Chapter 1 (HWZ §§1.1–1.4)

1V1.1

sc-Banach spaces, sums and shifts

restated

to confirmAn sc-Banach space is a sequence of Banach spaces $E_0 \supset E_1 \supset \cdots$ with compact inclusions and $E_\infty$ dense in every $E_m$, taken as an indexed family with injective compact inclusions; finite-dimensional spaces carry the constant structure, sums have levels $E_m \oplus F_m$, and $E^k$ has levels $E_{k+m}$.

indexed family, not nested subspacesinjectivity of the inclusions a fieldonly one structure in finite dim. (V1.31)
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.1 (preprint 1.1), p. 5 (preprint p. 6)

An sc-structure on a Banach space $E$ is a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \cdots$ such that (1) every inclusion $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ is compact and (2) $E_\infty = \bigcap_m E_m$ is dense in every $E_m$. A Banach space with an sc-structure is an sc-Banach space; points of $E_\infty$ are smooth, points of $E_m$ have regularity $m$. A finite-dimensional space has exactly one sc-structure, the constant one. A subset $A$ inherits the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$, and $A^k$ is $A_k$ with the filtration $(A^k)_m = A_{k+m}$. The direct sum $E \oplus F$ has levels $E_m \oplus F_m$.

Example 1.1.3 (preprint 1.2), the weighted Sobolev spaces $H^{m,\delta_m}(\mathbb R \times S^1)$, is not formalized (G.1).

Verified edition V1.1

A scale consists of real Banach spaces $E_m$, $m \in \mathbb N$, and injective compact continuous linear maps $E_{m+1} \to E_m$; $\iota_m : E_m \to E_0$ is the composite, $E_\infty \subseteq E_0$ the subspace of points that lie in $\iota_m(E_m)$ for every $m$, and $E_\infty \cap E_m := \iota_m^{-1}(E_\infty)$. An sc-Banach space is a scale in which $E_\infty \cap E_m$ is dense in $E_m$ for every $m$. Consequences: the image of $E_{m+k}$ in $E_m$ is dense. Constructions: for a finite-dimensional normed space $V$ the constant family $E_m = V$, with identity inclusions, is an sc-Banach space all of whose points are smooth; for sc-Banach spaces $E$, $F$, the family $E_m \times F_m$ with the product inclusions is an sc-Banach space $E \oplus F$ whose smooth points at level $m$ are the pairs of smooth points; the family $E_{m+1}$ with the inclusions of $E$ is an sc-Banach space $E^1$ whose smooth points at level $m$ are those of $E$ at level $m + 1$; $E^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate. For $U \subseteq E_0$, the level set $U_m := \iota_m^{-1}(U) \subseteq E_m$. Book: Definition 1.1.1 (preprint 1.1), p. 5 (preprint p. 6): a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset \cdots$ with compact inclusions and $E_\infty = \bigcap E_m$ dense in every $E_m$; the constant structure on a finite-dimensional space; $(E \oplus F)_m = E_m \oplus F_m$; the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$ of a subset and the shift $A^k$. Hidden hypotheses: the inclusions are injective (implicit in "$\subset$") and continuous (part of compactness). Deviation (restated): the $E_m$ are separate Banach spaces, not subsets of one space; the two pictures are equivalent and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family. The text's remarks that a finite-dimensional space has only the constant structure and that the constant family on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure are V1.31.

What differs (the comparison)

  • The text's $E_m$ are subsets of one space $E$; the formal scale is a family of separate Banach spaces with injective compact inclusions, and "$x \in E_m$" for $x \in E_0$ means $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$. The two pictures are equivalent, and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family.
  • Injectivity of the inclusions, implicit in "$E_{m+1} \subset E_m$", is a field of the structure; continuity is part of being a compact operator in Mathlib's sense.
  • Condition (2) is taken exactly as stated, density of $E_\infty \cap E_m$ in every $E_m$. The weaker "$E_{m+1}$ is dense in $E_m$" is derived, not assumed.
  • That a finite-dimensional space has only the constant structure, and that the constant sequence on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure, are proved separately (V1.31).
2V1.2

sc-operators and sc-isomorphisms

restated

to confirmAn sc-operator is a linear map continuous $E_m \to F_m$ on every level, given by its level maps; an sc-isomorphism is one that is a continuous linear equivalence on every level.

the level maps are the dataIsScOperator is the text's formcontinuity on the levels is automatic
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.4 (preprint 1.3), p. 6 (preprint p. 7)

A linear map $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is an sc-operator if $T(E_m) \subset F_m$ and the induced $T : E_m \to F_m$ is continuous for every $m$. A linear sc-isomorphism is a bijective sc-operator whose inverse is an sc-operator.

Verified edition V1.2

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is a family of continuous linear maps $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota^F_m T_{m+1} = T_m \iota^E_m$; the family is determined by $T_0$, and a continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator exactly when for each $m$ some continuous linear $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ satisfies $\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m$ (the two formulations correspond). Sc-operators compose, add, and map smooth points to smooth points. An sc-isomorphism is a family of continuous linear equivalences $E_m \simeq F_m$ commuting with the inclusions; inverses and composites are sc-isomorphisms. A continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ with $T_0(E_m) \subseteq F_m$ for every $m$ is an sc-operator (the continuity of $T_0 : E_m \to F_m$ is the closed graph theorem), and an sc-operator bijective on every level is an sc-isomorphism (the open mapping theorem). Book: Definition 1.1.4 (preprint 1.3), p. 6 (preprint p. 7). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the level maps are data, with the text's predicate on the base map recovered as Polyfold.IsScOperator; the continuity of the inverse of a bijective sc-operator on each level, which the text's definition of an sc-isomorphism demands, is built into the formal notion, and derived from the open mapping theorem separately (Polyfold.ScIso.ofBijective); the continuity on the levels asked by Definition 1.1.4 (preprint 1.3) is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 233).

What differs (the comparison)

  • In the family picture an sc-operator carries its level maps as data; the text's "one linear map $T$ mapping $E_m$ into $F_m$ continuously" is the predicate IsScOperator on the base map, and the two are interchangeable (ScOperator.isScOperator, IsScOperator.toScOperator).
  • An sc-isomorphism is given by level-wise continuous linear equivalences; that the inverse of a bijective sc-operator is continuous on each level (the open mapping theorem) is built into this definition, and proved separately (ScIso.ofBijective). Likewise the continuity of $T : E_m \to F_m$ asked by Definition 1.1.4 (preprint 1.3) is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (isScOperator_of_mapsTo, the closed graph theorem; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). 3V1.3

sc⁺-operators

as in the book

to confirmAn sc⁺-operator is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$; it is compact $E_m \to F_m$ on every level.

the first condition is the secondsc-compactness proved
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.5 (preprint 1.4), p. 7 (preprint p. 7)

An sc-operator $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator if $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator. Since the inclusion $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ is compact, an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator is sc-compact: $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$.

Verified edition V1.3

An $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator $E \to F$ is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$, i.e. continuous linear $S_m : E_m \to F_{m+1}$ commuting with the inclusions. Composed with the inclusion $F^1 \to F$ (an sc-operator) it is an sc-operator $E \to F$ whose level-$m$ map $E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$, and which raises the level: $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$ implies $S_0 x \in \iota_{m+1}(F_{m+1})$. Book: Definition 1.1.5 (preprint 1.4), p. 7 (preprint p. 7), and the remark that follows it: an sc-operator $S$ with $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ an sc-operator is sc-compact. Hidden hypotheses: none; the condition $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ is contained in "$S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator" and is dropped.

4V1.4

sc-subspaces and sc-splittings

restated

to confirmAn sc-subspace is a closed subspace whose smooth points are dense in each $F \cap E_m$; an sc-splitting $E = F \oplus G$ consists of two sc-subspaces with $F_m$ and $G_m$ complementary on every level.

compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ automatictopological sum from IsCompl + closedness
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.6 (preprint 1.5), p. 7 (preprint p. 7)

A subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if $F$ is closed and $F_m = F \cap E_m$ defines an sc-structure on $F$. An sc-subspace $F$ has an sc-complement if there is an algebraic complement $G$ such that $G_m = G \cap E_m$ is an sc-structure on $G$ and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ is a topological direct sum on every level; $E = F \oplus G$ is then an sc-splitting.

Verified edition V1.4

For a subspace $A \subseteq E_0$ let $A_m := \iota_m^{-1}(A) \subseteq E_m$, closed if $A$ is. $A$ is an sc-subspace if $A$ is closed and $A_m$ is contained in the closure of $A_m \cap E_\infty$ for every $m$. A closed $A$ with the levels $A_m$ and the restricted inclusions is a scale (the restricted inclusions are compact), and an sc-subspace is in this way an sc-Banach space. $E = F \oplus G$ is an sc-splitting if $F$ and $G$ are sc-subspaces and $F_m$, $G_m$ are complementary subspaces of $E_m$ for every $m$; then $F_m$ is closed complemented in $E_m$, and the splitting is symmetric in $F$ and $G$. Book: Definition 1.1.6 (preprint 1.5), p. 7 (preprint p. 7): $F$ closed with $(F \cap E_m)$ an sc-structure; an sc-complement $G$ with $(G \cap E_m)$ an sc-structure and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ a topological direct sum on every level. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the closedness of $F_m$ in $E_m$ and the compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ are automatic and are not conditions; "topological direct sum" is read as complementary closed subspaces, the continuity of the projections following from the closed graph theorem (Polyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.closedComplemented).

Polyfold.ScBanach.levelSubPolyfold.ScBanach.isClosed_levelSubPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSubspacePolyfold.ScBanach.ofSubspaceScalePolyfold.ScBanach.ofSubspacePolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplittingPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.closedComplementedPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.symm

What differs (the comparison)

  • Of the conditions in "$(F_m)$ is an sc-structure on $F$", the closedness of $F_m$ in $E_m$ and the compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ follow from the closedness of $F$ (restriction of a compact operator), so IsScSubspace asks only for closedness and the density of $F \cap E_\infty$ in each $F_m$; the sc-Banach space $F$ is then built (ScBanach.ofSubspace).
  • "Topological direct sum $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$" is read as: $F_m$ and $G_m$ are complementary closed subspaces of $E_m$; by the closed graph theorem the sum is then topological, which is recorded as a consequence (IsScSplitting.closedComplemented). The text's "$G$ an algebraic complement with $(G_m)$ an sc-structure" is the requirement that $G$ be an sc-subspace.

Proposition 1.1.7 (preprint 1.6)

as in the book

to confirmA finite-dimensional subspace is an sc-subspace iff it lies in $E_\infty$, and then has an sc-complement.

proof: a continuous projection onto $F$
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.1.7 (preprint 1.6), p. 7 (preprint p. 7)

A finite-dimensional subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \subset E_\infty$. A finite-dimensional sc-subspace always has an sc-complement.

Verified edition V1.5

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $F \subseteq E_0$ a finite-dimensional subspace. $F$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \le E_\infty$; and if $F \le E_\infty$ there is a subspace $G \subseteq E_0$ such that $E = F \oplus G$ is an sc-splitting. Book: preprint p. 7, the same. Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: as in the text, with a continuous projection $E_0 \to F$ from Mathlib (Hahn–Banach), lifted to each level through $F_m \cong F$.

Polyfold.ScBanach.proposition_1_6_iffPolyfold.ScBanach.proposition_1_6

What differs (the comparison)

  • The proof follows the text: a continuous projection $p : E_0 \to F$ (Mathlib's closed complementation of finite-dimensional subspaces, i.e. Hahn–Banach) is lifted to each level through $F_m \cong F$, $G = \ker p$, and the density of $G \cap E_\infty$ in $G_m$ comes from $g = (1 - P_m)g$ with $P_m$ the level projection, exactly as on preprint p. 8.

Proposition 1.1.8 (preprint 1.7)

stronger

to confirmFor a closed subspace $A$ of an sc-Banach space $E$, the quotients $E_m/A_m$ form an sc-Banach space $E/A$ with the quotient map an sc-operator whose level kernels are the $A_m$.

any closed $A$, not only sc-subspaces$(E/A)_\infty$ identified in V1.33
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.1.8 (preprint 1.7), p. 8 (preprint p. 8)

If $E$ is an sc-Banach space and $A \subset E$ an sc-subspace, then $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m = \{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$.

Verified edition V1.6

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $A \subseteq E_0$ a closed subspace. The quotient Banach spaces $E_m/A_m$, with the inclusions $E_{m+1}/A_{m+1} \to E_m/A_m$ induced by $\iota$ (injective and compact), and with the smooth points dense on every level, form an sc-Banach space $E/A$, and the quotient maps $E_m \to E_m/A_m$ form an sc-operator $E \to E/A$. As a statement: there exist an sc-Banach space $Q$ and an sc-operator $q : E \to Q$ with every $q_m$ surjective and $\ker q_m = A_m$. Book: preprint p. 8, for an sc-subspace $A$: $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m$ is identified with $\{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): only closedness of $A$ is used, not that $A$ is an sc-subspace. The text's identification of $E_m/A_m$ with a subset of $E/A$ is the injectivity of the induced inclusion, which holds because $A_m$ is the full preimage of $A$. The text's description of $(E/A)_\infty$ as the classes of points of $E_\infty$ is V1.33; only the trivial inclusion is used here.

sc-Fredholm operators and the index

restated

to confirmAn sc-Fredholm operator is an sc-operator with sc-splittings $E = \ker T \oplus X$, $F = C \oplus \operatorname{range} T$, $\ker T$ and $C$ finite-dimensional, and $T$ bijective $X_m \to \operatorname{range}(T)_m$ on every level; its index $\dim\ker T - \dim C$ is $\dim\ker T_0 - \dim\operatorname{coker} T_0$, and each $T_m$ is Fredholm.

(3) read as bijections $X_m \to Y_m$index independent of the splittingFredholm on every level
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.9 (preprint 1.8), p. 8 (preprint p. 9)

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm if there are sc-splittings $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ with (1) $K = \ker T$ finite-dimensional, (2) $C$ finite-dimensional and $Y = T(E)$, (3) $T : X \to Y$ an sc-isomorphism. Then $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and $F = C \oplus T(E_m)$. The index is $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$.

Verified edition V1.7

An sc-Fredholm splitting of an sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is given by subspaces $K, X \subseteq E_0$ and $C, Y \subseteq F_0$ such that $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ are sc-splittings, $K = \ker T_0$, $Y = \operatorname{range} T_0$, $K$ and $C$ are finite-dimensional, and for every $m$ the map $T_m$ is a bijection of $X_m$ onto $Y_m$. $T$ is sc-Fredholm if a splitting exists. The index $\dim K - \dim C$ of a splitting equals $\dim \ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range} T_0)$, hence does not depend on the splitting. Moreover $K \le E_\infty$; $\ker T_m = K_m$ and $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$; and every $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib's sense (finite-dimensional kernel, closed range of finite codimension, strict, with closed complemented kernel). Book: Definition 1.1.9 (preprint 1.8), p. 8 (preprint p. 9), with the remarks that $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and "$F = C \oplus T(E_m)$" (read $F_m$), and $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): condition (3), "$T : X \to Y$ is an sc-isomorphism", is taken as the bijectivity of $T_m : X_m \to Y_m$ for every $m$; the continuity of the inverses is automatic by the open mapping theorem on the closed subspaces $X_m$, $Y_m$. The independence of the index from the splitting and the level-wise Fredholm property are not stated in the text.

  • Condition (3), "$T : X \to Y$ is an sc-isomorphism", is taken as: $T_m$ restricts to a bijection $X_m \to Y_m$ for every $m$. The continuity of the inverses is automatic (open mapping theorem between the closed subspaces $X_m$, $Y_m$), so nothing is lost.

Proposition 1.1.10 (preprint 1.9)

as in the book

to confirmAn sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing: $T e \in F_m$ implies $e \in E_m$; conversely, an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm.

the text's proofconverse: $T_0$ Fredholm and regularizing
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.1.10 (preprint 1.9), p. 9 (preprint p. 9)

An sc-Fredholm operator $T : E \to F$ is regularizing: if $e \in E$ and $T(e) \in F_m$, then $e \in E_m$.

Verified edition V1.8

Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-operator with an sc-Fredholm splitting, $e \in E_0$ and $m \in \mathbb N$. If $T_0 e \in \iota_m(F_m)$ then $e \in \iota_m(E_m)$. As a property of sc-operators (Polyfold.ScOperator.IsRegularizing): every sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing. Conversely, an sc-operator $T$ with $T_0$ Fredholm that is regularizing is sc-Fredholm (V1.9); so $T$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm and $T$ is regularizing. Book: preprint p. 9, the same ("an sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing"). Hidden hypotheses: none; the step "$c = 0$" uses $C \cap Y = 0$ on level $0$, as in the text. The converse is not stated in the text; it is the tool for the text's unargued “is sc-Fredholm” for operators obtained by conjugation and restriction in Chapter 3 (V3.8, V3.46, V3.96; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233).

Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10)

as in the book

to confirmThe sum of an sc-Fredholm operator and an sc⁺-operator is sc-Fredholm.

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10), p. 9 (preprint p. 10) (proof §1.4.1, pp. 14–16 (preprint pp. 14–15))

Let $E$ and $F$ be sc-Banach spaces. If $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm and $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator, then $T + S$ is sc-Fredholm.

Verified edition V1.9

Let $E$, $F$ be sc-Banach spaces, $T : E \to F$ an sc-Fredholm operator and $S : E \to F$ an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator. Then $T + S$ (with $S$ read as an sc-operator $E \to F$) is sc-Fredholm. Along the way, $T + S$ is regularizing in the sense of V1.8. Book: preprint p. 10, the same; the proof is in §1.4.1, pp. 14–16 (preprint pp. 14–15). Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: the text's, with three additions. The opening claim that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm is the classical compact-perturbation theorem, proved here since Mathlib lacks it (V1.24–V1.25). The step "$y = (T+S)e$, so by Proposition 1.9 $e \in E_m$" needs a bootstrap, since $Se$ is only one level up: $Te = y - Se \in F_1$ gives $e \in E_1$, then $Se \in F_2$, and so on $m$ times; the same bootstrap gives $K_m = K_{m+1}$. The complement $C$ is the range of a linear right inverse of $F_0 \to F_0/Y$ with values in $F_\infty$ rather than the span of a lifted basis, and condition (3) of Definition 1.1.9 (preprint 1.8) for $T + S$, which the text does not verify, is proved as the bijectivity of $(T + S)_m : X_m \to Y_m$. The text does not assert that the index is preserved; it is, and this is V1.30. The construction uses only two properties of $T + S$, that it is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing; with these as hypotheses it is proved as a criterion: an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm, and every level map is then Fredholm of the level-$0$ index (not stated in the text).

What differs (the comparison)

  • §1.4.1 says "since $T$ is regularizing, $e \in E_m$"; the hypothesis gives only $Te = y - Se \in F_1$, so the regularizing step must be iterated $m$ times (ScPlus.regularizing_add). The same bootstrap gives $K_m = K_{m+1}$.
  • The complement $C$ is built from a linear right inverse of $F_0 \to F_0/Y$ with values in the smooth points rather than from a lifted basis; condition (3) of Definition 1.1.9 (preprint 1.8), which the text does not verify, is proved as the bijectivity of $(T+S)_m : X_m \to Y_m$.
  • The classical fact that opens §1.4.1, a compact perturbation of a Fredholm operator is Fredholm, is not in Mathlib and is proved here (V1.25). The text does not record that the index is preserved; the formalization proves it separately (V1.30).
  • §1.4.1 uses two properties of $T + S$ only: it is Fredholm on level $0$, and it is regularizing (so its kernel lies in $E_\infty$, it maps $E_m$ onto $Y \cap F_m$, and its range has a complement spanned by smooth points). With these as hypotheses the construction is a criterion for sc-Fredholm operators (isScFredholm_of_isRegularizing), not stated in the text (Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). partial quadrants and tuples

as in the book

to confirmA partial quadrant is a set $C = T^{-1}([0,\infty)^n \oplus W)$ for an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$; a tuple $(U, C, E)$ has $U = O \cap C$ with $O$ open.

closed and convex derived, not assumed$C^1$ a partial quadrant in $E^1$: V1.36
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.12 (preprint 1.11), p. 9 (preprint p. 10)

A partial quadrant in an sc-Banach space $E$ is a closed convex subset $C \subset E$ such that there is an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^n \oplus W$. One considers tuples $(U, C, E)$ with $U$ a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$.

Verified edition V1.10

In the sc-Banach space $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ (with $\mathbb R^n$ constant) the quadrant on level $m$ is $\{(a, w) : a_i \ge 0 \text{ for all } i\}$; it is closed and convex with non-empty interior, and the level sets of the level-$0$ quadrant are the level quadrants. $C \subseteq E_0$ is a partial quadrant if there are $n$, an sc-Banach space $W$ and an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})$. Then every $C_m$ is closed, convex, with non-empty interior in $E_m$, and $C_m$ has unique differentiability (in Mathlib's sense) at each of its points; $E_0$ itself is a partial quadrant ($n = 0$). $(U, C, E)$ is a tuple, i.e. $U$ is a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$, if $C$ is a partial quadrant and $U = O \cap C$ with $O \subseteq E_0$ open. Book: Definition 1.1.12 (preprint 1.11), p. 9 (preprint p. 10), and the sentence after it. Hidden hypotheses: none; "closed convex" is derived from the model. Deviation: none in the definition. The text's tacit use of $C_k$ as a partial quadrant in $E^k$ is V1.36 (for $k = 1$, and by iteration).

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.13 (preprint 1.12), p. 9 (preprint p. 10)

For tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$, a map $f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ (sc-continuous) if $f(U_m) \subset U'_m$ and the induced maps $f : U_m \to U'_m$ are continuous for all $m \ge 0$.

Verified edition V1.11

For $f : E_0 \to F_0$ the level map $f_m : E_m \to F_m$ sends $x$ to the unique $y \in F_m$ with $\iota_m y = f(\iota_m x)$, when such $y$ exists (and to a junk value otherwise). $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U \subseteq E_0$ if for every $m$ and $x \in U_m$ the point $f(\iota_m x)$ lies in $\iota_m(F_m)$, and $f_m$ is continuous on $U_m$. Then $f$ is continuous on $U$; if $f(U) \subseteq V$ then $f_m(U_m) \subseteq V_m$; the property depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$ and passes to subsets of $U$; the composition of an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on $U$ with values in $V$ and an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on $V$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; the identity and every sc-operator are $\mathrm{sc}^0$, the latter with level maps $T_m$. Book: Definition 1.1.13 (preprint 1.12), p. 9 (preprint p. 10): $f(U_m) \subset V_m$ (meaning $U'_m$) and $f : U_m \to U'_m$ continuous for all $m$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): maps are total functions on $E_0$, and the target tuple enters only through $f(U) \subseteq U'$.

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.14 (preprint 1.13), p. 9 (preprint p. 10)

The tangent of $(U, C, E)$ is the tuple $T(U, C, E) = (TU, TC, TE)$ with $TU = U^1 \oplus E$, $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$. It is again a tuple: $TU$ is relatively open in the partial quadrant $TC$ of the sc-Banach space $TE$.

Verified edition V1.12

The tangent of an sc-Banach space $E$ is $TE := E^1 \oplus E$, with levels $E_{m+1} \times E_m$. For $U \subseteq E_0$, $TU \subseteq (TE)_0 = E_1 \times E_0$ is $\{(x, h) : x \in U_1\}$, with level-$m$ part $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; $U \subseteq V$ implies $TU \subseteq TV$. If $U$ is an sc-domain (V1.27), $TU$ is an sc-domain in $TE$; and the level-$1$ part of $TU$ is $T(U_1)$ in $T(E^1) = (TE)^1$. to confirmA map is sc¹ on $U$ if it is sc⁰, differentiable from $U_1$ into $F_0$ at every point of $U_1$ with a derivative $Df(x)$ bounded on $E_0$, and $(x, h) \mapsto (f(x), Df(x)h)$ is sc⁰ on $TU$; $Df(x)$ is unique on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants; $x \mapsto Df(x)$ need not be norm continuous (an example on a weighted $c_0$ scale).

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1.15 (preprint 1.14), pp. 10 ff. (preprint pp. 10–11)

$f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded linear $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ as $|h|_1 \to 0$, $h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$; (3) the tangent map $Tf : TU \to TU'$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. In general $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is not continuous into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm, but it is with the compact-open topology; the $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps.

The text writes $Df(x)$ as if it were unique.

Verified edition V1.13

Let $f : E_0 \to F_0$, $U \subseteq E_0$ and $D : E_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ a family of bounded operators. The tangent map $T_Df : (TE)_0 \to (TF)_0$ is $(x, h) \mapsto (f_1(x), D(x)h)$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $D$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$, the map $f \circ \iota_1 : E_1 \to F_0$ has derivative $D(x) \circ \iota_1$ at $x$ within $U_1$; (3) $T_Df$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $TU$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if some $D$ makes it so; Polyfold.scDeriv is a chosen such $D$ (junk if none exists) and Polyfold.tangentMap the tangent map built from it. If $D$ and $D'$ both satisfy (2) at a point $x \in U_1$ where $U_1$ has unique differentiability, then $D(x) = D'(x)$, because $E_1$ has dense image in $E_0$; hence on an sc-domain the chosen derivative agrees on $U_1$ with any admissible one, and the tangent map on $TU$. The property depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$. Level $0$ of condition (3) is the continuity of $(x, h) \mapsto D(x)h$ on $U_1 \times E_0$, and it implies: for $x \in U_1$, a compact $K \subseteq E_0$ and $c > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $\|D(x')w - D(x)w\| \le c$ for all $x' \in U_1$ with $\|x' - x\|_1 < \delta$ and all $w \in K$ (continuity of $x \mapsto D(x)$ in the compact-open topology). It need not be norm continuous: on $E = \mathbb R \oplus X$, with $X$ the sc-Banach space whose level $m$ consists of the real sequences with $(k+1)^m x_k \to 0$, normed by $\sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$ (every level a copy of $c_0$, the inclusions $\mathrm{diag}(1/(k+1))$), the map $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with $Df(t, x)(\tau, \xi)_k = -k\sin(kt)x_k\tau + \cos(kt)\xi_k$, and for every derivative family $D$ of $f$ the map $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $E_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, X_0)$ with the operator norm: $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$. Book: Definition 1.1.15 (preprint 1.14), pp. 10 ff. (preprint pp. 10–11), with conditions (1)–(3) as stated, and the remarks that $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous for the compact-open but not in general for the norm topology, and that sc¹ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps. Hidden hypotheses: the uniqueness of $Df(x)$, without which "the tangent map" is undefined; it holds because $E_1$ is dense in $E_0$ and $U_1$ has unique differentiability (true for relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, V1.10). Deviation (hypotheses explicit): the derivative family is an explicit parameter of Polyfold.IsSc1With, with Polyfold.IsSc1 the text's notion. The compact-open remark is V1.34, its negative half the example above, which the text does not give (Findings, Chapter 1, follow-up item 1), and the finite-dimensional remark is V1.35 (on relatively open subsets of quadrants, with boundary; the open case is also in Polyfold/Test.lean, isSc1_iff_contDiffOn_of_finiteDimensional).

Inductively, an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^2$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $Tf : TU \to TV$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; then $T^2f = T(Tf)$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$, and $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^3$ if $T^2f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, and so on. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^\infty$, or sc-smooth, if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

By recursion: $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$ in the sense of V1.11; $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ on $U$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ and its tangent map (built from the chosen derivative) is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $TU \subseteq (TE)_0$ as a map into $(TF)_0$. $f$ is sc-smooth on $U$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for every $k$. Then $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ implies $\mathrm{sc}^k$, and $\mathrm{sc}^l$ for $l \le k$; $f$ is sc-smooth iff it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with sc-smooth tangent map; on an sc-domain, $\mathrm{sc}^k$ depends only on the values on $U$. to confirmAn sc⁰ map on an sc-domain is sc¹ iff on every level $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable with a derivative extending to a bounded $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ that depends jointly continuously on $(x, h) \in U_{m+1} \times E_m$; then $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$, and $Df(x)$ is an sc-operator at smooth points.

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.2.1 (preprint 1.16), p. 11 (preprint p. 12)

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. An $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f : U \to F$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if and only if (1) for every $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$, so that $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ is continuous; and (2) for every $m \ge 1$ and $x \in U_m$, $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$. In particular, at a smooth point $x \in U_\infty$ of an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map, $Df(x) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator.

Verified edition V1.15

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if and only if there is a family $D_m(x) \in \mathcal L(E_m, F_m)$, $m \in \mathbb N$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, such that for every $m$: (a) $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ has derivative $D_m(x) \circ \iota$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ within $U_{m+1}$; (b) $(x, h) \mapsto D_m(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. For any such family, $x \mapsto D_m(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$ in the operator norm, so $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$ within $U_{m+1}$; and $\iota_m D_m(x) = D_0(\iota x) \iota_m$, so all $D_m(x)$ are restrictions of the single operator $Df(x) := D_0(x)$. In the direction "sc¹ ⇒ levels" the family is the level operators of V1.26; in particular $f \circ \iota_1 : U_1 \to F_0$ is $C^1$. If $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $Df$ and $x \in U_1$ is a smooth point, $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator. Book: preprint p. 12: an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ iff (1) for $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$ with $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ continuous and (2) $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$; in particular $Df(x)$ is an sc-operator at smooth points. Hidden hypotheses: the compatibility of the extensions $Df(x)$ across levels, which the text's notation assumes and the direction (⇐) needs (Lemma 3.H of the exposition); it is proved. Deviation (restated): the extensions form an explicit family; the $C^1$ property and the norm continuity of $df$ are consequences of (a)–(b) rather than part of the condition; the hypothesis on $U$ is the weaker sc-domain condition.

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.2.2 (preprint 1.17), p. 13 (preprint p. 12)

Also proved, under the stronger hypothesis that every level map $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ is $C^{k+1}$ within $U_m$: $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$; for $k = 0$, where the two hypotheses agree, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with $Df(x)$ the derivative of $f : U_0 \to F_0$ within $U$ at $\iota_1 x$; and if $f$ maps $U_m$ into $F_m$ for every $m$ and every $f_m$ is $C^\infty$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. The induction cannot be run on the hypothesis itself: if $f$ satisfies it with $k$, then $Tf$ in general does not satisfy it with $k - 1$, since its second component $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h : U_{m+l+1} \times E_{m+l} \to F_m$ is only $C^l$. Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $V \subseteq D \subseteq F$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $G$ an sc-Banach space, $f : E_0 \to F_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $g : F_0 \to G_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$. Then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$, and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TU$. More precisely: if $g$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$ with derivatives $Dg$, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $Df$, $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $V_1$ is the intersection of an open and a convex set, then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $x \mapsto Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x)$, with no hypothesis on $U$; and $g \circ f \circ \iota_1$ has this derivative at every $x \in U_1$ within $U_1$. Verified edition V1.26

Compact-open lemma. Let $X$, $Y$, $Y'$, $Z$ be real normed spaces, $\iota : Y' \to Y$ a compact operator and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$. If $(x, y) \mapsto A(x)y$ is continuous on $s \times Y$, then $x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous on $s$ into $\mathcal L(Y', Z)$ with the operator norm; if $s$ is the intersection of an open and a convex set with unique differentiability at every point and $(x, y) \mapsto A(x)y$ is $C^k$ within $s \times Y$, then $x \mapsto A(x) \circ \iota$ is $C^k$ within $s$. Level operators. Let $f$ be $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $Df$, $m \in \mathbb N$ and $x \in U_{m+1}$. There is a unique continuous linear $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ (written levelDeriv) with $\iota_m \circ Df(x) = Df(\iota x) \circ \iota_m$, namely the second component of the level-$m$ tangent map, which is $(x, h) \mapsto (f_{m+1}(x), Df(x)h)$ on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; $x \mapsto Df(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$. If $U$ is an sc-domain, $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ has derivative $Df(x) \circ \iota$ at $x$ within $U_{m+1}$, hence is $C^1$ within $U_{m+1}$; and if $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ has derivative $L$ at $\iota x$ within $U_m$, then $L = Df(x)$. Book: not stated as such; the compactness argument of the 2010 paper's Propositions 2.1–2.3 (quoted in §1.2) and its integral identity $f(x+h) - f(x) = \int_0^1 Df(x + \tau h)h\,d\tau$. Deviation (not in the book): the $C^k$ case of the lemma, proved by induction with the mean value inequality, replaces the multilinear maps $\Gamma(x)$ and the differentiation under the integral sign of the 2010 paper; the integral identity is formed as a Bochner integral in $F_m$ and identified with $f(x+h) - f(x)$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus for the $C^1$ map $f : U_1 \to F_0$.

the Fredholm index and its invariance

to confirmThe index $\dim\ker - \dim\operatorname{coker}$ is additive under composition, and the Fredholm index between Banach spaces is invariant under small and under compact perturbations.

HWZ §1.4.1, preprint p. 14 (quoted as classical)

Not stated. The proof of Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10) uses that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm; that its index is that of $T$ is the classical invariance of the index under compact perturbations, which the text does not invoke.

Verified edition V1.28

For a linear map $u : E \to F$ over a field let $\operatorname{ind}(u) := \dim\ker u - \dim(F/\operatorname{range}u) \in \mathbb Z$, meaningful when both dimensions are finite ("finite index"). If $u$ and $v : F \to G$ have finite index, so has $v \circ u$, and $\operatorname{ind}(v \circ u) = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)$. If $a$ is bijective and $r$ has finite rank, $a + r$ has finite index $0$ (in particular $1 + r$). If $v \circ u$ and $u \circ v$ have finite index, so has $u$. For real Banach spaces $E$, $F$: a Fredholm operator $u : E \to F$ has finite index, and $\operatorname{ind}(u)$ is its Fredholm index. If $v : F \to E$ is a quasi-inverse of $u$ ($vu - 1$ and $uv - 1$ have finite rank) and $\|v\|\,\|s\| < 1$, then $u + s$ has finite index and $\operatorname{ind}(u + s) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$. If $u$ is Fredholm and $k : E \to F$ is compact, then $\operatorname{ind}(u + k) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$. Book: not stated; the classical fact behind the exposition's (F2) (Kato IV.5.26), which the text's §1.4.1 would need to conclude that the index is preserved. Deviation (not in the book): infrastructure Mathlib v4.33.1 lacks (it has Fredholm operators but no index). Proof: additivity by rank–nullity along the exact sequence $0 \to \ker u \to \ker vu \to \operatorname{range} u \cap \ker v \to F/\operatorname{range}u \to G/\operatorname{range}vu \to G/\operatorname{range}v \to 0$; small perturbations through $v(u + s) = (1 + vs) + (vu - 1)$ and $(u+s)v = (1 + sv) + (uv - 1)$, where $1 + vs$, $1 + sv$ are invertible by the Neumann series; compact perturbations by the local constancy of $t \mapsto \operatorname{ind}(u + tk)$ on $\mathbb R$ (each $u + t_0k$ is Fredholm by V1.25), not by Kato's argument.

HWZ §1.1, after Definition 1.1.15 (preprint 1.14), preprint p. 11

The $\mathrm{sc}^1$-maps between finite-dimensional Banach spaces are the familiar $C^1$-maps.

Verified edition V1.35

Let $V$, $W$ be finite-dimensional real normed spaces with their constant sc-structures, $f : V \to W$ and $U \subseteq V$ an sc-domain (V1.27), for instance a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant of $V$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if and only if $f$ is $C^1$ within $U$; equivalently, $f$ is differentiable within $U$ at every point of $U$ and the derivative within $U$, $x \mapsto \mathrm{fderivWithin}\,f\,U\,x$, is continuous on $U$. And $f$ is sc-smooth on $U$ if and only if it is $C^\infty$ within $U$. Book: preprint p. 11: "the $\mathrm{sc}^1$-maps between finite dimensional Banach spaces are the familiar $C^1$-maps". Hidden hypotheses: the meaning of $C^1$ at boundary points of a quadrant, never defined in the text; here the derivative within $U$, which at a boundary point is the one-sided derivative along $U$ and is unique because the quadrant has non-empty interior. Deviation (hypotheses explicit): none beyond this; by V1.31 every sc-structure on a finite-dimensional space is the constant one up to sc-isomorphism. Proof: Propositions 1.2.1 and 1.2.4 (preprint 1.16 and 1.19) at $k = 0$ (V1.15, V1.18) for the levels of the constant structure, which all equal $U$.

The proof of Proposition 1.2.4 (preprint 1.19) in the 2010 paper writes $d^jf(x)$ for the $j$-th derivative of $f$ on whichever level pair $U_{m+l} \to F_m$ the argument needs, with one symbol for all of them: the derivatives taken with a finer domain level or a coarser target level are tacitly identified.

Verified edition V1.37

A derivative tower of order $k + 1$ for $f : E_0 \to F_0$ on $U$ consists of maps $\Phi_i : E_0 \times E_0^i \to F_0$ with $\Phi_0(x) = f(x)$ and, for $x \in U_{m+l}$, continuous $i$-linear maps $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x) : E_{m+l}^i \to F_m$, for $i \le l + 1$ and $i \le k + 1$, such that (a) $\iota_m \Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i) = \Phi_i(\iota_{m+l} x)(\iota_{m+l} h_1, \dots, \iota_{m+l} h_i)$; (b) $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is continuous on $U_{m+l}$ into the space of continuous $i$-linear maps; (c) for $i \le l$ and $i \le k$, $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is differentiable within $U_{m+l}$ at every point, with derivative $\xi \mapsto \Psi_{i+1,m,l}(x)(\xi, \cdot)$. If $U$ is an sc-domain, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$ and $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$ for all $m$ and $l \le k$, then the iterated derivatives within the level sets, $\Psi_{i,m,l} := d^i(f_m \circ \iota)$ on $U_{m+l}$ and $\Phi_i$ the $i$-th derivative of $f : U_{i-1} \to F_0$ at lifts to $E_{i-1}$, form a derivative tower of order $k + 1$. In a tower, two values $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h)$, $\Psi_{i,m,l'}(x')(h')$ with the same images in $E_0$ are equal. Book: not stated; the 2010 paper's proof of Proposition 2.4 (pp. 51–53) writes one symbol $d^jf(x)$ for the derivatives on all level pairs. Hidden hypotheses: the compatibility (a) is the identification the text makes tacitly. Deviation (not in the book): a tool of the formalization. Proof: (a) from the chain rule for iterated derivatives within a set composed on the left and on the right with continuous linear maps (the inclusions), and the uniqueness of derivatives on the level sets; for $l > k$ the hypothesis is used with order $k + 1$, restricted from $U_{m+k}$.

Remark 1.1.2, Banachable spaces and equivalent norms

restated

to confirmTwo norms on a vector space that induce the same topology are equivalent; two complete norms one of which dominates the other induce the same topology (open mapping theorem).

two readingssame topology: no completeness needed
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Remark 1.1.2, p. 5 (new in the 2021 edition)

"Banach space" means a Banachable space: a vector space with a topology induced by a complete norm. All norms inducing the given topology are equivalent, in view of the open mapping theorem; where the choice matters, a norm is fixed.

Verified edition V1.40

Let $E_1$, $E_2$ be real normed spaces and $e : E_1 \to E_2$ a linear equivalence (one vector space carrying two norms). (1) If $e$ and $e^{-1}$ are continuous (the two norms induce the same topology), there is $c > 0$ with $\|e x\| \le c\|x\|$ and $\|x\| \le c\|e x\|$ for all $x$. (2) If both spaces are complete and $e$ is continuous, then $e^{-1}$ is continuous, and the two norms are equivalent as in (1). Book: Remark 1.1.2, p. 5, new in the 2021 edition: "Banach space" means a Banachable space, a vector space with a topology induced by a complete norm, and all norms inducing that topology are equivalent "in view of the open mapping theorem". Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the remark is a convention, not a statement; the Lean records its mathematical content in two readings. Part (1) needs neither completeness nor the open mapping theorem (a continuous linear map between normed spaces is bounded); the open mapping theorem is what gives part (2), two complete norms one of which dominates the other. Proof: (1) by the operator norms of $e$ and $e^{-1}$; (2) by Mathlib's open mapping theorem (ContinuousLinearEquiv.ofBijective), then (1).

Definition 2.3.2 (preprint 2.11), charts

to confirmA chart is a homeomorphism of an open set onto a retract; charts are compatible when both transition maps are sc-smooth between the overlap retracts.

HWZ §2.3 (preprint §2.2), Definition 2.3.2 (preprint 2.11), pp. 34 ff. (preprint pp. 23–24)

A chart around $x$ in a space $X$ is $(V, \varphi, (O, C, E))$ with $V$ an open neighbourhood of $x$, $(O, C, E)$ an sc-smooth retract and $\varphi : V \to O$ a homeomorphism. Two charts are sc-smoothly compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(V \cap V') \to \psi(V \cap V')$ and its inverse are sc-smooth (Definition 2.1.14 (preprint 2.7)); $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract by Proposition 2.3.1(1) (preprint 2.10).

Verified edition V2.10

A chart on a space $X$ is a local model $(O, C, E)$ and a partial equivalence $\varphi$ between $X$ and $E_0$ with open source $V$ and target $O$, continuous on $V$, with inverse continuous on $O$. The overlap $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract. Two charts are compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth from $(\varphi(V \cap V'), C, E)$ to $(\psi(V \cap V'), C', E')$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ back. A chart is compatible with itself, compatibility passes to restrictions, and two charts each compatible with every chart of a family covering $V \cap V'$ are compatible. Book: Definition 2.3.2 (preprint 2.11), pp. 34 ff. (preprint pp. 23–24). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the chart is a partial equivalence; the last statement, the locality of compatibility, is not in the text and is what makes the maximal atlas (V2.12) work.

HWZ §2.3 (preprint §2.2), Definition 2.3.12 (preprint 2.17), pp. 38–39 (preprint pp. 25–26)

For $x \in O_1$, $T_xO = p^{-1}(x)$, the image of $Dr(x)$. Tuples $(x, V, \varphi, (O, C, E), h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart around $x$ and $h \in T_{\varphi(x)}O$ are equivalent, $(x, \varphi, h) \sim (x', \psi, h')$, if $x = x'$ and $T(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})(\psi(x))h' = h$.

Verified edition V2.18

A tangent tuple is $(x, \varphi, h)$ with $x \in X_1$, $\varphi$ a chart of the structure around $x$ and $(\varphi(x), h) \in TO$. Its transport to a chart $\psi$ around $x$ is $T(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}) (\varphi(x), h)$, computed on the overlap retract; it lies in $TO'$ over $\psi(x)$, transport to $\varphi$ is the identity, and transport to $\psi$ followed by transport to $\chi$ is transport to $\chi$. Two tuples are equivalent if their points agree and the transport of the first to the chart of the second is the second; this is an equivalence relation. Book: Definition 2.3.12 (preprint 2.17), pp. 38–39 (preprint pp. 25–26). Hidden hypotheses: that the relation is an equivalence relation (the text does not check it); it needs Theorem 2.1.15 (preprint 2.8) on the triple overlap and the locality of $Tf$ (V2.8). $TX$ is the set of equivalence classes of tangent tuples, with $p : TX \to X_1$, $[(x, \varphi, h)] \mapsto x$, and $T_xX = p^{-1}(x)$. Moreover, for every sc-smooth retraction $r$ in $C = T^{-1}([0, \infty)^n \oplus W)$ and every smooth $x \in O$ (no tameness), $T_xO$ and $T^R_xO$ are sc-subspaces of $E$ and $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in the sc-Banach space $T_xO$ (with the sc-structure induced from $E$), of dimension $r = \operatorname{rank} M = \dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) \le d_C(x)$, where $M$ is the matrix of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x \cong \mathbb R^{I(x)}$. A retraction $r$ is tame for $T$ if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ for $x \in U$ and (2) for every smooth $x \in O_1$ there is a subspace $A \le E_x$ such that $E = Dr(x)E_0 \oplus A$ is an sc-splitting. $r$ is tame if it is tame for every presentation of $C$; tameness for one presentation implies it. For $P : Y \to X$ (Y paracompact Hausdorff, fibres Banachable), a strong bundle chart $(\Phi, P^{-1}(V), K, U \triangleleft F)$: $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$, $V$ open with a homeomorphism $\varphi : V \to O$, $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K$ a homeomorphism covering $\varphi$, bounded linear on fibres. Charts are compatible if $(\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1})[i]$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, $i = 0, 1$; atlases and their equivalence.

Verified edition V2.57

For $P : Y \to X$ with linear structures on the fibres: a strong bundle chart is a chart $\varphi$ of the M-polyfold $X$, an sc-Banach space $F$, a strong bundle retraction $R$ on a relatively open $U \subseteq C$ with base retract $O$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K = R(U \times F_0)$ with $\Phi(y)_1 = \varphi(P(y))$ and linear on each fibre (hence continuous on fibres). Two charts are compatible if $\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1}$ and $\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1}$ are sc-smooth between the overlaps on $[0]$ and, through the lift to $F_1$, on $[1]$, and carry fibre components in $F_1$ to fibre components in $F'_1$. Atlases and their equivalence as in V2.11; two atlases are equivalent iff every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other, and the relation is an equivalence relation (it rests on the locality of compatibility: near a point of the overlap a transition factors through a chart of the middle atlas, on $[0]$ and on $[1]$). A strong bundle chart restricts to every open $s \subseteq V$ (retraction domain $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$ for $\varphi(s) = O \cap W$, $K_s = \{(u, h) \in K \mid u \in \varphi(s)\}$, $\Phi$ unchanged), and restrictions of compatible charts are compatible. A space is Banachable if it is linearly homeomorphic to a Banach space. Book: Definition 2.6.4 (preprint 2.50), pp. 67–68 (preprint pp. 51–52). Hidden hypotheses: $\varphi$ a chart of $X$ (the text: a homeomorphism onto $O$); the $[1]$-transition condition. Deviation (hypotheses explicit): both stated. The transitivity of the equivalence, which “an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases” (Definition 2.6.5 (preprint 2.51)) presupposes, and the restriction of charts, which the text uses silently (Lemma 5.1.2 (preprint 5.2)), are proved (Findings, Chapter 2, items 40, 42); a restriction whose retraction domain lies inside a given open $W \ni 0$ of $E$ is not, since $U \cap W$ need not be invariant under $r$.

HWZ §2.6 (preprint §2.5), Definition 2.6.5 (preprint 2.51) and the remarks after it, preprint p. 52

A strong bundle over $X$ is $P : Y \to X$ (continuous surjection, $Y$ paracompact Hausdorff) with an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases. The charts induce a double filtration $Y_{m,k}$ and M-polyfolds $Y[i]$, $Y[i]_m = Y_{m,m+i}$; $P[i] : Y[i] \to X$ are sc-smooth.

Verified edition V2.58

A strong bundle is a continuous surjection $P : Y \to X$, $Y$ Hausdorff paracompact, with Banachable fibres and a strong bundle atlas. The charts $\Phi$ form an sc-smooth atlas of $Y$ (the M-polyfold $Y[0]$), and $P : Y[0] \to X$ is sc-smooth. $Y_{m,k}$ ($k \le m + 1$) is the set of $y$ with $\Phi(y) \in E_m \times F_k$ in the charts of the atlas around $y$; one chart around $y$ suffices. The charts $\Phi[1] : y \mapsto (\Phi(y)_1, \Phi(y)_2$ lifted to $F_1)$, defined on $Y_{0,1}$ with the topology they generate and onto the retracts $K[1]$, are pairwise compatible, their transition maps being the $[1]$-transitions of Definition 2.6.4 (preprint 2.50), and make $Y[1]$ an M-polyfold; $P[1] : Y[1] \to X$ is sc-smooth. The charts of the strong bundle (compatible with the atlas) are those of the maximal atlas, which is equivalent to the given one: a chart is one iff it belongs to some atlas of the class, any two are compatible, restrictions of charts are charts, and equivalent atlases have the same charts. Book: Definition 2.6.5 (preprint 2.51) and the remarks after it, preprint p. 52. Hidden hypotheses: the paracompactness of $Y[1]$ (proved, V2.64); for the chart-independence of $Y_{m,m+1}$ and of $Y_{0,1}$, the $F_1$-condition on the $[1]$-transition (V2.57). Deviation (restated): $Y[1]$ carries the topology generated by the charts $\Phi[1]$, as $X_m$ in §2.3 (preprint §2.2); the charts are those induced by the given atlas. The notions defined through the charts compatible with the atlas depend only on the class; those defined with the charts of the given atlas itself ($Y_{m,k}$, $Y[1]$ and its atlas, sc⁺-sections) are not shown invariant (Findings, Chapter 2, item 43).

HWZ §2.6 (preprint §2.5), Proposition 2.6.8 (preprint 2.54), p. 69 (preprint p. 53)

$P_f : f^*Y \to Z$ carries a natural structure of a strong bundle over $Z$ (\"the easy proof is left to the reader\").

Let $P : Y \to X$ be a strong bundle and $f : Z \to X$ sc-smooth. Then $f^Y$ is paracompact, and $P_f : f^*Y \to Z$ is a strong bundle whose atlas consists of the pulled-back charts: for a strong bundle chart $\Phi$ over $\varphi$ and a chart $\psi$ of $Z$ with $f(\operatorname{dom}\psi) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}\varphi$ and $g = \varphi \circ f \circ \psi^{-1}$, the chart $\Phi_f(z, y) = (\psi(z), \mathrm{pr}_F\Phi(y))$ onto $K_g = \{(w, h) : w \in O_Z, (g(w), h) \in K\}$, the image of the strong bundle retraction $R_g(w, h) = (r_Z(w), \Gamma(g(r_Z(w)), h))$. Its fibres are $P_f^{-1}(z) \cong P^{-1}(f(z))$ (a linear homeomorphism). Transition maps of pulled-back charts are $(w, h) \mapsto (\psi_2\psi_1^{-1}(w), \mathrm{pr}_F(\Phi_2\Phi_1^{-1})(g_1(w), h))$ and are sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$. *Book: Proposition 2.6.8 (preprint 2.54), p. 69 (preprint p. 53) ("the easy proof is left to the reader"). HWZ §2.7.2 (preprint §2.6.2), Theorem 2.7.1 (preprint 2.55), p. 72 (preprint p. 56)

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable (quoted from Smirnov).

Verified edition V2.62

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable. More generally, a space $Y$ with open metrizable subspaces $V_i$ and a locally finite family of continuous $\rho_i \ge 0$ with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq V_i$, not all vanishing at any point, is metrizable, with the metric $\sum_i |\rho_i(x) - \rho_i(y)| + \min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y)) \min(d_i(x, y), 1)$; and if $\pi : Y \to X$ is continuous into a paracompact Hausdorff $X$ whose points have open neighbourhoods $U$ with $\pi^{-1}(U)$ metrizable, $Y$ is metrizable. Metrizable spaces are paracompact. Book: Theorem 2.7.1 (preprint 2.55), p. 72 (preprint p. 56), quoted from Smirnov. Deviation (stronger): proved, in the pull-back form used for $X_m$ and $TX$.

Then $W$ can be chosen inside any neighbourhood of $x$, and $X$ is regular, $T_1$ and Hausdorff. Let $X$ be tame. A chart datum of $bX$ consists of a triple $(x, V, \theta)$ with $V$ centred at $x$ (V2.84), a chart $\varphi$ of $X$, an open $V_1 \subseteq \mathrm{dom}\, \varphi$, an sc-isomorphism $T$ of the model space of $\varphi$ with $\mathbb R^{k+1} \oplus W$ and a coordinate $i$ vanishing on $T\varphi(\theta \cap V_1)$, such that the image of $\varphi(\theta \cap V_1)$ under the face projection $\pi$ (Proposition 2.5.15 (preprint 2.43)) is a tame retract of $[0, \infty)^k \oplus W$ and $d_X(y) = d(\pi\varphi(y)) + 1$ on $\theta \cap V_1$. Its chart is $p \mapsto \pi(\varphi(B(p)))$ on $U(x, V, \theta) \cap B^{-1}(V_1)$; two such charts are compatible, with transition map $\pi' \circ (\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ \iota$ ($\iota$ the face inclusion); every point of $\theta$ lies in the $V_1$ of a chart datum with the triple $(x, V, \theta)$, so the charts cover $bX$. With the topology $T_{bX}$, paracompact by V2.88, they make $bX$ a tame M-polyfold (2); $B : bX \to X$, which is $\iota$ in these charts, is sc-smooth (3); and $d_X(B(p)) = d_{bX}(p) + 1$, hence $d_X(B(p)) - 1 = d_{bX}(p)$ (4). Book: Theorem 2.7.13 (2)–(4), pp. 83–84, new in the 2021 edition. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none. Proof: the charts are the charts $\pi \circ \varphi$ of the face $\theta$ composed with $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)}$; the local faces of $\theta$ in a tame chart inside $V$ are found as in Theorem 2.5.17 (preprint 2.45).

Definition 3.1.1 (preprint 3.1), sc-germs of neighbourhoods

restated

to confirmA germ of neighbourhoods is a nested sequence of relatively open neighbourhoods $U_m$ of $0$ in $C_m$, with tangent germ $(U_{m+1} \times E_m)_m$; a germ is a fixed sequence of sets.

a germ is a fixed sequence of sets
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1.1 (preprint 3.1), p. 89 (preprint p. 62)

An sc-germ of neighbourhoods $\mathcal O(C, 0)$ around $0$ in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$ is a decreasing sequence $U_0 \supset U_1 \supset \cdots$ with $U_m$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C_m = C \cap E_m$; its tangent $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$ is $U_1 \oplus E_0 \supset U_2 \oplus E_1 \supset \cdots$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ with $U_m = U \cap E_m$ is an example; \"the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter\".

Verified edition V3.1

An sc-germ of neighbourhoods around $0$ in $C \subseteq E_0$ is a family $U_m \subseteq E_m$, each of the form $O \cap C_m$ with $O$ open in $E_m$, containing $0$, with $\iota U_{m+1} \subseteq U_m$. Its tangent germ has levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ in $C$ gives the germ $U_m = U \cap E_m$. $C$ is quadrant-like if $0 \in C$ and every $C_m$ is convex with nonempty interior; partial quadrants are. Book: Definition 3.1.1 (preprint 3.1), p. 89 (preprint p. 62). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): a germ is a fixed sequence, not a class up to shrinking; the text's "the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter" is not built in, and the theorems say on which germ they hold. $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ only when all levels coincide (finite-dimensional $E$).

An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ is a continuous $f : U_0 \to F$ with $f(U_m) \subseteq F_m$ and $f : U_m \to F_m$ continuous. It is sc$^1$ if for $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x + h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ ($h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$) and $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$ is an sc$^0$-germ on $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$; sc$^k$ inductively, sc-smooth if sc$^k$ for all $k$.

An sc^k map on a relatively open $U \ni 0$ is an sc^k-germ on $(U \cap E_m)$. Book: Definition 3.1.2 (preprint 3.2), pp. 90–91 (preprint pp. 62–63). HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1.3 (preprint 3.3), p. 91 (preprint p. 63)

An sc-smooth section germ $(f, x_0)$ of $P : Y \to X$ is a continuous section $f : V \to P^{-1}(V)$ near the smooth point $x_0$ such that in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has $\mathbf f \circ r : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ an sc-smooth germ.

Verified edition V3.5

$(f, x_0)$ is an sc-smooth section germ of the strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ if $x_0$ is smooth and in some strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, centred at $x_0$, the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $f$ satisfies: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ of $0$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$. An sc-smooth section is an sc-smooth section germ at every smooth point that has a centred chart (with the germ $U \cap E_m$). Book: Definition 3.1.3 (preprint 3.3), p. 91 (preprint p. 63). Hidden hypotheses: "a strong bundle chart" means a chart compatible with the atlas (a chart of the atlas need not be centred); the notion does not depend on the atlas within its class (Polyfold.StrongBundle.isChart_congr, V2.58). Deviation (hypotheses explicit): the chart, as just said. Since a fourth addendum the germ is the text's: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, as for Definitions 3.1.4, 3.1.6 and 3.1.11 (preprint 3.4, 3.6 and 3.11) since phase 2. Until then it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart, which is stricter (a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$, Polyfold.exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth), and the item was "narrower". No theorem assumes the definition (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260).

Since the fourth addendum of this page the definition is in the text’s germ reading: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, as for Definitions 3.1.4, 3.1.6 and 3.1.11 (preprint 3.4, 3.6 and 3.11) since phase 2. Before, it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart (levels $U \cap E_m$), which is stricter: a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$ (exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth). No theorem assumes the definition. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” from the third addendum until the fourth) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260; round-trip item V3.5).

Not stated: the fibrewise sum of sections, principal parts in a chart, the sum rule of the sc-calculus, and the sc-smoothness of the local representatives of sc$^+$-sections in a chart that is not in the atlas.

Verified edition V3.6

Sums, differences and negatives of sc-smooth maps on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants are sc-smooth. The fibrewise sum $f + s$ of sections is a section, with principal part $\mathbf f + \mathbf s$ in every chart; $f(x) = 0$ iff $\mathbf f(\varphi(x)) = 0$; the fibres of $K$ over $O$ are linear. In every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, the representative $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf f(z))$ of an sc-smooth section is sc-smooth $O \to K$, and the representative $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf s_1(z))$ of an sc⁺-section is sc-smooth $O \to K[1]$. Book: not stated; used in Theorems 3.1.13, 3.1.18 (preprint 3.12, 3.15). Hidden hypotheses: the compatibility on $[1]$ of Definition 2.6.4 (preprint 2.50) (its first use). Deviation (not in the book).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4), p. 91 (preprint p. 64)

For a tame strong local bundle $K = R(U \triangleleft F) \to O$, $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r(0) = 0$, an sc-smooth section germ $(f, 0)$ has a filling $(g, 0)$ (an sc-smooth section germ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$) if (1) $f = g$ on $O$ near $0$; (2) $g(y) = \rho(r(y))g(y)$ for $y \in U$ near $0$ forces $y \in O$; (3) the linearization of $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ at $0$, restricted to $\ker Dr(0)$, is a topological isomorphism onto $\ker\rho(0)$.

Verified edition V3.7

For a strong bundle retraction $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$ on $U \triangleleft F$ with $O = r(U)$, $0 \in U$: $g$ is a filling of $f$ if $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$ and (1) $f = g$ on $O$ near $0$; (2) a point $y \in U$ near $0$ with $g(y) = \rho(r(y))g(y)$ lies in $O$; (3) $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ is an sc¹-germ on $G$ with a derivative family $Dk$, and $Dk(0)$ restricts to a topological linear isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$. ($\rho(u)$ is a bounded operator, $\rho(x)$ a projection for $x \in O$.) Book: Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4), p. 91 (preprint p. 64). Hidden hypotheses: the map in (3) is differentiable at $0$ (true for every sc-smooth germ $g$, and $Dk(0)$ is unique). Deviation (hypotheses explicit): stated for the principal parts; tameness unused. Since the switch of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) to the text's germ reading (phase 2) $g$ and the map in (3) are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$; the stricter whole-chart filler (Polyfold.IsFillerOf, the map in (3) sc¹ on all of $U$, the sc-smoothness of $g$ on $U$ added in Definition 3.1.6 (preprint 3.6)) is kept for the whole-chart notions (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261, 330). to confirmFor a filler with $g(0) = 0$, $Tf(0) = Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E}$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with the same index; if $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm, so is $Tf(0)$, and condition (3) holds on every level.

the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §3.1, the paragraph after Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4) and Proposition 3.1.5 (preprint 3.5), pp. 91–93 (preprint pp. 64–65)

If $f$ has the filling $g$ and $f(0) = 0$, then in the splittings $E = Dr(0)E \oplus \ker Dr(0)$, $F = \rho(0)F \oplus \ker\rho(0)$, $Dg(0) = \begin{pmatrix} Tf(0) & * \\ 0 & C \end{pmatrix}$ with $C$ an isomorphism, and (1) $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is; (2) $Tf(0)$ is Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with equal index.

Verified edition V3.8

Let $g$ be sc-smooth on $U$ and fill the section $f$ of $K \to O$, with $g(0) = 0$. Then $D(\rho(r(\cdot))g)(0) = \rho(0)Dg(0)$, $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$, $D(f \circ r)(0) = Dg(0)Dr(0)$; and $Tf(0) := Dg(0)$ restricted to $Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is surjective iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, and has the same index ($\dim\ker - \dim\mathrm{coker}$). The linear algebra holds for any idempotents $p$, $q$ and $L$ with $(1 - q)Lp = 0$ and $(1 - q)L : \ker p \to \ker q$ a topological isomorphism. In sc form: if $Dg(0)$ is an sc-Fredholm sc-operator, then $Dr(0)E$, $\rho(0)F$, $\ker Dr(0)$ and $\ker\rho(0)$ are sc-subspaces, $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is sc-Fredholm with the index of $Dg(0)$ on every level, and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0) : \ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$ is an sc-isomorphism (condition (3) on every level); for $Dg(0)$ an sc-operator, $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm iff $Tf(0)$ is sc-Fredholm and condition (3) holds on every level. Book: the paragraph after Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4) and Proposition 3.1.5 (preprint 3.5), pp. 91–93 (preprint pp. 64–65). Hidden hypotheses: $(u, h) \mapsto \rho(u)h$ differentiable at $(0, 0)$; $g(0) = 0$. Deviation (stronger): the index equality without any finiteness assumption, via isomorphisms of kernels and cokernels instead of the text's factorization. The text's target "$(1 - D\rho(0))F$" is $(1 - \rho(0))F$. The sc form needs condition (3) only on level $0$, as the text states it (the higher levels of $Tf(0)$ come from the regularity of $Dg(0)$); its converse needs condition (3) on every level and fails with level $0$ alone (an example with the shift on a weighted $\ell^2$, not formalized; Findings, Chapter 3, items 234, 237, 238). The same holds for a filling germ (V3.7), with $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of any derivative family of $g$ (Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5, Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc, Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc_iff; Findings, Chapter 3, items 272, 289, 314).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7), p. 94 (preprint p. 66)

A basic germ is an sc-smooth germ $f : \mathcal O([0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{n-k} \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$ and $P_W \circ f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ close enough to $(0, 0)$ on level $m$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$.

Verified edition V3.10

For a finite-dimensional $P$, a set $\widetilde C \subseteq P$, a finite-dimensional $Q$ and a germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$: $f$ is a basic germ with contraction map $B$ if $f$ is an sc-smooth germ on $G$ with $f(0) = 0$, the $W$-component of $f(a, w)$ is $w - B(a, w)$ on $U_0$, and $B$ is an sc⁰-contraction germ (V3.25). Book: Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7), p. 94 (preprint p. 66) (Remark 3.1.8 (preprint 3.8): historical). Hidden hypotheses: the points of the contraction estimate lie in $U_m$. $(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if $x_0$ is smooth and in a strong bundle chart of $P$ centred at $x_0$ the principal part has a filling $g$ (V3.9: an sc-smooth germ on a germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$), there is an sc⁺-germ $s$ (IsScPlusGerm: $s : E_0 \to F_1$ an sc-smooth germ into $F^1$ on a germ inside $U$) with $\iota s(0) = g(0)$, and $k = g - \iota s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: strong bundle maps $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ and $\Psi'$ back, inverse to each other, with base map $\psi$, $\psi(0) = 0$, $U'$ relatively open in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant of a finite-dimensional space), a basic germ $h$ on a germ inside $U'$, and $(\Psi(u, k(u)))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ for $u \in U$ near $0$. Book: Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11), p. 96 (preprint p. 69). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the identity is required for $u \in U$; tameness unused; $C' = T\psi(0)C$ not imposed (it is proved, V3.48). The witnesses of the conjugation are also available as data (Polyfold.ConjugationData, V3.46). Since the switch to the text's germ reading (phase 2) the filling and the sc⁺-section are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$; $\Psi$ on all of $U$ is no restriction (on a relatively open $U_0 \subseteq U$ it is the same after restricting the chart on level $0$). The project's earlier notion, with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on the whole $U$ (IsScFredholmGermWholeChart), implies this one and is exactly this one with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on $U$; whether the two agree for sections sc-smooth on $X$ is open, and no theorem depends on it (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261–264, 330). The existential over charts is essential: a filling in a chart gives a topological isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \cong \ker\rho(0)$, a condition on the chart (Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.nonempty_kerEquiv), so a filling in one chart gives none in another unless these normal spaces match; a compatible tame chart of the trivial bundle carries no filling of any section (Polyfold.TrivialBundle.not_isFillingGerm_evenBundleChart; Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–352).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21), pp. 102–103 (preprint pp. 76–77)

A finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N \subseteq E$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has an sc-complement $P$ (a good complement) with: for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ implies ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). A merely topological complement is allowed for non-smooth $N$.

Verified edition V3.20

A subspace $P$ is a good complement of $N$ with respect to $C$ if $E_0 = N \oplus P$ (algebraically) and for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $n \in N$, $p \in P$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ imply ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). $N$ is in good position to $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has a good complement. Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21) as written (IsScGoodComplement: $E = N \oplus P$ an sc-splitting with the constant $\varepsilon$; IsInGoodPositionSc) implies this; on a partial quadrant a smooth finite-dimensional $N$ in good position is in good position with an sc-complement, also inside any sc-subspace $T \supseteq N$, and for smooth $N$ the text's good complements are the project's closed ones. Book: Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21), pp. 102–103 (preprint pp. 76–77) (an sc-complement, or a topological one). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): only the algebraic splitting is required, as a hypothesis. As a conclusion the algebraic form is weaker (an algebraic good complement need not be closed, round-trip item V3.20), so the text's form is formalized as well and proved where the theorems conclude good position (V3.47, V3.94; Findings, Chapter 3, items 210, 211).

If the finite-dimensional subspace $N$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$, then $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$. HWZ §3.3, Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28), p. 109 (preprint p. 85)

An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ if $f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ on level $m$ sufficiently close to $(0, 0)$.

Verified edition V3.25

For a germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$: $B$ is an sc⁰-contraction germ if $B$ is an sc⁰-germ, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m$ there is $r > 0$ such that the points $(a, w)$ with $a \in \widetilde C$, $|a| < r$, $|w|_m < r$ lie in $U_m$ and $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for such $(a, w)$, $(a, w')$. Every such $B$ has a working form: open $N(0) \supseteq N(1) \supseteq \cdots \ni 0$ in $P$ and $0 \in K(m) \subseteq O(m) \subseteq W_m$ ($K$ closed, $O$ open, $\iota K(m+1) \subseteq K(m)$) with $\{a\} \times O(m) \subseteq U_m$, $B_m(a, \cdot)$ a $\tfrac12$-contraction on $O(m)$ mapping $K(m)$ into itself, for $a \in N(m) \cap \widetilde C$. Book: Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28), p. 109 (preprint p. 85). Hidden hypotheses: the points lie in $U_m$. Deviation (restated): explicit regions, needed for Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31).

An sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ admits a uniquely determined sc$^0$-solution germ $\delta : \mathcal O(\widetilde C, 0) \to (W, 0)$ with $f(a, \delta(a)) = 0$; proof by \"the parametrized version of Banach's fixed point theorem\".

For a contraction germ in working form with quadrant-like $\widetilde C$: the level-$0$ fixed point $\delta(a)$ of $B(a, \cdot)$ is an sc⁰-germ on $V_m = N(m) \cap \widetilde C$ with $\delta(0) = 0$, $(a, \delta_m(a)) \in U_m$ for $a \in V_m$, $B(a, \delta(a)) = \delta(a)$ on $V_0$, and every $w \in O(0)$ with $B(a, w) = w$, $a \in V_0$, equals $\delta(a)$. HWZ §3.6, Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52), p. 135 (preprint p. 110)

If $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $f(x) = 0$, then $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator (of the index $n - N$ of the basic germ, as the proof of Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54) uses).

Verified edition V3.46

Let $f$ be a section of a strong bundle with $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ and $f(x_0) = 0$. In the strong bundle chart of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) centred at $x_0$, with the filling germ $g$ (a derivative family $Dg$ on a germ inside $U$) and the local sc⁺-germ $s$ for which $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ, $Dg(0) : E_0 \to F_0$ and $Tf(x_0) := Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E_0} : Dr(0)E_0 \to \rho(0)F_0$ are Fredholm operators, and for every conjugation of $g - s$ to a basic germ $h : O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $\widetilde C \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, both have index $n - N$ (ConjugationData: the witnesses of a conjugation, Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11), as data). In particular $n - N$ is the same for all conjugations of one germ: for $k$ sc-smooth with $k(0) = 0$ and any conjugation of $k$ to a basic germ, $Dk(0)$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$. They are sc-Fredholm operators: $Dg(0) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator, $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ and $K_0 = \rho(0)F$ are sc-subspaces, and $Tf(x_0) : T_0O \to K_0$ is sc-Fredholm, both of index $n - N$ on every level; for an sc-Fredholm section the same holds in every strong bundle chart around a zero $y$, at the point $z$ over $y$, for $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$. Book: Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52), p. 135 (preprint p. 110) ($Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is sc-Fredholm); the index $n - N$ is used in the proof of Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): in charts ($T_xX$ carries no linear structure here, Chapter 2). The hypothesis is the text's since the switch to the germ reading (phase 2): the filling and the sc⁺-section are germs (V3.13), and $Dg(0)$ is the value at $0$ of any derivative family of the filling germ; the forms for germ data on the whole chart are the _wholeChart declarations of the same names (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 289, 310, 331). Formerly "narrower", for that hypothesis. The sc-Fredholm property, first proved on level $0$ only, follows the text's argument with two steps it leaves out: $D(g - s)(0) = \Gamma(0)^{-1}Dh(0)D\psi(0)$ is sc-Fredholm by the criterion of V1.8, and $T_0O$, $K_0$ are sc-subspaces (Definition 2.6.1 (preprint 2.47) at the smooth point $0$, the closed graph theorem); in other charts the levels are transported by the chart change at smooth points (Findings, Chapter 3, items 235, 239). The first version (Polyfold.proposition_3_52, kept for its consumers) states the index as "$n - N$ for some natural numbers $n$, $N$", which carries no information; proposition_3_52_index identifies $n$ and $N$ with the dimensions of the conjugating basic germ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 120). In every other strong bundle chart around $x_0$ the linearization is Fredholm of the same index (V3.96).

HWZ §3.6, Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53), p. 136 (preprint p. 111)

An sc-Fredholm germ $(f, x)$ of a tame strong bundle with $f(x) = 0$ is in good position if (1) $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is surjective and (2) if $d_X(x) \ge 1$, $\ker f'(x)$ is in good position to the partial cone $C_xX$ in $T_xX$.

Verified edition V3.47

In a chart centred at the zero, with the filling germ $g$ and $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of a derivative family of $g$ (the same for all): the germ is in good position if $Tf(0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ is onto and $\ker Dg(0)$ is in good position to $T_0O \cap C$ inside $T_0O$ (interior of $\ker Dg(0) \cap C$ in $\ker Dg(0)$ nonempty, a good complement inside $T_0O$). For a section, $(f, x_0)$ is in good position if it has the data of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) at $x_0$ with the germ in good position in that chart. With the text's sc-complement (IsGoodPositionAtSc; for a section IsGoodPositionGermSc, in a tame chart) the kernel has a good sc-complement inside $T_0O$ ($T_m = N_m \oplus P_m$ on every level); at a zero of an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data the two forms agree. Book: Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53), p. 136 (preprint p. 111). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): in a chart rather than in $T_xX$; no case distinction $d_X(x) \ge 1$, which is recovered as a theorem for tame germ data: at a zero with $d_X = 0$ good position in a tame chart is the surjectivity of the linearization (V3.100). At a zero the linearization and the two conditions do not depend on the chart (V3.78); Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53) at a zero from a chart not centred there is V3.79, and in any chart of the germ data V3.107. The form in a tame chart, which the theorems of §3.6 assume and conclude, is V3.103. The germ data are the text's since the switch to the germ reading (phase 2, V3.13); the whole-chart forms are IsGoodPositionGermWholeChart, IsGoodPositionGermScWholeChart (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 280, 320, 330); that "an sc-splitting of $T_0O$", written in $E$, is an sc-splitting of the sc-Banach space $T_0O$ is not formalized (item 214).
