HWZ §3.6, Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54), p. 136 (preprint p. 111) (proof pp. 136–140 (preprint pp. 111–115))

Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section of a tame strong bundle with $f(x) = 0$ and $(f, x)$ in good position. There is an open $V \ni x$ such that $S = \{y \in V \mid f(y) = 0\}$ has: (1) at every $y \in S$, $(f, y)$ is in good position; (2) $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is equivalent to a smooth manifold with boundary with corners. The proof shows (3): $\psi\varphi(S) = \{v + \sigma(v) \mid v \in V'\}$ for the $\sigma$ of Theorem 3.5.11 (preprint Corollary 3.47) applied to $\Psi_*(g) = h + t$.

Verified edition V3.48

Let $f$ be a section of a strong bundle, with $f(x_0) = 0$ and $(f, x_0)$ in good position in a tame chart (V3.103). Then there are: a tame strong bundle chart $\varphi$ centred at $x_0$ (compatible with the atlas, with tame base retraction); an sc-smooth $\psi$ on its $U$ with $\psi(0) = 0$ into a relatively open $U'$ of $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant), with an sc-smooth inverse $\psi'$ on $U'$; the data of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) and a basic germ $h'$ with $D(h' + \iota t)(0)$ surjective and kernel $K$ in good position, $K$ a smooth subspace; a closed good complement $Y$ of $K$; a relatively open $V' \ni 0$ in $K \cap (\widetilde C \oplus W)$; $\sigma$ with values in $Y$ and $W$-components on level $1$, $C^1$ on $V'$, $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$, such that every $v + \sigma(v)$, $v \in V'$, is a zero of $h' + \iota t$ in its germ, and for every $k \ge 1$ a $C^k$-lift $\sigma_k : V_k \to E'_k$ of $\sigma$ on a relatively open $V_k \ni 0$, $V_k \subseteq V'$ (Theorem 3.5.11 (1) (preprint Corollary 3.47)); and an open $V_x \ni x_0$ in the chart domain on which $\psi\varphi$ is injective, $f(y) = 0 \iff (h' + \iota t)(\psi\varphi(y)) = 0$, and $\psi\varphi(\{y \in V_x \mid f(y) = 0\}) = \{v + \sigma(v) \mid v \in V'\}$. On the way: in the chart, $Dg(0)$ is surjective with kernel in good position to $C$ in $E$, $x \in C \iff D\psi(0)x \in C'$, and $D(\Psi_*g)(0) = \Gamma(0)Dg(0)D\psi(0)^{-1}$ is surjective Fredholm with kernel in good position. Book: Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54), p. 136 (preprint p. 111), the step (3) of its proof, pp. 137–139 (preprint pp. 113–114). Hidden hypotheses: the tameness of the chart at $x_0$, used only as $(1 - Dr(0))E \subseteq E_0$; the neighbourhood $V$ made explicit; the kernel is smooth (the text: without comment). Deviation (narrower): only the graph description (3) of the proof; conclusions (1) and (2) of the theorem are V3.82 and V3.85, the choice of $Y$ with the projection property V3.77.

HWZ §3.6, Lemma 3.6.9 (preprint 3.55), p. 139 (preprint p. 114) (proof §3.8.4 (preprint §3.8.3), pp. 160–164 (preprint pp. 132–135))

$C \subseteq E$ a partial quadrant, $N$ a finite-dimensional smooth subspace in good position with good complement $Y$, $V \subseteq N \cap C$ relatively open, $\tau : V \to Y_1$ of class $C^1$ with $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$. Then for $v$ in a relatively open $V' \ni 0$: (1) $v + \tau(v) \in C_1$; (2) $Y$ is a topological complement of $N_v = \{n + D\tau(v)n\}$; (3) there is $\gamma_v > 0$ with $n \in C_x \iff n + y \in C_x$ for $n \in N_v$, $y \in Y$, $|y|_0 \le \gamma_v|n|_0$, $x = v + \tau(v)$.

Verified edition V3.49

In $E = \mathbb R^n \oplus W$, $C = [0, \infty)^n \oplus W$: let $N$ be finite-dimensional in good position with good complement $Y$, $Y$ closed, and $\tau : N \to E$ with values in $Y$, $C^1$ on $N \cap C$, $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$. There is $\rho > 0$ such that for $v \in N \cap C$ with $|v| < \rho$: $v + \tau(v) \in C$, and $Y$ is a good complement of $N_v = \{n + D\tau(v)n \mid n \in N\}$ with respect to the partial quadrant $C_{v + \tau(v)}$ (so $E_0 = N_v \oplus Y$, both closed, with the good-complement constant independent of $v$). The core holds for any $C$ cut out by coordinate functionals. Book: Lemma 3.6.9 (preprint 3.55), p. 139 (preprint p. 114), proof pp. 160–164 (preprint pp. 132–135). Hidden hypotheses: $Y$ closed (needed for $D\tau(v)n \in Y$). Deviation (narrower): the added closedness; $\tau$ given on all of $N \cap C$. The form used in Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54) — for a relatively open $V \subseteq N \cap C$ and any presentation of $C$, with the good position of $N_v$ — is Polyfold.lemma_3_55_relOpen (V3.80).

Used without statement: in the proof of Proposition 3.2.2 (preprint 3.26), “$X' = \psi(X)$ is tame”; in the proof of Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54), the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ onto $\psi(O)$ is a chart of the tame M-polyfold $X$.

Verified edition V3.71

Let $\psi : U \to U'$ be an sc-diffeomorphism between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants ($\psi$ sc-smooth on $U$, $\psi'$ sc-smooth on $U'$, mapping $U$ and $U'$ into each other, inverse to each other) and $r : U \to U$ a tame sc-smooth retraction onto $O$ whose domain is $U$. Then $r' = \psi \circ r \circ \psi'$ is a tame retraction of $U'$ onto $\psi(O)$, so $(\psi(O), C', E')$ is a tame retract; on the way $d_{C'}(\psi(x)) = d_C(x)$ (Theorem 1.3.5 (preprint 1.25)), $Dr'(y) = D\psi(x)Dr(x)D\psi'(y)$ at the level-$1$ points $y = \psi(x)$ with $x \in O$, and an sc-operator with an sc-operator inverse carries sc-subspaces and sc-splittings. The restriction of a tame retraction to $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$, $W$ open, is tame; an open subset $O \cap W$ of a tame retract is a tame retract; the model $\varphi(s)$ of a chart restricted to an open $s$ of its domain is tame if the model of $\varphi$ is. Book: used without statement in the proof of Proposition 3.2.2 (preprint 3.26) ("$X' = \psi(X)$ is tame", preprint p. 80) and in the proof of Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54) (the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ of a tame M-polyfold, preprint p. 114). Hidden hypotheses: condition (2) of Definition 2.5.2 (preprint 2.34) is transported at smooth points, where $D\psi(x)$ is an sc-isomorphism, with $D\psi(x)E_x \subseteq E'_{\psi(x)}$ (the one-sided sign argument). Deviation (not in the book).

HWZ §3.2, proof of Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27), preprint p. 84

In the proof of Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27): $\delta$ is an sc$^\infty$-germ near every $v_0 \in V$. With the data $(\psi, N', Y', V', \tau)$ at $x_0 = \varphi^{-1}(v_0 + \delta(v_0))$, the map $w \mapsto \pi\varphi\psi^{-1}(w + \tau(w))$ has an invertible linearization at $0$, so it is a local diffeomorphism and $\delta$ is regular near $v_0$.

Verified edition V3.73

Let $\chi_1$, $\chi_2$ be charts of an M-polyfold $X$ and $S \subseteq X$. Suppose that $\chi_1(S \cap V_{x_1}) = \{v + \sigma_1(v) \mid v \in V_1\}$ for an open $V_{x_1}$ in the domain of $\chi_1$, where $K_1$ is a finite-dimensional smooth subspace in good position to $C_1$ with a closed complement $Y_1$, $V_1$ is relatively open in $K_1 \cap C_1$, and $\sigma_1$ has values in $Y_1$ and is of class $C^1$ on all of $V_1$; that $\chi_2$ is centred at a point $y \in V_{x_1} \cap V_{x_2}$ and $\chi_2(S \cap V_{x_2})$ is the graph of $\sigma_2$ over a relatively open $V_2 \ni 0$ in $K_2 \cap C_2$ (the same conditions on $K_2$, $Y_2$), with $\sigma_2$ continuous, $\sigma_2(0) = 0$, $D\sigma_2(0) = 0$ and $C^k$-lifts $\sigma_{2,k} : V_{2,k} \to E_{2,k}$ on relatively open neighbourhoods of $0$ for every $k \ge 1$; and that $\chi_1(y) = v_0 + \sigma_1(v_0)$, $v_0 \in V_1$. Then $\dim K_1 = \dim K_2$, and for all $m$, $k$ there is a relatively open $B' \ni v_0$ in $K_1 \cap C_1$, $B' \subseteq V_1$, on which $\sigma_1$ takes values in $E_{1,m}$ and is of class $C^k$ into $E_{1,m}$. On the way: a map differentiable on a set whose image has nonempty interior does not lower the dimension (Sard's lemma in fixed dimension); and a $C^k$ map between relatively open subsets of convex sets with nonempty interior in finite-dimensional spaces, with a continuous left inverse on its relatively open image and an invertible derivative at a point, has a $C^k$ inverse near the image of that point. Book: the step "$\delta$ is an sc$^\infty$-germ near every point $v_0 \in V$" of the proof of Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27), preprint p. 84. Hidden hypotheses: $\sigma_1$ differentiable at $v_0$ (here $C^1$ on $V_1$; without it the step fails, V3.24); $Y_1$, $Y_2$ closed; the lifts at $0$ (Theorem 3.5.11 (1) (preprint Corollary 3.47), V3.42). Deviation (narrower): for two graph descriptions of one set, with $\sigma_1$ of class $C^1$ on $V_1$. Proof: the linearization of $\beta = \pi_1 \circ \chi_1\chi_2^{-1} \circ (1 + \sigma_2)$ at $0$ is injective by the chain rule for the transition and its inverse on level $1$ and the tangency of the graph of $\sigma_2$ to the retract; it is onto by the dimension count, not by the symmetric chain rule (which would need $\sigma_1$ differentiable into level $1$ at $v_0$); the inverse is $C^k$ by V3.90, not by Theorem 3.8.15 (preprint 3.72) (which would need $d_C(x) = d_C(\beta(x))$).

In the proof of Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27) the set $\Sigma = \{v + y \in C \mid v \in V, y \in Y\}$ is asserted to be relatively open in $C$; the retraction $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$ is defined on it.

Verified edition V3.75

ProjectsInto C N Y means: $z \in C$, $k \in N$, $z - k \in Y$ imply $k \in C$; for $E_0 = N \oplus Y$ the projection onto $N$ along $Y$ maps $C$ into $N \cap C$. If the finite-dimensional subspace $N$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ of the sc-Banach space $E$, there is a continuous projection $\pi : E_0 \to N$ with $\pi(C) \subseteq N \cap C$ whose kernel $Y$ is a good complement of $N$; $Y$ is closed and ProjectsInto C N Y holds. The property is carried by continuous linear isomorphisms $S$ with $x \in C \iff Sx \in C'$. Book: not stated; the proof of Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27) (preprint p. 83) asserts that $\Sigma = \{v + y \in C \mid v \in V, y \in Y\}$ is relatively open in $C$, which fails for an arbitrary good complement (V3.24) and holds when $\pi(O) \subseteq C$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): the construction keeps the coordinates of a set $S$ of indices; when no coordinate vanishes at a nonzero point of $N \cap C$ and $N \cap C \ne N$, one coordinate is kept (the natural choice $S = \Sigma$ fails there: for $C = [0, \infty)^2$, $N = \mathbb R(1, 1)$, the projection along the good complement $\mathbb R(1, 2)$ maps $(0, 1)$ to $-(1, 1)$).

HWZ §3.4, Corollary 3.4.3 (preprint 3.39), p. 116 (preprint p. 93)

If the sc-germ $g$ is equivalent by a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi$ to a basic germ and $s$ is an sc$^+$-germ, there is a strong bundle map $\Psi$ such that $((\Psi \circ \Phi)_*(g + s))^1$ is a basic germ.

Verified edition V3.76

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ with $0 \in U$, $g : U \to F$ sc-smooth and conjugated to a basic germ (V3.13), and $s : U \to F_1$ sc-smooth into $F^1$ with $s(0) = 0$. Then the level-$1$ map $(g + \iota s)^1 : U_1 \to F_1$ is conjugated to a basic germ on the shifted structures $E^1 \triangleleft F^1$. Explicitly, for a conjugation $\Phi$ of $g$ to the basic germ $h$, with $t = \Phi[1]_*s$ ($t(0) = 0$) and $h' = h + (t_{\mathbb R^N}, 0)$, there are the data of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) (V3.34) for $t_W$ such that: $h'$ is a basic germ and $\Phi_*(g + s) = h + t$ near $0$; the composite $\Gamma = \Lambda \circ \Phi^1$ of the index raise of $\Phi$ and the linear coordinate change $\Lambda$ of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) is a strong bundle isomorphism of the shifted structures onto a relatively open subset of $(\widetilde C \oplus C) \oplus X^1$, with base map vanishing at $0$ and $\Gamma_* = \Lambda_* \circ \Phi^1_*$; and $(\Gamma(u, (g + s)^1(u)))_2 = (\Lambda_*(h + t))^1(\gamma(u))$ for $u \in U_1$ near $0$, a basic germ. The text's form "$\Gamma = \Psi \circ \Phi$, then raise the index" is the same map (compIso_eq_strongShift). On the way: a pair of sc-isomorphisms, the index raise of a strong bundle isomorphism and a composition of strong bundle isomorphisms are strong bundle isomorphisms, and push-forwards compose. Book: Corollary 3.4.3 (preprint 3.39), p. 116 (preprint p. 93). Hidden hypotheses: the index raise of a strong bundle isomorphism is one (used silently). Deviation (restated): "sc-germ" read as sc-smooth on $U$, $s$ as an sc⁺-map on all of $U$ with $s(0) = 0$; the conclusion is a conjugation of $(g + s)^1$ on the shifted structures; the text's "strong bundle map $\Psi$" is an isomorphism; the $\mathbb R^N$-component of $t$ is absorbed into $h$; the text's $\tau : Z \to C$ is not applied.

HWZ §3.6, Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53), p. 136 (preprint p. 111); §2.5 (preprint §2.4), Definition 2.5.8 (preprint 2.38), p. 57 (preprint p. 42)

Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53) is stated with $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ and the partial cone $C_xX$; Definition 2.5.8 (preprint 2.38) asserts that $T^R_xX$ and $C_xX$ do not depend on the chart (Proposition 2.4.10 (preprint 2.30)). The linearization is defined at the centre of a chart, through a filler.

Verified edition V3.78

In a strong bundle chart (retraction $r$ on $U$ onto $O$, fibre projections $\rho$, principal part $\mathbf f$), $\mathrm{Lin}(z) = D(\mathbf f \circ r)(z)|_{T_zO}$, $T_zO = Dr(z)E$, at every level-$1$ point $z$ of the retract. At a zero its values lie in $K_z = \rho(z)F$; it equals $Dg(z)$ on $T_zO$ for every $g$ sc¹ on $U$ agreeing with $\mathbf f$ on $O$ near $z$, and for every sc¹-germ $g$ agreeing with $\mathbf f$ near $z$ with $z$ in its germ ($Dg(z)$ the value of its derivative family; Findings, Chapter 3, item 284); at a centred zero it is the $Tf(0)$ of Proposition 3.1.5 (preprint 3.5) (V3.8), also for a filling germ. For strong bundle charts $c$, $c'$ whose transition is sc-smooth on $[0]$, a section with sc-smooth principal parts in both, and a zero $y$ in both domains with level-$1$ points $z$, $z'$ over $\varphi(y)$, $\varphi'(y)$: there are topological linear isomorphisms $A : T_zO \to T_{z'}O'$ and $\Gamma : K_z \to K'_{z'}$ with $\Gamma \circ \mathrm{Lin}(z) = \mathrm{Lin}'(z') \circ A$ and, on $T_zO$, $x \in C_z \iff Ax \in C'_{z'}$ (the partial quadrants at the two points). Hence for two strong bundle charts of $P$ and an sc-smooth section, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ and $\mathrm{Lin}'(z')$ are simultaneously onto, simultaneously Fredholm with the same index, and their kernels are simultaneously in good position to the partial quadrants inside $T_zO$, $T_{z'}O'$ (good position inside a subspace is carried by isomorphisms respecting the cones). Book: Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53) (p. 136 (preprint p. 111)) presupposes it; Definition 2.5.8 (preprint 2.38) (p. 57 (preprint p. 42)) asserts the chart independence of $T^R_xX$, $C_xX$ by Proposition 2.4.10 (preprint 2.30); nothing is said about $f'(x)$. Hidden hypotheses: the point is a zero (away from zeros the linearization is not chart independent). Deviation (not in the book): the chart form of what gap G.13 leaves open; of the compatibility of Definition 2.6.4 (preprint 2.50) only the sc-smoothness of the transition on $[0]$ is used; level-$1$ points suffice; no tameness.

(a) Let $C \subseteq V$ be closed under nonnegative scaling with $0 \in C$ and $N \subseteq V$ a subspace. For every good complement of $\mathbb R \times N$ with respect to $\mathbb R \times C$, the $V$-components of its vectors lie in the lineality space $C \cap (-C)$; so $\mathbb R \times N$ is in good position only if $N + (C \cap -C) = V$. (b) Let $K$, $Y'$ be subspaces of $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ and $j : \Lambda \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ linear, $\Lambda$ finite-dimensional, with $K \cap j(\Lambda) = 0$, $(K + j(\Lambda)) \oplus Y' = \mathbb R^n \oplus W$, $Y'$ in the lineality space of $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($v + y \in \widetilde C \oplus W \iff v \in \widetilde C \oplus W$ for $y \in Y'$), and $K + j(\Lambda)$ meeting the interior of $\widetilde C \oplus W$. Then $\{((\lambda, a), w) \mid (a, w) + j(\lambda) \in K\}$ is in good position to $(\Lambda \times \widetilde C) \oplus W$. Let $U$ be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space $V$ with unique differentiability at its points, $f : V \to V$ of class $C^j$ ($j \ge 1$) on $U$ with $\|Df(x) - 1\| \le \tfrac12$ for $x \in U$, and let $f(U)$ have unique differentiability. Then $f$ is injective on $U$ ($\tfrac12|x - x'| \le |f(x) - f(x')|$), its inverse $g$ is differentiable within $f(U)$ with $Dg(y) = [Df(g(y))]^{-1}$, and $g$ is of class $C^j$ on $f(U)$. Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1): at a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ is the Fredholm index of $(f - s)'(x)$ for a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$; it does not depend on $s$. Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2): over a tame M-polyfold, if $x_0$, $x_1$ are smooth points connected by an sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$, then $\mathrm{ind}(f, x_0) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x_1)$. Verified edition V3.98

Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section of a strong bundle with tame germ data (V3.103), $f(x_0) = 0$, $(f, x_0)$ in good position in a tame chart. Then there are an open $V_x \ni x_0$ and $d$ such that IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d holds at every zero $y \in V_x$: $f'(y)$ is onto with $\mathrm{ind}\,f'(y) = \dim\ker f'(y) = d = \mathrm{ind}\,f'(x_0)$ (theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant). Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54) with the index (theorem_3_54_index): moreover every zero in $V_x$ is in good position in a tame chart, and $S$ has at $x_0$ regular data of dimension $d$ whose chart domain is $V_x$, every datum at a point of $S$ in $V_x$ having dimension $d$. On the way: at a zero in good position in a tame chart at which every datum of Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25) for $S$ has dimension $d$, IsSurjLinOfIndex f y d ($f$ sc-smooth). In sc form, at every zero in $V_x$ and in every chart, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm, onto on every level, of index $d$ on every level (theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_sc); at any zero of an sc-Fredholm section, in every chart, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm with the same index on every level (linAt_isScFredholm). Without good position, with the text's hypotheses: if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data and $f(x_0) = 0$, there are an open $V \ni x_0$ and $i \in \mathbb Z$ such that at every zero $y \in V$, in every strong bundle chart, $f'(y)$ is Fredholm of index $i$ (IsLinOfIndex f y i; index_locally_constant_tame) and $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm of index $i$ on every level (theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general_tame); no bump functions are assumed (the first forms, for $X$ admitting sc-smooth bump functions, Definition 5.3.1 (preprint 5.9): index_locally_constant_of_admitsBumpFunctions, theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general). Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1), with the text's locally defined section: an sc-Fredholm section $f$ has index $i$ at a smooth point $x$ (IsIndexAtLocal f x i) if for some open $V \ni x$ and some sc⁺-section $s$ of the restriction $P|V$ of $P$ to $V$ (StrongBundle.restrictOpen: the strong bundle over the M-polyfold $V$ whose atlas consists of the charts of $P$ with base domain inside $V$), $(f|_V + s)(x) = 0$ and $(f|_V + s)'(x)$ is Fredholm of index $i$ in every strong bundle chart of $P|V$; the index is unique, at a zero it is the index of $f'(x)$, and it exists at every smooth point. With an sc⁺-section on all of $X$ in place of $s$ (IsIndexAt f x i) the index is unique as well and implies the local one; if $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions it exists at every smooth point and the two readings agree (isIndexAtLocal_iff_isIndexAt). Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2): if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data, then for every sc-smooth path $\varphi : \mathbb R \to X$ the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, \varphi(t))$ (local reading) is the same for all $t$ (proposition_6_2_local), and any two values of the index at $\varphi(0)$ and $\varphi(1)$ agree (proposition_6_2_local'); if $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, the same holds for the global reading (proposition_6_2). Book: Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1), pp. 237–240 (preprint pp. 200–201); Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2), p. 240 (preprint p. 201) (over a tame M-polyfold, the index is constant along sc-smooth paths $[0, 1] \to X$ of smooth points; the proof: "we do not need a sc-smooth partition of unity", preprint p. 202), whose proof uses the step of V3.82; in Chapter 3 the statement along the solution set is implicit in Theorem 3.6.8 (1) (preprint 3.54). Hidden hypotheses: tameness as in V3.68; for Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1), the text's local sc⁺-section $s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ is a section of the restriction of the bundle to an open neighbourhood of $x$ ($-s$ here), a construction the text uses without comment. Deviation (narrower): the path is defined on $\mathbb R$, not on $[0, 1]$ ($\mathbb R \times X$ is the product of Theorem 3.1.21 (preprint 3.18) and has no boundary, and the text's tame M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ is not used): a path on $[0, 1]$ that extends sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is covered, a path sc-smooth on $[0, 1]$ only is not, and the project has no M-polyfold $[0, 1]$. This is the only narrowing left; the hypotheses on $f$ are the text's, in the reading of tameness of V3.103 (as in V3.94), and no bump functions are assumed. Proof: Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) is proved by the text's device, run on the restriction $P|V$ to the domain $V$ of a chart around $\varphi(t_0)$, where the text's sections need no cut-off — for each $t_0$ an sc⁺-section $S$ of the pull-back to $\mathbb R \times V$ with $\tilde f + S = 0$ along the graph of the path near $t_0$ (the text's $R(x, f(\varphi(t)))$ in the chart), the local constancy of the index of $\tilde f + S$ along its zero set, the count $\mathrm{ind}(\tilde f + S)'(t, x) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x) + 1$ through the slice $S(t, \cdot)$, and the connectedness of $\mathbb R$; the earlier form for M-polyfolds with bump functions cuts the sections off instead (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340–349, 360–367). The local constancy along the zero set without good position is the same device: sc⁺-sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$ on $P|V$ put the parametrized section of Theorem 3.1.21 (preprint 3.18) into general position at $(0, x_0)$, its index is constant along its solution set, at $(0, y)$ it is $k + \mathrm{ind}\,f'(y)$, and the index at a zero is the same for $P$ and $P|V$, through the germ datum (items 240–242, 360–363). Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1) is well defined because two local sections are compared on the intersection of their domains; its independence of $s$ is proved from the germ data and Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15), not by the text's appeal to Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10); and it exists at every smooth point through the section $-R(\cdot, f(x))$ on a chart domain (items 340, 364). Under bump functions a local section is cut off to a global one with the same index (item 367). The candidate counterexample of items 188 and 243 is excluded by Theorem 3.6.8 (1) (preprint 3.54). Without tame germ data the local constancy is open: it amounts to the index $0$ of the block $(1 - \rho(z))Dg(z)|_{\ker Dr(z)}$ of the filling at the nearby zeros, which condition (3) of Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4) gives at $z = 0$ only (items 243, 343).

What differs (the comparison)

  • Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) is proved with the text’s hypotheses (fifth addendum of this page; in the fourth, with bump functions), by the text’s device run on the restriction $P|V$ of $P$ to the domain $V$ of a strong bundle chart around $\varphi(t_0)$ (StrongBundle.restrictOpen), for each $t_0$: an sc$^+$-section $S$ of the pull-back to $\mathbb R \times V$ with $\tilde f + S = 0$ along the graph of the path near $t_0$ (the text’s $s(t, x) = R(x, f(\varphi(t)))$ in the chart, with no cut-off, since the chart covers $V$), the local constancy of the index of $\tilde f + S$ along its zero set (stabilizing sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$ in the product chart, again without cut-off, and the implicit function theorem), the index count $\mathrm{ind}(\tilde f + S)'(t, x) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x) + 1$ through the slice $S(t, \cdot)$ (isIndexAt_of_pullback_isLinOfIndex), and the connectedness of $\mathbb R$ (proposition_6_2_local). No bump functions are assumed (“we do not need a sc-smooth partition of unity”, preprint p. 202); tame germ data are the project’s reading of the text’s tameness (V3.103), as in V3.94, where they are no narrowing. With bump functions the proposition holds for the global reading of Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1) as well (proposition_6_2, the form of the fourth addendum, whose section along the path is cut off by a bump; exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_path) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340–349, 360–367).
  • Why still “narrower”. The path is $\varphi : \mathbb R \to X$, not $[0, 1] \to X$: $\mathbb R \times X$ is the product of Theorem 3.1.21 (preprint 3.18) and has no boundary, and the text’s tame M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ is not used. A path on $[0, 1]$ that extends sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is covered; a path sc-smooth on $[0, 1]$ only, in the sense of M-polyfolds with boundary, is not, and the project has no M-polyfold $[0, 1]$. This is the one narrowing left: the bump functions are gone, Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1) has the text’s local sections, and the hypotheses on $f$ are the text’s in the project’s reading of tameness.
  • Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1) has no row of its own. It is IsIndexAtLocal: the text’s locally defined sc$^+$-section is a section of the restriction $P|V$ to an open $V \ni x$ — the restriction of a strong bundle to an open set, which the text uses without comment, is constructed (StrongBundle.restrictOpen, whose atlas consists of the charts of $P$ inside $V$) — and the text’s $f - s$, $s(x) = f(x)$, is written $f + s$, $(f + s)(x) = 0$. It is well defined, two local sections being compared on the intersection of their domains (IsIndexAtLocal.unique), and it exists at every smooth point without bump functions, through the section $-R(\cdot, f(x))$ on a chart domain (exists_isIndexAtLocal). The global reading IsIndexAt of the fourth addendum implies it, and when $X$ admits bump functions the two agree, the local section being cut off (isIndexAtLocal_iff_isIndexAt). The independence of $s$ is proved from the germ data and Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15), without the text’s appeal to Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10), for which the project has no lemma that the linearization of an sc$^+$-section is compact (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340, 364, 367).
  • Along the solution set the formal proof combines the good position of the nearby zeros (V3.94), the local constancy of the dimension (V3.85) and dimension = index at each zero (V3.97); the text’s proof of Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) uses the step of V3.82 for an extended section, which along solution sets is repaired by V3.93 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 171, 188). Added in the second addendum of this page.
  • Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (htame), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).

(3.50) For an sc-smooth section $f$ of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and a smooth point $x$: $(f, x)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if there is a strong bundle chart $\Phi : \Phi^{-1}(V) \to K$ around $x$ covering $\varphi : (V, x) \to (O, 0)$, “where $K \to O$ is a tame strong local bundle”, in which the local section has a filling $g$ near $0$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ and $g - s$ conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ. A strong bundle chart of $P$ is tame (IsTameChart) if it is compatible with the atlas and its base retraction $r : U \to U$ is tame (Definition 2.5.2 (preprint 2.34)). IsScFredholmGermTame f x (Definition 3.6.3 (preprint 3.50), "tame germ data at $x$"): $x$ is a smooth point and there are the data of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) (V3.13: a strong bundle chart centred at $x$, a filling germ $g$ of the principal part, a local sc⁺-germ $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$, and $g - s$ conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ; the text's germ reading) in a tame chart. IsGoodPositionGermTame f x ("good position in a tame chart"): the same data with the germ in good position in that chart (Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53) in the chart form of V3.47). IsScFredholmSectionTame f (Definition 3.6.4 (preprint 3.51), "tame germ data"): $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section (V3.16) with tame germ data at every smooth point. Each of these implies the form without tameness (V3.13, V3.47), good position in a tame chart gives tame germ data, and the strengthened good position of V3.82 is stated in a tame chart and implies good position in it. A retraction agreeing on its domain with a tame retraction is tame; hence a compatible chart whose base retraction is the identity of $U$ (the retract $O = U$ relatively open in the partial quadrant) is tame, so the hypotheses can be met. Book: Definition 3.6.3 (preprint 3.50), p. 135 (preprint p. 110) (a strong bundle chart around $x$ "where $K \to O$ is a tame strong local bundle", as in Definition 3.1.6 (preprint 3.6), p. 93 (preprint p. 66)); Definition 3.6.4 (preprint 3.51), p. 135 (preprint p. 110), and Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53), p. 136 (preprint p. 111) (for a tame strong bundle); a strong bundle retraction is tame when its $r$ is (preprint p. 49); the proof of Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52) starts from "a tame strong bundle chart" (p. 135 (preprint p. 110)). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (hypotheses explicit): these are the hypotheses of the implicit function theorems of §3.6 (V3.48, V3.68–V3.70, V3.80–V3.82, V3.84–V3.87, V3.94–V3.102), in place of the reading of "tame strong bundle" as the tameness of the base retraction of every compatible chart, under which they were first proved and which cannot be met (V3.104). Whether germ data in some chart (V3.13) can be moved to some compatible tame chart when the atlas consists of tame charts is open; it cannot be done by re-centring a chart of the tame atlas, since whether a filling exists in a chart depends on the chart: the trivial bundle with a one-chart tame atlas has sc-Fredholm sections with tame germ data in compatible charts and no germ data in the chart of the atlas (Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–353). The text builds the tame chart into Definition 3.6.3 (preprint 3.50), and so do the theorems. Since the switch to the text's germ reading (phase 2) the three notions carry the text's germ data (V3.13, V3.45); the earlier whole-chart forms are IsScFredholmGermTameWholeChart, IsGoodPositionGermTameWholeChart, IsScFredholmSectionTameWholeChart, and the non-vacuity witnesses satisfy both readings (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 304, 330). For Definition 3.6.6 (preprint 3.53) the comparison is that of V3.47. Formerly "restated", for the whole-chart reading (round-trip item V3.103).

In the setting of V3.91, if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (V3.103) and $s_1, \dots, s_n$ are sc⁺-sections, then $F(r, x) = f(x) + \sum_i r_is_i(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $\pi^P$ with tame germ data. On the way: the product chart $(r \mapsto r - r_0) \times c$ of a strong bundle chart $c$ of $P$ (V3.92) has the base retraction $1 \times r$ on $\mathbb R^n \times U$, which is tame when $r$ is ($\mathbb R^n$ carries the identity retraction of the whole space, so $d(a, u) = d_C(u)$, and the minimal subspaces and tangent spaces are products); so $\tilde f(r, x) = f(x)$ has germ data at every smooth $(r_0, x)$ in the tame product chart, and V3.105 adds $\tilde s$. *Book: Theorem 3.1.21 (preprint 3.18), p. 100 (preprint p. 74) (for a tame strong bundle). Hidden hypotheses: none. Definition 4.1.1 (preprint 4.1), corner charts and corner structures

to confirmA corner chart is a chart onto a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant in a finite-dimensional space with the constant structure; a corner structure is an equivalent atlas of corner charts, of possibly varying dimension, and makes $X$ tame.

HWZ §4.1, Definition 4.1.1 (preprint 4.1), p. 175 (preprint p. 147)

An M-polyfold $X$ has a compatible smooth manifold structure with boundary with corners if it admits an atlas of sc-smoothly compatible charts $(V, \varphi, (U, C, \mathbb R^n))$, $\varphi : V \to U$ an sc-diffeomorphism from an open $V \subseteq X$ onto a relatively open subset $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$ in $\mathbb R^n$ (or in a finite-dimensional vector space).

Verified edition V4.1

A chart of $X$ is a corner chart if its local model is $(U, C, V)$ with $V$ a finite-dimensional real normed space carrying the constant sc-structure, $C$ a partial quadrant in $V$, $U$ relatively open in $C$, and the identity retraction. $X$ has a corner structure if it has an atlas of corner charts equivalent to its atlas; equivalently, every point of $X$ lies in a corner chart that is a chart of the M-polyfold structure. The dimension of $V$ may vary from chart to chart. The model of a corner chart is a tame retract and an sc⁺-retract, and an M-polyfold with a corner structure is tame. Book: Definition 4.1.1 (preprint 4.1), p. 175 (preprint p. 147). Hidden hypotheses: "sc-smoothly compatible charts" with "$\varphi$ an sc-diffeomorphism" is read as compatibility with the atlas of $X$ (equivalence of atlases, as for tameness). Deviation (restated): the classical manifold structure with corners is represented by the atlas of corner charts; local constancy of the dimension is neither stated by the text nor formalized.

HWZ §4.1, Remark 4.1.3 (preprint 4.3), p. 176 (preprint p. 148)

If $X_0 = X_\infty$, $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ has the inverse $1_1^0$, which is always sc-smooth; so if $1_0^1$ is sc-smooth it is an sc-diffeomorphism. It is possible that $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds although the underlying sets agree. A finite-dimensional space with the constant structure has $X = X^1$.

Verified edition V4.6

The inclusion $1_1^0 : X^1 \to X$ is always sc-smooth; in the charts $(V_1, \varphi, (O_1, C_1, E^1))$ and $\varphi$ it is the sc-operator $\iota : E^1 \to E$. If every point of $X$ lies in $X_1$ and $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ is sc-smooth, then $1_0^1$ is an sc-diffeomorphism with inverse $1_1^0$. For a finite-dimensional $V$ with the constant structure, $V^1 = V$ as sc-Banach spaces, the lift $V \to V^1$ is the identity, and every sc-smooth retract in $V$ is an sc⁺-retract. The levels of $X^1$ are those of $X$ shifted by one, as sets: $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$. The example: there is an M-polyfold all of whose points are smooth ($X_0 = X_\infty$) for which $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ is not sc-smooth, so $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds. It is a retract $O \subseteq \mathbb R \oplus X$, $X$ the weighted sequence space of V1.13 ($|x|_m = \sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$), with a single chart: the image of $r(t, z) = (t, L(t)z)$, $L(t)$ the projection onto $\cos\theta\,e_{n_k} + \sin\theta\,e_{n_{k+1}}$ ($n_k = 2^k$), the angle $\theta$ turning from $0$ to $\pi/2$ with flat ends while $t$ runs through $[1/(k+2), 1/(k+1)]$, and $L(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$. Its points are smooth, and the lift $O \to E_1$ is discontinuous at $0$, so $O$ is not an sc⁺-retract (Proposition 4.1.8 (preprint 4.8)). The sc-smoothness of $r$ comes from a criterion proved for it: for level operators $L(p)_m : Z_m \to W_m$ depending on a finite-dimensional parameter $p$, compatible with the inclusions, with $(p, z) \mapsto L(p)_mz$ continuous and $p \mapsto L(p)_m$ of class $C^\infty$ as a map into the operators $Z_{m+1} \to W_m$ (one level of loss), $(p, z) \mapsto L(p)z$ is sc-smooth. Book: Remark 4.1.3 (preprint 4.3), p. 176 (preprint p. 148). Hidden hypotheses: $1_0^1$ is defined on $X_1$ (the text: when $X_0 = X_\infty$). Deviation (stronger): the sc-diffeomorphism clause needs only $X = X_1$, not $X_0 = X_\infty$; "$X^1 \ne X$ is possible" has an example, which the text does not give, and in it $X$ and $X^1$ even have different topologies on the same set. "$X^1 \ne X$" is read as "$1_0^1$ is not sc-smooth", equivalently "the identity is not an sc-diffeomorphism". An example needs a retraction that loses a level in its first derivative, as the splicings of HWZ do (a retraction with $C^1$ level maps gives none: an argument, not formalized), so its sc-smoothness does not follow from Proposition 1.2.4 (preprint 1.19). "$(X^1)_m = X_{m+1} = X_i$" misprints $X_0$; the topologies of the iterated levels agree (Polyfold.MPolyfold.shiftLevelHomeomorph; gap G.6, closed) (Findings, items 5, 125, 140–146). Formerly "narrower", for the missing example (gap G.31, now closed).

There are an sc-Banach space $E$, the identity retraction of $E$ onto $O = E$ (with $C = E$), vector fields $A$, $B$ on $(O, C, E)$ and a point $x \in O_2$ with $[A, B](x) \notin E_1$; so the statement "$[A, B](x) \in E_1$ for every local model, all vector fields $A$, $B$ and all $x \in O_2$" does not hold. Every sc-operator $E^1 \to E$ is a vector field on $(E, E, E)$, and the bracket of two of them is the commutator $S_0T_1 - T_0S_1$. The example: $E$ the weighted sequence space of V1.13 ($|x|_m = \sup_k(k + 1)^m|x_k|$), $(Sx)_k = (-1)^k(k + 1)x_k$, $(Tx)_k = (k + 1)x_{k+1}$, $x_k = (k + 1)^{-3}$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): both sentences, read as $[A, B](x) \in E_1$, do not hold as we read them: $[S, T]x = ((-1)^k(k + 1)(2k + 3)x_{k+1})_k$, and for this $x$ the level-$1$ coordinates have absolute value $P^3 + P^2 \ge 1/4$, $P = (k + 1)/(k + 2)$, so they do not tend to $0$ (here $T_xO = E_0$, so $(T_xO)_1 = E_1$). Read as "a tangent vector at the point $x$ of level $1$ of $X^1$", that is $x \in O_{m+2}$ gives $[A, B](x) \in E_m$, the sentence is V4.72, and Proposition 4.4.5 is not affected. For sc-smooth vector fields $A$, $B$ on the M-polyfold $X$, the Lie bracket $[A, B] : X^2 \to TX$, $X^2 = (X^1)^1$, is the tangent vector at $x$ represented by $[A_\varphi, B_\varphi](\varphi(x))$ in a chart $\varphi$ chosen around $x$. In every chart $\psi$ around $x$, $T\psi([A, B](x)) = (\psi(x), [A_\psi, B_\psi](\psi(x)))$, so $[A, B]$ depends neither on the chart nor on the retraction chosen for its model; $p([A, B](x)) = x$; and $[A, B]$ is continuous and sc-smooth from $X^2$ to $TX$. Book: Proposition 4.4.5 (preprint 4.26), p. 196 (preprint p. 167), with the proof in §§4.5.1–4.5.2, pp. 200–202: the bracket, defined in local coordinates by the usual formula, is an sc-smooth section of $TX|X^2 \to X^2$, the pull-back of $TX \to X^1$ by the inclusion $X^2 \to X^1$ (the preprint and 2017 texts quote it from another paper, as a vector field on $X^1$). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): "an sc-smooth section of $TX|X^2 \to X^2$" is read as an sc-smooth map $X^2 \to TX$ that covers the inclusion $X^2 \to X^1$; the pull-back bundle itself is not built (gap G.92). The earlier statement, a vector field on $X^1$, would through $\Phi$ (V4.78) put $[A, B](x)$ in $E_1$ for $x \in X_2$, which the example of V4.73 excludes; as we read it, it does not hold, and the 2021 statement does. With V4.72, V4.75 and V4.77 this closes gap G.38 (Findings, item 161). Proof: in the chart $(\psi^1)^1$ of $X^2$ and the tangent chart $T\psi$, $[A, B]$ reads $z \mapsto (z, [A_\psi, B_\psi](z))$, sc-smooth by V4.72; the chart does not matter by V4.75.

Let $X$ be an M-polyfold, $X^i$ its $i$-th lift ($X^0 = X$, $X^{i+1} = (X^i)^1$), and $\Phi_i : T(X^i) \to (TX)^i$, $J_i : (X^1)^i \to (X^i)^1$ the sc-diffeomorphisms of Proposition 2.3.17 for every $i$. For an sc-smooth vector field $A$ on $X$ put $A^{(0)} = A$ and $A^{(i+1)} = (A^{(i)})^{(1)}$, the index raise of V4.78 on $X^i$. Then for every $i \ge 0$: $A^{(i)}$ is an sc-smooth vector field on $X^i$, a section of $T(X^i) \to X^{i+1}$; it is $A$, in that its image under the inclusion $T(X^i) \to TX$ at $x \in X^{i+1}$ is $A(x)$; and $\Phi_i \circ A^{(i)} \circ J_i$ is the $i$-th index raise $(X^1)^i \to (TX)^i$ of $A : X^1 \to TX$. HWZ §5.1, preprint p. 169

"The fibers $Y_x := P^{-1}(x)$ have the structure of Banach spaces"; $|h|_1$ is the norm of the fibre component in Lemma 5.1.2 (preprint 5.2).

Verified edition V5.2

The points of the fibre $P^{-1}(x)$ that lie in $Y_{0,1}$ form a linear subspace $(Y_{0,1})_x$; its zero is the point $0_x$ of $Y[1]$. In a strong bundle chart around $x$ the fibre component of $\Phi[1]$ is an injective linear map $(Y_{0,1})_x \to F_1$ onto the slice $\{h \in F_1 \mid (\varphi(x), h) \in K[1]\}$, which is closed in $F_1$, so $(Y_{0,1})_x$ is complete for $|h|_1$. The norms $|\cdot|_1$ of two charts around $x$ are comparable, with one constant, on the fibres over a neighbourhood of $x$. Book: §5.1, preprint p. 169 ("the fibers $Y_x$ have the structure of Banach spaces"; $|h|_1$ in Lemma 5.1.2 (preprint 5.2)). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the text takes the linear and Banach structure of the fibres of $Y_{0,1}$ for granted; it is constructed, and $|h|_1$ depends on the chart up to equivalence (Findings, item 1).

HWZ §5.1, Definition 5.1.1 (preprint 5.1), p. 205 (preprint p. 169)

An auxiliary norm is a continuous $N : Y_{0,1} \to \mathbb R$ such that (1) its restriction to a fibre is a complete norm; (2) if $P(w_k) \to x$ and $N(w_k) \to 0$, then $w_k \to 0_x$ in $Y_{0,1}$.

Verified edition V5.3

An auxiliary norm is a continuous $N : Y[1] \to \mathbb R$ such that (1) on every fibre $(Y_{0,1})_x$, $N$ is a norm ($N(v) = 0 \Rightarrow v = 0$, $N(tv) = |t|N(v)$, the triangle inequality) for which every Cauchy sequence converges, and (2) if $P(w_k) \to x$ in $X$ and $N(w_k) \to 0$, then $w_k \to 0_x$ in $Y[1]$. It is non-negative and homogeneous. Book: Definition 5.1.1 (preprint 5.1), p. 205 (preprint p. 169). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): "complete norm" is read as a norm on $(Y_{0,1})_x$ with complete normed space; the topology of $Y_{0,1}$ is that of $Y[1]$ (Findings, item 1).

HWZ §5.2, Definition 5.2.1 (preprint 5.4), p. 209 (preprint p. 171)

(1) $f^{-1}(0)$ compact; (2) weakly proper: moreover for every $N$ an open $U \supseteq f^{-1}(0)$ with $\{f = s\}$ compact for every sc⁺-section $s$ supported in $U$ with $N(s) \le 1$; (3) proper: moreover $\operatorname{cl}_{X_0}\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact, $N(f(x)) = \infty$ off $Y_{0,1}$. "Obviously proper implies weakly proper, which in turn implies compactness."

Verified edition V5.7

A section $f$ has a compact solution set if $f^{-1}(0)$ is compact in $X$; it is weakly proper if moreover for every auxiliary norm $N$ there is an open $U \supseteq f^{-1}(0)$ such that $\{f = s\}$ is compact for every sc⁺-section $s$ with support in $U$ and $N(s(y)) \le 1$ for all $y$; it is proper if moreover for every $N$ there is an open $U \supseteq f^{-1}(0)$ with $\operatorname{cl}_X\{x \in U \mid N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ compact, where $N(f(x)) \le 1$ includes $f(x) \in Y_{0,1}$. Verified edition V5.14

The shifted strong bundle. $P^1 : Y^1 \to X^1$ is a strong bundle over the M-polyfold $X^1$ (Definition 2.6.5 (preprint 2.51)): its total space is $Y_{1,1}$, the level $1$ of the M-polyfold $Y[0]$ with its level topology; $P^1$ is the restriction of $P$; the fibre over $x$ is $P^{-1}(x) \cap Y_{1,1}$, a linear subspace, carrying the topology of $F_1$; and the atlas consists of the index raises $\Phi^1$ of the strong bundle charts $\Phi$ of $P$ (base chart the level chart $\varphi^1$, fibre model $F^1$, retraction $R$ restricted to $U^1 \triangleleft F^1$), compatible charts having compatible index raises. Its double levels are $(Y^1)_{m,k} = Y_{m+1,k+1}$. $f^1$ is sc-Fredholm. For every sc-Fredholm section $f$ (no compactness needed), $f^1 = f|_{X_1}$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $P^1$: it is sc-smooth, regularizing, and at every smooth point of $X^1$ it has the data of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) in the index raise $\Phi^1$ of the chart $\Phi$ of a datum $(g, s)$ of $f$ there. The principal part of $f^1$ is the level-$1$ map of that of $f$; $g^1$ is a filling germ of it, including condition (3) of Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4) on level $1$, which comes from a regularity statement at the centre of every datum of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11): $v \in \ker Dr(0)$ and $Dk(0)v \in F_m$ imply $v \in E_m$, $k$ the fill defect. In a chart. The level shift $f^1$ of a basic germ $f$ on $\tilde C \oplus W$, $\tilde C$ a partial quadrant, is a basic germ on $\tilde C \oplus W^1$ with $B^1$ in place of $B$; if a principal part $k$ is conjugated to a basic germ $h$ by $\Psi$, then $k^1$ is conjugated to $h^1$ by the index raise $\Psi^1$. Hence for an sc-Fredholm section with compact solution set: the zeros in $X_1$ form a compact subset of $X_1$, and at every smooth point $x$, in the chart $\Phi$ centred at $x$ of the germ $(f, x)$ with filling germ $g$ and sc⁺-germ $s$ (the text's germ reading of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11)), the level-$1$ germ $(g - s)^1$ is conjugated to a basic germ (by the germ form of the index raise, which uses $g - s$ only near $0$) and $s^1$ is an sc⁺-germ on the shifted germ of $s$. Book: Corollary 5.2.5 (preprint 5.8), p. 213 (preprint p. 173) ("it is a priori clear that $f^i$ is sc-Fredholm", as a section of $P^i : Y^i \to X^i$). Hidden hypotheses: the bundle $Y^1 \to X^1$, which the text does not define ($Y[i]$ is defined for $i = 0, 1$ only): $Y^1 = Y_{1,1}$, the convention of $E^1$, forced by "$f^i$ is obtained by raising the index" (an sc-smooth section maps $X_1$ into $Y_{1,1}$, in general not into $Y_{1,2}$); $\tilde C$ a partial quadrant. Deviation: none; "it is a priori clear" hides condition (3) of the filling on level $1$, which does not follow from level $0$ alone (an sc-operator can be bijective on level $0$ and not onto on level $1$); it is proved for the data of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) by reducing to $g(0) = 0$ with Lemma 3.1.20 (preprint 3.17) (subtracting the section $z \mapsto \Gamma(z, -g(0))$, which leaves the fill defect unchanged) and applying Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52) in sc form. No hypothesis beyond the text's is added; tameness is not used, and the tame form (germ data in tame charts of $P^1$) is not stated (Findings, items 22, 140–146). Formerly "narrower": the bundle was not built and the filler on level $1$ not verified (gap G.41, now closed for each fixed $i$). In the text's germ reading of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) (phase 2; Findings, Chapter 3, item 333) $s^1$ is an sc⁺-germ on the shifted germ; in the whole-chart reading it was sc⁺ on all of $U^1$.

$X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions if for every $x$ and every open $U \ni x$ there is an sc-smooth $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq U$. Definition 5.5.2 (preprint 5.29) as written ("$f$ not identically zero") is a separate notion, implied by the first. A point $x$ is a bump point if every open $U \ni x$ carries an sc-smooth $f$ with $f(x) \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq U$: the first notion says that every point is a bump point, and the second follows if the bump points are dense. On an sc-Banach space $E$ (as an M-polyfold with the identity chart) the second notion makes every smooth point a bump point; on M-polyfolds built on sc-Hilbert spaces the first notion holds. Book: Definition 5.3.1 (preprint 5.9), p. 216 (preprint p. 173); Definition 5.5.2 (preprint 5.29), p. 229 (preprint p. 192). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): "$f \ne 0$" is read as $f(x) \ne 0$, the reading Proposition 5.5.3's (preprint 5.30) proof uses. Whether the weak reading implies it is open only at non-smooth points: at a smooth point of an sc-Banach space a bump that is non-zero near $x$ is translated to $x$ by a smooth vector, and translation by a non-smooth vector does not preserve the levels; that the weak reading is exactly the density of the bump points is argued, one direction formalized (Findings, items 41, 160–163).

On an sc-Banach space this is now settled at every point: a bump at one point is moved to any other by a smooth vector close to the difference, so the bump points are all points or none, and the weak and pointwise readings agree (MPolyfold.admitsBumpFunctionsWeak_iff_admitsBumpFunctions_scPolyfold; Findings, Chapter 5, item 180); for a general M-polyfold the question stays open. Updated in the fourth addendum of this page.

$\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ and the metric $\rho$

to confirm$\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ is the set of sc⁺-sections supported in $U$ with $N \le 1$; $\rho = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$ is a metric on it, not complete for the trivial bundle over $\mathbb R$, complete for $U = \emptyset$.

“not complete” read as “in general”not complete over $\mathbb R$ (an example)complete for $U = \emptyset$
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §5.3, preprint p. 174

$\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$: the $s \in \Gamma^+(P)$ with $\operatorname{supp}(s) \subseteq U$ and $N(s(x)) \le 1$ for all $x$, a metric space for $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$, not complete.

Verified edition V5.21

For an auxiliary norm $N$ and an open $U$, $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ is the set of sc⁺-sections $s$ with $\operatorname{supp} s \subseteq U$ and $N(s(x)) \le 1$ for all $x$ (the allowable sections). For two sc⁺-sections $N(s(x) - s'(x))$ is the norm of the difference in the fibre $(Y_{0,1})_x$. The uniform distance $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$ is finite ($\rho \le 2$) and, for an auxiliary norm, a metric on $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$; $\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon$ iff $N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$. For the trivial bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $N(x, v) = |v|$ and $U = \mathbb R$ the metric space is not complete; for $U = \emptyset$ (any bundle) and over a point with fibre $\mathbb R^k$ (any $U$) it is complete. Book: §5.3, preprint p. 174 ("a metric space ... not complete"). Hidden hypotheses: none for the metric. Deviation (restated): the text's "not complete" is false without a hypothesis (the cases $U = \emptyset$ and a point base) and is read as "not complete in general", proved by the example: $s_j(x) = (x, \sqrt{x^2 + 1/(j+1)^2}/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2}))$ is a $\rho$-Cauchy sequence of allowable sections whose pointwise limit has the fibre part $|x|/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2})$, not differentiable at $0$, while the fibre part of an sc⁺-section of the trivial bundle is $C^1$. Non-completeness in the text's setting ($U$ containing a non-isolated point over which $Y_{0,1} \ne 0$) is expected by the same mechanism and not formalized (Findings, items 47, 150–153).

Let $f$ be a section of a strong bundle. HWZ §6.2 (preprint §6.1), Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1), p. 239 (preprint p. 201) (with preprint pp. 200–201, 219)

For an sc-Fredholm section $f$ and a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x) = \{(f - s)'(x) + a \mid a : T_xX \to Y_x$ an sc⁺-operator$\}$, where $s$ is a local sc⁺-section with $s(x) = f(x)$, made in a strong bundle chart as $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$. Its members differ by sc⁺-operators and are sc-Fredholm of one index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$; §6.6 (preprint §6.5) adds that $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex (preprint p. 219).

Verified edition V6.1

At a chart point $p = (c, z)$ of a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is the set of operators $(f + s)'(x) + a : T_zO \to K_z$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$ and an sc⁺-operator $a$; for one such $s$ it is $(f + s)'(x)$ plus the sc⁺-operators. Two such sections give linearizations that differ by an sc⁺-operator; the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are Fredholm on level $0$, all of the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of V3.98; $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex, and it is not empty when $P$ has sc⁺-sections through the smooth points of its fibres, which bump functions give. Book: §6.2 (preprint §6.1), pp. 237–240 (preprint pp. 200–201) (the sections $s$ and the paragraph before the definition), Definition 6.2.1 (preprint 6.1), p. 239 (preprint p. 201), and preprint p. 219 (convexity); the index and Proposition 6.2.2 (preprint 6.2) are V3.98. Hidden hypotheses: an sc⁺-section through $f(x)$; the text constructs a local one in a chart, the project uses global ones (HasScPlusSectionsThrough), which exist under the standing bump functions. Deviation (restated): made in a chart point; global sections; "sc-Fredholm" is proved on level $0$, which is what the determinant lines use, and not on every level (gap G.64). HWZ §6.3 (preprint §6.2), pp. 241–243 (preprint pp. 203–204)

$\lambda(E) = \Lambda^{\max}E$ and $\lambda^(E) = (\lambda(E))^$. For $\Phi : E \to F$ between spaces of the same dimension, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi(a_n)$, nontrivial iff $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, with $\lambda(\Psi \circ \Phi) = \lambda(\Psi) \circ \lambda(\Phi)$; $\lambda^(\Phi)$ is the dual of $\lambda(\Phi)$. The dual vector $v^$ of $v \ne 0$ in a line is fixed by $v^*(v) = 1$ (preprint p. 204).

Verified edition V6.2

$\lambda(E)$ is the top exterior power of a finite-dimensional real space and $\lambda^(E)$ its dual, both lines; a change of basis multiplies the wedge by the determinant, also in one block of a two-block wedge, and adding to one block vectors of the span of the other does not change the wedge. For $v \ne 0$ in a line, $v^$ is the functional with $v^(v) = 1$. For $\dim E = \dim F$, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi a_n$, with $\lambda(\Psi\Phi) = \lambda(\Psi)\lambda(\Phi)$, nonzero iff $\Phi$ is bijective; $\lambda^(\Phi)$ is its dual. Book: §6.3 (preprint §6.2), pp. 241–243 (preprint pp. 203–204). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none.

A good left-projection for a Fredholm $T : E \to F$ is a bounded projection $P : F \to F$ with (1) $\dim F/R(P) < \infty$ and (2) $R(P \circ T) = R(P)$; $\Pi_T$ is their set. HWZ §6.6 (preprint §6.5), Definition 6.6.2 (preprint 6.27), p. 263 (preprint pp. 219–220)

An orientation of $(f, x)$, $x$ smooth, is a choice of one of the two orientations of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$. The objects of a category are the sets $\mathrm{Or}^f_x = \{o_x, -o_x\}$; for smooth $x$, $y$ in the same path component the morphisms are the two bijections $\pm o_x \mapsto \pm o_y$ and $\pm o_x \mapsto \mp o_y$.

Verified edition V6.31

At a chart point, $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ is the pull-back of $\mathrm{DET}(T_zO, K_z)$ to $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ is the set of its orientations, with exactly two elements; for each $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $o \mapsto o(L)$ is a bijection onto the two orientations of $\det(L)$. Between two two-element sets there are bijections, and one value determines a bijection. Book: Definition 6.6.2 (preprint 6.27), p. 263 (preprint pp. 219–220). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): made in a chart point (V6.53 compares charts); the category $\mathcal O_f$ is read through its objects, with bijections as morphisms, and $\{o_x, -o_x\}$ as "exactly two elements" (Findings, item 44).

For a path $\varphi$ and $t_0 \in [0, 1]$ one chooses an orientable neighbourhood $U(\varphi(t_0))$ and an open interval $I(t_0)$ on which orientations propagate; using the compactness of $[0, 1]$ and a finite covering, $o_0$ is transported to $o_1$; "by a covering argument" $\varphi_*$ depends only on $[\varphi]$, and the uniqueness of $\Gamma_f$ is called obvious.

From local data (good open sets covering $X_\infty$ and push-forwards along paths in a good set, compatible with concatenation and independent of the good set) the transport along an sc-smooth path is the composite of the push-forwards along its $2^N$ dyadic pieces, for any $N$ at which every piece lies in a good set (such $N$ exist by the Lebesgue number lemma). It is the push-forward on a path in a good set, homotopy invariant, compatible with concatenation and reparametrization, the identity on constant paths, and the only family with these properties. narrower

to confirmFor a proper $f$ in general position at its zeros, $S$ is a compact manifold with boundary with corners, and the tangent orientations $o_x$ of $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ vary continuously along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart.

the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §6.6 (preprint §6.5), Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41) and its proof, preprint p. 229; the paragraph after it, pp. 274–276 (preprint pp. 229–230)

Over a tame $X$, for a proper sc-Fredholm section $f$ with $(f, x)$ in general position to $\partial X$ at every zero and an orientation $o^f$ of $f$, the solution set $S = f^{-1}(0)$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners with a natural orientation. Proof: $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ is oriented by $o^f_x$ since $f'(x)$ is onto, and the local prolongation of this orientation on $S$ is the Fredholm one. For $f$ not generic, a small perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set orients $S_{f+s}$.

Verified edition V6.61

Over a tame $X$, for a proper sc-Fredholm section $f$ with tame germ data in general position (Definition 5.3.9 (preprint 5.17)) at every zero, the solution set $S$ is compact, a smooth submanifold in general position with the induced structure of a tame manifold with boundary with corners (the conclusions of Theorem 5.3.10 (preprint 5.18)), and $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$, read in a chart. At a zero, $f'(x)$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ and is onto, so an element $o_x$ of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ gives a ray of $\det f'(x) \cong \lambda(\ker f'(x)) = \lambda(T_xS)$, the tangent orientation. For an orientation $o$ of $f$ (Definition 6.6.16 (preprint 6.40)) and every sc-smooth path $\gamma$ of zeros in an orientable neighbourhood $V \subseteq U$, the kernels $\ker f'(\gamma_q)$ form a continuous family of subspaces, and the tangent orientations of $o$ form an orientation of its line bundle. The Fredholm side is the push-forward for the datum $S = 0$, $k = 0$, which along a path of zeros is the continuation between tangent orientations. Book: Theorem 6.6.18 (preprint 6.41) and its proof, preprint p. 229; the paragraph after it on $S_{f+s}$, pp. 274–276 (preprint pp. 229–230). Hidden hypotheses: tame germ data (the standing hypothesis of Chapter 5); the orientation $o$ exists iff $f$ is orientable (V6.60). "Proper" is the text's hypothesis (StrongBundle.IsProper); the proof uses only the compactness of $S$, which for sc-Fredholm sections is equivalent to it (V5.10). Deviation (narrower): "a natural orientation" is read as the tangent orientations with their continuity along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart, and "the local prolongation of the orientation on $S$ is the Fredholm one" as the identity of continuation and push-forward along such paths. Not formalized: an orientation of $S$ as an abstract manifold (gap G.67), the compatibility of the tangent orientations read in two charts at one point (gap G.68), and the perturbation paragraph after the theorem, with $S_{f+s}$ and $\mathrm{Lin}(f + s, x) = \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ (gap G.69) (Findings, items 90–93).

HWZ §6.6 (preprint §6.5), Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42), p. 276 (preprint p. 230)

For an oriented $(f, o)$ and an sc⁺-section $s$ of $Y \to X \times [0, 1]$, $\hat f(x, t) = f(x) + s(x, t)$ has a natural orientation from $o$ and the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$: for $L = (f - t)'(x)$ oriented by $h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^$, the operator $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ on $T_{(x,t)}(X \times [0, 1])$ is oriented by $\tilde h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n \wedge e) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^$, $e$ the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$, and $\tilde L$ lies in the linearization space of $\hat f$ at $(x, t)$.

Verified edition V6.62

For Fredholm $L$, $\tilde L = L \oplus 0 : E \times \mathbb R \to F$ is Fredholm with $\ker\tilde L = \ker L \times \mathbb R$ and $\operatorname{coker}\tilde L = \operatorname{coker} L$, and $h \mapsto \tilde h$, $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes d^* \mapsto ((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_n, 0) \wedge e) \otimes d^$ with $e = (0, 1)$, is an isomorphism $\det(L) \cong \det(\tilde L)$; in local determinant charts its coordinate is $(-1)^{\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ times a continuous nowhere-zero function, and $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}\,h \mapsto \tilde h$ pulls continuous orientations back along $L \mapsto \tilde L$. In charts: for an sc-Fredholm $f$, an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R \times X$, $\hat f = \tilde f + S$ with $\tilde f(t, y) = f(y)$, and the product chart point $(t, z)$, the operator $\hat L(\sigma, v) = Lv$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(\hat f, (t, x))$ for every $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, and an orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ gives exactly one orientation $\hat o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ with $\hat o(\hat L)$ the image of $o(L)$ for every $L$; $o \mapsto \hat o$ is injective. *Book: Remark 6.6.19 (preprint 6.42), p. 276 (preprint p. 230). Hidden hypotheses: $x$ smooth and $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ nonempty (implied by bump functions, V6.1); only the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ at the one point is used. Deviation (narrower): at a point. As we read it, the literal $h \mapsto \tilde h$ is not continuous in $L$ where the parity of $\dim\operatorname{coker}L$ changes, so the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ it defines could depend on the choice of $L$; the sign $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ (the sign of V6.40) is used, which agrees with the text's map when $L$ is onto. $X \times [0, 1]$ is read as $\mathbb R \times X$ (decision D2), with the parameter first, so $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ is conjugated by the swap of the factors. That $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.6.16 (preprint 6.40), built from an orientation of $f$, is not formalized (gap G.66) (Findings, items 95–97).

There exists a Hausdorff topology on $O_f$ with (1): $\pi_f : O_f \to X_\infty$ is a local homeomorphism. "In view of Proposition 6.6.3 and Theorem 6.6.11" the easy proof is left to the reader.

Let $L$ be local transport data for the sets $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ (good open sets covering $X_\infty$ with push-forwards, V6.56). A continuous orientation over an open $U$ is a family $y \mapsto o_y$ carried along by the transport of $L$ along every sc-smooth path in $U$. The topology $\mathcal T_L$ on $O_f$: $W$ is open iff $\{y \in U_\infty : (y, o_y) \in W\}$ is open in $X_\infty$ for every continuous orientation $o$ over an open $U$. For every $L$: two continuous orientations agree near a smooth point iff they agree at it; the sets $\{(y, o_y) : y \in U_\infty\}$ are open, $y \mapsto (y, o_y)$ is continuous on $U_\infty$ and $\pi_f$ is continuous; every point of $O_f$ lies on a continuous orientation over an open set inside a good set of $L$; $\pi_f$ restricted to $\{(y, o_y) : y \in U_\infty\}$ is a homeomorphism onto $U_\infty$, so (1) $\pi_f$ is a local homeomorphism; and $\mathcal T_L$ is Hausdorff. Book: Theorem 6.6.17, p. 275, new in the 2021 edition: "a uniquely defined Hausdorff topology" with (1); the text leaves the proof to the reader, in view of Proposition 6.6.3 and Theorem 6.6.11 (preprint 6.28, 6.35). Hidden hypotheses: none (every $L$). Deviation (not in the book): the construction of the topology. Points over different smooth points are separated through $\pi_f$ ($X_\infty$ is metrizable); the two points over one $y$ lie on two continuous orientations that differ at $y$, hence near $y$ (Findings, item 118).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.1.1 (2017: 7.1) and the paragraph after it, pp. 287–288 (2017 pp. 225–226)

A groupoid $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is a small category consisting of the set $X$ of objects, denoted by $x$, and the set $\mathbf X$ of morphisms (arrows), which are assumed to be invertible, and the following five structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$. (1) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ assign to every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ in $\mathbf X$ its source $s(\varphi) = x$ and its target $t(\varphi) = y$. (2) The associative multiplication (composition) map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $m(\varphi, \psi) = \varphi \circ \psi$, is defined on the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X = \{(\varphi, \psi) \in \mathbf X \times \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) = t(\psi)\}$, so that if $\psi : x \to z$ and $\varphi : z \to y$, then $\varphi \circ \psi : x \to y$. (3) For every object $x \in X$ there exists the unit morphism $1_x : x \to x$ in $\mathbf X$, a 2-sided unit for the composition: $\varphi \circ 1_x = \varphi$ and $1_x \circ \psi = \psi$ for all $\varphi, \psi \in \mathbf X$ satisfying $s(\varphi) = x = t(\psi)$; these define the unit map $u : X \to \mathbf X$, $u(x) = 1_x$. (4) For every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ there exists the inverse morphism $\varphi^{-1} : y \to x$, a 2-sided inverse: $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = 1_y$ and $\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = 1_x$; these define the inverse map $\iota : \mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $\iota(\varphi) = \varphi^{-1}$.

After the definition: $\mathrm{mor}(x, y) \subset \mathbf X$ is the set of all morphisms $\varphi$ with $s(\varphi) = x$ and $t(\varphi) = y$. The orbit space $|X| = X/\sim$ is the quotient of the set of objects by the equivalence relation $x \sim y$ if and only if there exists a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; the class of $x$ is $|x| := \{y \in X \mid y \sim x\}$, and $\pi : X \to |X|$, $\pi(x) = |x|$, is the quotient map.

Verified edition V7.1

A groupoid is a set of objects and a set of invertible morphisms with source, target, an associative composition on composable pairs, units and inverses; $|X|$ is the quotient by $x \sim y$ iff there is a morphism $x \to y$, with projection $\pi$. Book: Definition 7.1.1 (2017: 7.1) and the paragraph after it, pp. 287–288 (2017 pp. 225–226). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): a structure of maps on types, the laws required on composable pairs and the composition total with a junk value; the saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$ of Definition 7.1.21 (2017: 7.10) is defined here; the bridge to Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Groupoid is added so that "full" and "faithful" are Mathlib's (Findings, item 1).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3), pp. 288 ff. (2017 pp. 226–227)

An ep-groupoid $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ consists of a groupoid equipped with M-polyfold structures on the object set $X$ and the morphism set $\mathbf X$ having the following properties. (1) (étale) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms. (2) The unit map $u$ and the inverse map $\iota$ are sc-smooth. (3) (Properness) Every point $x \in X$ possesses an open neighborhood $V(x)$ of $x$ in $X$ such that the map $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper. Since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ is in a natural way an M-polyfold in view of Lemma 2.8 in [38], and we require (4) the multiplication map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$ is sc-smooth. In particular, all the structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$ are sc-smooth maps.

Verified edition V7.3

An ep-groupoid is a groupoid with M-polyfold structures on objects and morphisms such that (1) $s, t$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, (2) $u$ and $\iota$ are sc-smooth, (3) every $x$ has an open $V(x)$ with $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V(x)) \to X$ proper, (4) $m$ is sc-smooth on the fibred product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$; all structure maps are then sc-smooth. Book: Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3), pp. 288 ff. (2017 pp. 226–227). Hidden hypotheses: Obj and Mor Hausdorff and paracompact (the project's M-polyfolds). Deviation (restated): (3) existential per point, with Mathlib's proper maps; the universal form "for every open $V \ni x$" fails (the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$), and every smaller open neighbourhood works. (4) on the sub-M-polyfold of Part I's Proposition 2.5.20 (2017: 2.15), the book's statement of the text's citation "Lemma 2.8 in [38]" (an external reference, not a misprint); the proofs use the equivalent sheet form (Findings, items 3, 4, 103).

Definition 7.1.3 (3) (2017: 7.3) asks that $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ be proper. The proofs use this in the form: if $s(\varphi_k) \in \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))$ and $t(\varphi_k)$ converges in $X$, then, "after perhaps taking a subsequence", $(\varphi_k)$ converges in $\mathbf X$ (Proposition 7.1.10 (2017: 7.3), 2017 p. 230; Lemma 7.1.11 (2017: 7.1), p. 292 (2017 p. 230); Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7), p. 307 (2017 p. 238); Proposition 7.3.9 (2017: 7.11), 2017 p. 248; Lemma 7.6.2 (2017: 7.8), 2017 p. 254), or through the compactness of preimages of compact sets (Proposition 7.5.9 (2017: 7.13), p. 342 (2017 p. 251)). After Definition 7.1.4 (2017: 7.4) (p. 289 (2017 p. 227)) the text points out that this properness differs from that of classical Lie groupoids, which requires $(s, t) : \mathbf X \to X \times X$ to be proper, a requirement too weak for some of the constructions.

Verified edition V7.4

For the restriction of $t$ to a closed $s^{-1}(Q)$ between metrizable spaces, properness is equivalent to: every sequence with convergent targets has a convergent subsequence; it passes to smaller closures, and proper restrictions have closed images and finite fibres. Book: the notion of Definition 7.1.3 (3) (2017: 7.3), 2017 p. 227, used in sequential form in Proposition 7.1.10 (2017: 7.3), Lemma 7.1.11 (2017: 7.1) (p. 292 (2017 p. 230)), Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7) (p. 307 (2017 p. 238)), Proposition 7.3.9 (2017: 7.11) (2017 p. 248), Proposition 7.5.9 (2017: 7.13) (p. 342 (2017 p. 251)) and Lemma 7.6.2 (2017: 7.8) (2017 p. 254). HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.1.4 (2017: 7.4) and the paragraph before it, 2017 p. 227

Since $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ of an ep-groupoid has an extension to a local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ satisfying $\hat\varphi(x) = y$, defined as follows: there exist open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi) \subset \mathbf X$ and $U(x), U(y) \subset X$ such that $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(x)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, and $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} : U(x) \to U(y)$. In the case that $\varphi$ is smooth, i.e. $\varphi \in \mathbf X_\infty$, there is an associated sc-isomorphism $T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}X$ defined by $T\varphi := T\hat\varphi(x)$; more generally $T\hat\varphi : TU(s(\varphi)) \to TU(t(\varphi))$. $T\varphi$ can be defined for $\varphi$ on level at least $1$ and gives a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$; only in the case that $\varphi$ is smooth is $T\varphi$ an sc-operator. Definition 7.1.4 (2017: 7.4): associated to a smooth morphism $\varphi$ we have the so-called associated local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$, as well as its tangent $T\varphi$.

HWZ §7.1, pp. 289–291 (2017 pp. 227–228)

The M-polyfolds $X$ and $\mathbf X$ are equipped with the filtrations $X = X_0 \supset X_1 \supset X_2 \supset \dots \supset X_\infty = \bigcap_{k \ge 0} X_k$ and similarly for $\mathbf X$; $X_\infty$ is dense in every $X_k$. For $x$ in the M-polyfold $X$, $ml(x) \in \mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$ is the largest non-negative integer $m$, or $\infty$, such that $x \in X_m$. Since the source and target maps are local sc-diffeomorphisms and therefore preserve the levels, $ml(x) = ml(y) = ml(\varphi)$ for every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; consequently the filtration of $X$ induces the filtration $|X| = |X_0| \supset |X_1| \supset \dots \supset |X_\infty| = \bigcap_{k \ge 0}|X_k|$ of the orbit space. The degeneracy indices $d_X : X \to \mathbb N$ and $d_{\mathbf X} : \mathbf X \to \mathbb N$ are invariant under local sc-diffeomorphisms (Proposition 2.4.4 (2017: 2.7)), so $d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t(\varphi))$ for every morphism $\varphi$; in particular $d_X(x) = d_X(x')$ if $x \sim x'$.

Verified edition V7.6

$s$ and $t$ preserve the levels, so $ml(x) = ml(\varphi) = ml(y)$ for $\varphi : x \to y$; $d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t(\varphi))$, so $d_X$ is constant on classes; $|X_k| = \pi(X_k)$. Book: pp. 289–291 (2017 pp. 227–228), with Part I's Proposition 2.4.4 (2017: 2.7). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the set $|X_\infty|$ and $|X_\infty| = \bigcap_k |X_k|$ are not stated (gap G.72); the density of $X_\infty$ in every $X_k$, stated on 2017 p. 227 without proof, is not formalized and is not in Part I for M-polyfolds (gap G.73; Findings, items 6, 112, 116).

HWZ §7.1, after Definition 7.1.7 (2017: 7.7), pp. 290 ff. (2017 pp. 228–229)

It is sufficient to require that the functor $f$ is sc-smooth between the object spaces $X \to Y$, because the sc-smoothness of $f : \mathbf X \to \mathbf Y$ follows from the properties of the source map $s : \mathbf X \to X$: given $\varphi \in \mathbf X$ and $f(\varphi) = \psi \in \mathbf Y$ there exist open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi)$, $\mathbf U(\psi)$, $U(s(\varphi))$ and $U(s(\psi))$ satisfying $f(U(s(\varphi))) \subset U(s(\psi))$ and $f(\mathbf U(\varphi)) \subset \mathbf U(\psi)$; moreover, $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(s(\varphi))$ and $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(s(\psi))$ are sc-diffeomorphisms. Therefore the claim follows from the formula $f(\gamma) = (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(f(s(\gamma)))$ for all $\gamma \in \mathbf U(\varphi)$.

Verified edition V7.10

The text claims that a functor sc-smooth on objects is sc-smooth on morphisms, by $f(\gamma) = (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(f(s(\gamma)))$ on $\mathbf U(\varphi)$. Book: pp. 290–292 (2017 pp. 228–229). Hidden hypotheses: the argument needs $f(\mathbf U(\varphi)) \subseteq \mathbf U(\psi)$, i.e. continuity of $f$ on morphisms. Deviation (does not hold as we read it): a functor of the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action on $\mathbb R$, the identity on objects, is sc-smooth on objects and not continuous on morphisms; for functors continuous on morphisms the claim is proved, with a sheet $\mathbf U(\psi)$ at $\psi = f(\varphi)$ and $\mathbf U(\varphi) = f^{-1}(\mathbf U(\psi))$ (Findings, items 9, 104).

Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $x$ an object with the isotropy group $G = G_x$. Then for every open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ we find an open neighborhood $U \subset V$ of $x$, a group homomorphism $\Phi : G \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$, $g \mapsto \Phi(g)$, and an sc-smooth map $\Gamma : G \times U \to \mathbf X$ such that the following holds. (1) $\Gamma(g, x) = g$. (2) $s(\Gamma(g, y)) = y$ and $t(\Gamma(g, y)) = \Phi(g)(y)$ for all $y \in U$ and $g \in G$. (3) If $h : y \to z$ is a morphism between points in $U$, then there exists a unique element $g \in G$ satisfying $\Gamma(g, y) = h$, i.e., $\Gamma : G \times U \to \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in U\}$ is a bijection. (After the theorem: $(\Phi, \Gamma)$ are the data for the natural representation of $G_x$, and $g \ast y = \Phi(g)(y)$.)

HWZ §7.1, Proposition 7.1.15 (2017: 7.5), pp. 297–298 (2017 pp. 233–234) (proof pp. 297–305 (2017 pp. 234–236))

Let $(X, \mathbf X)$ be an ep-groupoid and $Y = \{y_1, \dots, y_k\}$ a finite set of distinct objects in $X$ which are mutually isomorphic. Denote by $\mathbf Y = (Y, \mathbf Y)$ the full subcategory associated with $Y$, whose morphism set is $\mathbf Y$. Then, given a neighborhood $V$ of $Y$ in $X$, there exists a functor $f$, which associates with the objects $y$ in $Y$ mutually disjoint connected open neighborhoods $U(y)$ contained in $V$, and with a morphism $\psi : y \to y'$ in $\mathbf Y$ an sc-diffeomorphism $f(\psi) : U(y) \to U(y')$. The set of morphisms $\mathbf U = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in \bigcup_{y \in Y}U(y)\}$ decomposes into the union of connected components $\mathbf U(\psi)$, $\psi \in \mathbf Y$, and the following holds true. (1) The isotropy group $G_y$ for $y \in Y$ acts via the natural action on $U(y)$. (2) For $\psi \in \mathbf Y$ the maps $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms. (3) If $\psi : y \to y'$ and $z \in U(y)$, then $f(\psi)(z) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(z)$.

Verified edition V7.25

For finitely many mutually isomorphic objects $Y$ and a neighbourhood $V$ of $Y$ there is a functor $f$ assigning disjoint connected open $U(y) \subseteq V$ and sc-diffeomorphisms $f(\psi) : U(y) \to U(y')$, such that the morphisms between the $U(y)$ split into components $\mathbf U(\psi)$ with (1) the natural action of $G_y$ on $U(y)$, (2) $s, t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ sc-diffeomorphisms, (3) $f(\psi) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}$. Book: Proposition 7.1.15 (2017: 7.5), pp. 297–304 (2017 pp. 233–236). Hidden hypotheses: none. HWZ §7.1, Proposition 7.1.19 (2017: 7.6), p. 304 (2017 p. 236) (proof pp. 299–306 (2017 pp. 236–237))

Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $z \in |X|$. We fix $x \in X$ satisfying $z = |x|$, denote the isotropy group of $x$ by $G_x$ and take an open neighborhood $U(x)$ of $x$ on which we have the natural $G_x$-action $\Phi$, which we abbreviate as $g \ast y := \Phi(g)(y)$ for $g \in G_x$ and $y \in U(x)$. Then the map $\tau : G_x\backslash U(x) \to |U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$, $G_x \ast y \mapsto |y|$, is a homeomorphism. In other words, the obvious functor $G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$, which on the object level is the inclusion map and on the morphism level the map $(g, y) \mapsto \Gamma(g, y)$, is a fully faithful functor, which on the orbit spaces defines a homeomorphism between the orbit spaces $|U(x)|_{G_x \ltimes U(x)} = G_x\backslash U(x)$ and $|U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$.

HWZ §7.1, 2017 p. 238

The set of morphisms $\mathbf A = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in A\}$ has in a natural way the structure of an M-polyfold. For $\varphi \in \mathbf A$ and $a = s(\varphi)$ choose open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi) \subset \mathbf X$ and $U(a) \subset X$ such that $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(a)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism and (shrinking) an sc-smooth retraction $r : U(a) \to U(a)$ with $r(U(a)) = U(a) \cap A$; then $\mathbf r : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to \mathbf U(\varphi)$, $\mathbf r(\psi) = (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} \circ r \circ s(\psi)$, is an sc-smooth retraction, and since $A$ is saturated, $\mathbf r(\mathbf U(\varphi)) = \mathbf U(\varphi) \cap \mathbf A$. This shows that $\mathbf A$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X$, and the properties listed for $A$ also hold for $\mathbf A$.

HWZ §7.1, Proposition 7.1.22 (2017: 7.7) and the argument before it, pp. 306–308 (2017 pp. 238–239)

Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $A$ a saturated subset of the object space $X$ such that $A$ is also a sub-M-polyfold. Then the full subcategory associated with $A$, also denoted by $A$, has in a natural way the structure of an ep-groupoid. In particular, $A$ and $\mathbf A = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi), t(\varphi) \in A\}$ are sub-M-polyfolds of $X$ and $\mathbf X$, respectively, and all the structure maps are the restrictions of the structure maps of $X$ and $\mathbf X$, respectively.
