HWZ §7.2, Definition 7.2.1 (2017: 7.11) and the sentences after it, 2017 p. 239

An ep-groupoid $X$ is said to be effective provided for every $x \in X$ and $g \in G_x \setminus \{1_x\}$, given an open neighborhood $\mathbf U(g) \subset \mathbf X$, there exists a morphism $\psi \in \mathbf U(g)$ satisfying $s(\psi) \ne t(\psi)$. An object $x \in X$ is said to be regular provided $G_x = \{1_x\}$. If $\varphi \in \mathbf X$ and $s(\varphi)$ is a regular object, the same has to be true for $t(\varphi)$. The regular part $X_{reg}$ of an ep-groupoid is the subset $X_{reg} = \{x \in X \mid G_x = \{1_x\}\}$ of the object space $X$.

Verified edition V7.33

$X$ is effective if every open neighbourhood of every $g \in G_x \setminus \{1_x\}$ contains a $\psi$ with $s(\psi) \neq t(\psi)$; $x$ is regular if $G_x = \{1_x\}$; if $s(\varphi)$ is regular, so is $t(\varphi)$. Book: Definition 7.2.1 (2017: 7.11) and the sentences after it, 2017 p. 239. Hidden hypotheses: none; satisfiable non-vacuously (Polyfold.EpGroupoid.Examples.isEffective_reflection_nonvacuous). Deviation: none (Findings, items 50, 101).

HWZ §7.2, before Definition 7.2.7 (2017: 7.12), p. 310 (2017 p. 241)

Every point $x$ of the object set possesses a suitable open neighborhood $U(x)$, which can be chosen arbitrarily small, on which $G_x$ acts by the homomorphism $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$. We say that $g \in G_x$ acts trivially if there exists an open neighborhood $U(x)$ equipped with the $G_x$-action $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$ such that $g$ belongs to the kernel of $\Phi$, i.e., $\Phi(g) = 1$. Clearly $1_x$ always acts trivially, but there might be other elements $g \in G_x$ acting trivially. Since $G_x$ is finite, we can choose $U(x)$ so small that the kernel of $\Phi$ is equal to the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$. We denote by $T_x \subset G_x$ the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$, which, as the kernel of a group homomorphism, is a normal subgroup of $G_x$.

Verified edition V7.37

$g$ acts trivially if $\Phi(g) = 1$ for some natural representation; for $U(x)$ small the kernel of $\Phi$ is the set $T_x$ of such $g$, a normal subgroup. Book: 2017 p. 241. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ with $\ker\Phi = T_x$ for every natural representation inside $N$; $g \in T_x$ iff $s = t$ near $g$; $\varphi T_x \varphi^{-1} = T_y$, which Definition 7.2.7 (2017: 7.12) needs and the text does not state. "$\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x)$" (possible misprint or extraction artefact) (Findings, item 54).

HWZ §7.2, Definition 7.2.7 (2017: 7.12), p. 310 (2017 p. 241)

The non-effective part $\mathbf X^T \subset \mathbf X$ is the subset of morphisms defined as $\mathbf X^T = \{\varphi \in T_x \subset G_x \mid x \in X\}$. The subset $\mathbf X^R$ of reduced morphisms of $\mathbf X$ is defined as follows. Two morphisms $\varphi$ and $\varphi' \in \mathbf X$ are called equivalent, $\varphi \sim \varphi'$, if the following two conditions are satisfied. (1) $s(\varphi) = s(\varphi') = x$. (2) $\varphi = \varphi' \circ g$ for some $g \in T_x$. The set $\mathbf X^R$ is the collection of all equivalence classes $[\varphi]$ of morphisms in $\mathbf X$.

$\mathbf X^T = \bigcup_x T_x$; $\varphi \sim \varphi'$ iff $s(\varphi) = s(\varphi') = x$ and $\varphi = \varphi' \circ g$ with $g \in T_x$; $\mathbf X^R$ is the set of classes. The ep-groupoid $(X, \mathbf X)$ is an ep-groupoid with paracompact orbit space if, in addition to the properties (1)–(4) of Definition 7.1.3 (2017: 7.3), it also possesses the following property (5): the orbit space $|X|$ is paracompact. HWZ §7.6.1 (2017 §7.5.1), Theorem 7.6.1 (2017: 7.5) and its proof, pp. 344–346 (2017 pp. 253–254)

Given an ep-groupoid $X$, an object $x_0 \in X$, and an open neighborhood $V \subset X$ of $x_0$. Then there exist an open neighborhood $U \subset V$ of $x_0$, a group homomorphism $\Phi : G_{x_0} \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$, $g \mapsto \Phi(g) = t_g \circ s_g^{-1}$, and an sc-smooth map $\Gamma : G_{x_0} \times U \to \mathbf X$ having the following properties: $\Gamma(g, x_0) = g$; $s(\Gamma(g, y)) = y$ and $t(\Gamma(g, y)) = \Phi(g)(y)$ for all $y \in U$ and $g \in G_{x_0}$; if $h : y \to z$ is a morphism connecting two objects $y, z \in U$, then there exists a unique $g \in G_{x_0}$ such that $\Gamma(g, y) = h$. In particular, every morphism between points in $U$ belongs to the image of the map $\Gamma$. The homomorphism $\Phi$ is called a natural representation of the stabilizer group $G_{x_0}$. (In the proof, for every $g \in G_{x_0}$ one chooses contractible open neighborhoods $N^t_g$, $N^s_g$ on which $t$ and $s$ are sc-diffeomorphisms onto some open neighborhood $U_0$ of $x_0$, the sets $N^t_g \cup N^s_g$ disjoint; $N_g := N^t_g \cap N^s_g$, $s_g := s|N_g$, $t_g := t|N_g$, and $\Gamma(g, y) = s_g^{-1}(y)$.)

Verified edition V7.62

Deviation (restated): Polyfold.EpGroupoid.theorem_7_5 is Polyfold.EpGroupoid.theorem_7_1 (V7.17); the proof starts at $U_0 := V \cap \bigcap_g s(N_g)$ so that $U \subseteq V$; the contractibility of $N^t_g$, $N^s_g$ is not needed; "$\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$" for $G_{x_0}$ (possible misprint) (Findings, item 29).

HWZ §7.6.2 (2017 §7.5.2), proof of Theorem 7.5.7 (2017: 7.4), pp. 346–347 (2017 pp. 255–256)

Consider the open covering $(|U_\lambda|)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ of $|X|$. For every $x \in X$ take an open neighborhood $V(x)$ with: (1) there exists an open neighborhood $W(x)$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action such that $V(x) \subset \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x)) \subset W(x)$ and $V(x)$ is invariant; (2) $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper; (3) there exists a $\lambda$ with $V(x) \subset U_\lambda$; (4) $(\pi^{-1}(|V(x)|) \setminus V(x)) \cap W(x) = \emptyset$. Take a locally finite refinement $(V'_i)_{i \in I}$ of $(|V(x)|)_{x \in X}$, with $V'_i \subset |V(x_i)|$, open $V''_i$ with $V''_i \subset \mathrm{cl}_{|X|}(V''_i) \subset V'_i$ and $|X| = \bigcup_i V''_i$; $U''_i = V(x_i) \cap \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$ is invariant under the $G_{x_i}$-action, with saturation $U_i = \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$. Take a continuous partition of unity $(\beta_i)$ subordinate to $(V''_i)$; $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ has support in $U''_i \subset V(x_i)$. Using the sc-smooth partitions of unity of $X$, approximate $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ by Lemma 7.6.5 (2017: 7.10) by an sc-smooth $f_i$ supported in $V(x_i)$ with $f_i \ge (\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$; average using the $G_{x_i}$-action, extend to the saturation of $V(x_i)$ and then by $0$ outside, which gives a function $h_i$ compatible with morphisms. The sum $h$ of all $h_i$ is locally finite and always bigger than $0$, and $(h_i/h)$ is the desired partition of unity for the ep-groupoid $X$.

HWZ §7.1, the remark after Definition 7.1.7, p. 291 (2017: after Definition 7.7, p. 228)

Let $f : X \to Y$ be a functor between ep-groupoids which is sc-smooth on the object M-polyfolds and continuous on the morphism spaces. HWZ §7.2, Definition 7.2.18, Remarks 7.2.19 and 7.2.20, p. 321 (new in the 2021 edition; Definition 7.4.1, p. 328, repeats it)

$X$ has the local unique continuation property (LUC) if every object $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U(x)$ with the natural $G_x$-action such that, for $g \in G_x$, $\hat g$ is the identity on $U(x)$ as soon as it is the identity on a nonempty open subset. Remark 7.2.19: there are ep-groupoids without LUC (Appendix 7.6.3). Remark 7.2.20: $U(x)$ may be taken inside any given neighbourhood $O(x)$.

Verified edition V7.80

$X$ has the local unique continuation property (LUC) if every object $x$ has a natural representation $U(x)$ such that $\Phi(g) = \mathrm{id}$ on a nonempty open subset of $U(x)$ forces $\Phi(g) = \mathrm{id}$ on $U(x)$. Under LUC every natural representation has this property, and there are such inside every open $O \ni x$. Not every ep-groupoid has LUC (V7.82). LUC holds for the trivial ep-groupoid of every M-polyfold, for every effective ep-groupoid ($\mathbf X^T$ is then the closed set of units), for $\mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$ by reflection, and for the non-effective trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action on $\mathbb R$. Book: Definition 7.2.18, Remarks 7.2.19, 7.2.20, p. 321, new in the 2021 edition; Definition 7.4.1, p. 328, repeats Definition 7.2.18. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): that the choice of $U(x)$ does not matter is proved (by V7.81, $\mathbf X^T$ is then closed, and a connectedness argument) (Findings, items 128, 144).

HWZ §7.4, the proofs of Lemma 7.4.6, Propositions 7.4.8, 7.4.10, 7.4.22 and Lemma 7.4.15, pp. 331–340 (new in the 2021 edition)

The proofs use, without stating them, facts about an M-polyfold $X$: $X_\infty$ is dense in every $X_m$ (stated on p. 289); $U(x) \cap X_\infty$ is connected for a connected open $U(x)$; tangent vectors at a point are approximated by tangent vectors at nearby smooth points; sc-smooth maps that agree near a smooth point in $X_\infty$ have the same tangent there; $(T_xX)_\infty$ is dense in $T_xX$.

Verified edition V7.86

For an M-polyfold $X$: DenseSmooth, $X_\infty$ is dense in every $X_m$; SmoothConnected, $U \cap X_\infty$ is connected in $X_\infty$ for connected open $U$; DenseSmoothTangent, $(T_xX)_\infty$ is dense in $T_xX$ for smooth $x$; TangentDeterminedSmooth, two sc-smooth maps agreeing near a smooth $y$ in $X_\infty$ have the same tangent on $T_yX$. SmoothRegular bundles the first, the second, the last and the openness of $p : TX \to X^1$. Consequences: $X_\infty$ is dense in $X$, and, if $p$ is open, a map continuous on an open $W \subseteq TX$ and the identity over a set $A \subseteq X_\infty$ is the identity over its closure in $X_\infty$. All hold for M-polyfolds on a subsingleton with every point smooth. Book: used in the proofs of Lemma 7.4.6, Propositions 7.4.8, 7.4.10, 7.4.22 and Lemma 7.4.15, pp. 331–340; the density of $X_\infty$ is stated on p. 289. Hidden hypotheses: these Part I facts, not proved in Part I for M-polyfolds. Deviation (explicit): explicit hypotheses of the §7.4 results that use them (gaps G.85, G.73, G.8) (Findings, item 134).

HWZ §7.6, Appendix 7.6.5.2, pp. 353–355 (new in the 2021 edition): the maps on $bX$ induced through sheets

With a sheet $\mathbf V$ on which $s : \mathbf V \to V$ is an sc-diffeomorphism, a class $[\varphi, \mathbf V, \theta]$ of $b\mathbf X$ is carried to the class $[s(\varphi), s(\mathbf V), s(\theta)]$ of $bX$; in the charts $\Phi$ the map becomes the sc-diffeomorphism $s : \theta \to s(\theta)$.

Verified edition V7.96

For a corner index $d$ (the degeneracy index of a tame M-polyfold, or any IsCornerIndex): a map $f$ that is a homeomorphism of an open $W$ onto an open set preserving the index carries faces to faces, face-structured neighbourhoods to face-structured neighbourhoods, and admissible triples $(y, V, \theta)$ to admissible triples, with a class independent of the chosen $W$. For an index-preserving local homeomorphism $f$, $[y, V, \theta] \mapsto [f(y), f(V), f(\theta)]$ is a well defined map $bf$ of the tame boundaries, continuous, open and a local homeomorphism; preimages of compact sets under $B$ are compact. An sc-diffeomorphism between open sets preserves the degeneracy index. Book: §7.6.5.2, pp. 353–355, new in the 2021 edition, where the maps (7.25)–(7.28) are defined through sc-diffeomorphisms of sheets. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (extra): a tool of the formalization: the topological content of those sc-diffeomorphisms (Findings, item 140).

HWZ §7.6, Theorem 7.6.9, p. 355 (new in the 2021 edition), and the characterization after it

For a tame ep-groupoid: (1) $bX$ and $b\mathbf X$ have natural metrizable topologies; (2) natural tame M-polyfold structures; (3) both maps $B$ are sc-smooth; (4) $d_X(B(p)) - 1 = d_{bX}(p)$, and likewise on $b\mathbf X$; (5) $(bX, b\mathbf X)$ with $s, t, u, \iota, m$ is a tame ep-groupoid. The topology and the M-polyfold structure are characterized by: every $U(x, V, \theta)$ is open and every $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)} : U(x, V, \theta) \to \theta$ is a homeomorphism and an sc-diffeomorphism.

Verified edition V7.98

For a tame ep-groupoid: (1) $bX$ and $b\mathbf X$ are metrizable, every $U(x, V, \theta)$ is open and every $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)}$ an open embedding, and these properties determine the topologies; (3) both maps $B$ are continuous; (4) a point of index $d$ has exactly $d$ preimages under $B$, on objects and on morphisms; (5) $s, t$ are local homeomorphisms, $u, \iota$ are continuous, $m$ is continuous on the composable pairs, $(bX, b\mathbf X)$ has the properness property of Definition 7.1.3 (3), and $B$ is a functor. The trivial ep-groupoid of the tame quadrant $[0, \infty)^n \oplus W$, $n \ge 1$, is tame, with $bX$, $b\mathbf X$ nonempty and $n$ classes over the corner. In the charts $\Phi_{(\varphi, \mathbf V, \theta)}$ and $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)}$ the map $s : U(\varphi, \mathbf V, \theta) \to U(x, V, \theta)$ becomes $s : \theta \to s(\theta)$, an sc-diffeomorphism; this gives the smoothness of $s$, and similarly of the other structure maps.

Let $A$, $B$ be tame M-polyfolds with the tame M-polyfold structures of Part I's Theorem 2.7.13 (2) on $bA$, $bB$ (Polyfold.MPolyfold.tameBoundaryPolyfold), and $f : A \to B$ sc-smooth on an open $U$. A map $g : bA \to bB$, continuous on an open $O \subseteq B^{-1}(U)$ with $B \circ g = f \circ B$ on $O$, is sc-smooth on $O$; in the charts $p \mapsto \pi(\varphi(B p))$ of $bA$ and $bB$ it reads $\pi' \circ (\varphi' \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ \iota$. Hence the lift $bf$, $[y, V, \theta] \mapsto [f(y), f(V), f(\theta)]$ (V7.96), of an sc-smooth index-preserving local homeomorphism is sc-smooth, and the lift of a local sc-diffeomorphism is a local sc-diffeomorphism: over a sheet $f : W \to V$ with inverse $\sigma$, $bf$ maps $B^{-1}(W)$ onto $B^{-1}(V)$, with an inverse that covers $\sigma$ and undoes $bf$. Book: §7.6.5.2, p. 355, new in the 2021 edition: the proof sketch of Theorem 7.6.9, which reads the structure maps in the charts $\Phi$ as sc-diffeomorphisms $s : \theta \to s(\theta)$ of faces. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (extra): a tool of the formalization; it replaces the sketch's sc-diffeomorphism of faces by the computation in the charts of $bA$, which needs only that $f$ is sc-smooth (Findings, item 146).

The sets $O \cap X_\infty$, $O$ open in some $X_{N+1}$, form a neighbourhood basis of $X_\infty$. A natural representation $U(x)$ of $x \in X_1$ with $U(x) \cap X_1$ connected in $X^1$ restricts to a natural representation of $x$ in $X^1$, the isotropy groups of $x$ in $X$ and in $X^1$ being identified; if every $U(x) \cap X_m$ is connected in $X_m$, so it is for the restriction. HWZ §8.1, (8.1)–(8.9), pp. 357–359 (2017 pp. 257–258)

The tangent of the ep-groupoid $(X, \mathbf X)$ is the pair $T(X, \mathbf X) = (TX, T\mathbf X)$ (8.1), to be equipped with the structure of an ep-groupoid with object M-polyfold $TX$ and morphism M-polyfold $T\mathbf X$. A tangent vector $(\varphi, h) \in T_\varphi\mathbf X$ is viewed as a morphism $(\varphi, h) : Ts(\varphi)(h) \to Tt(\varphi)(h)$ (8.2), so that $s_{T\mathbf X}(\varphi, h) = Ts(\varphi)(h)$ and $t_{T\mathbf X}(\varphi, h) = Tt(\varphi)(h)$ (8.3). If $s_{T\mathbf X}(\psi, k) = Ts(\psi)(k) = Tt(\varphi)(h) = t_{T\mathbf X}(\varphi, h)$ (8.4), which implies $s(\psi) = t(\varphi)$, the multiplication is $(\psi, k) \circ (\varphi, h) = (\psi \circ \varphi, Ts(\psi \circ \varphi)^{-1}(Ts(\varphi)(h))) \in T_{\varphi \circ \psi}\mathbf X$ (8.5), where $k = Ts(\psi)^{-1}(Tt(\varphi)(h))$; with the projection $\mathbf p : T\mathbf X \to \mathbf X^1$, shorter, $k \circ h = Ts(\mathbf p(k) \circ \mathbf p(h))^{-1}Ts(\mathbf p(h))(h)$ (8.6). The unit at $a \in T_xX$ is $1_a = (1_x, h_a)$ with $Ts(1_x)(h_a) = a = Tt(1_x)(h_a)$ (8.7), so $u_{T\mathbf X}(a) = (1_x, Ts(1_x)^{-1}(a))$ (8.8), and the inverse map is $\iota_{T\mathbf X}(\varphi, k) = (\varphi^{-1}, T\iota_X(\varphi)(k))$ (8.9).

Verified edition V8.1

The objects of $T(X, \mathbf X)$ are $TX$, the morphisms $T\mathbf X$; $s_T = Ts$, $t_T = Tt$ (8.3); for $Ts(k) = Tt(h)$ the composite $k \circ h$ is the vector over $p(k) \circ p(h)$ with $Ts(k \circ h) = Ts(h)$ (8.5), (8.6); $u_T(a) = (1_x, Ts(1_x)^{-1}a)$ (8.7), (8.8); $\iota_T = T\iota$ (8.9). Book: §8.1, pp. 357–359 (2017 pp. 257–258). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the composition is defined by choice and is total, with a junk value off composable pairs, as Chapter 7's composition; on composable pairs it is unique, since $Ts$ is injective on every fibre $T_\varphi\mathbf X$ (Polyfold.EpGroupoid.tangent_ext); $u_T$ is $Tu$, which is (8.8). $TX$ and $T\mathbf X$ live in Type (max u 1). (8.5) writes $T_{\varphi \circ \psi}\mathbf X$ for $T_{\psi \circ \varphi}\mathbf X$ (possible misprint) (Findings, items 1, 2).

HWZ §8.1, Remark 8.1.10 (2017: 8.1), pp. 364 ff. (2017 pp. 264–265)

There are equivalent ways to turn $T\mathbf X$ into an ep-groupoid. A morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ with $x \in X_1$ has a well-defined associated linear isomorphism $T\varphi : T_xX \to T_yY$, the tangent map of $t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1}$ at $x$; $(T\varphi, h)$ is a morphism from $h$ to $T\varphi(h)$, and $(T\psi, h) \circ (T\varphi, l) = (T\psi \circ T\varphi, l) = (T(\psi \circ \varphi), l)$ for $h = T\varphi(l)$. The map $G : (\varphi, h) \mapsto (T\varphi, Ts(h))$ is compatible with the functorial structures, and $G : T\mathbf X \to \{(T\varphi, a) \mid \varphi \in \mathbf X_1, a \in T_{s(\varphi)}X\}$ is a bijection; the right-hand side can be given an M-polyfold structure making $G$ an sc-diffeomorphism, and the pairs $(T\varphi, a)$ can be identified with the triples $(a, T\varphi, b)$, $b = T\varphi(a)$. Finally, $Tt(\varphi) \circ Ts(\varphi)^{-1} : T_xX \to T_yX$ is the linearization of $t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1}$ at $\varphi$, hence equal to $T\varphi$, and $t_{T\mathbf X} \circ (s_{T\mathbf X}|T_xX)^{-1} = T\varphi : T_xX \to T_yX$ is a linear isomorphism.

Verified edition V8.12

$t_T \circ (s_T|T_\varphi\mathbf X)^{-1} = T\varphi$; $T(\psi \circ \varphi) = T\psi \circ T\varphi$ on $T_{s(\varphi)}X$; $G(\varphi, h) = (T\varphi, Ts(h))$ is a bijection onto the pairs with $\varphi \in \mathbf X_1$, $a \in T_{s(\varphi)}X$, compatible with the compositions. Book: Remark 8.1.10 (2017: 8.1), pp. 364 ff. (2017 pp. 264–265). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): $T\varphi$ is Chapter 7's Polyfold.EpGroupoid.tangentMor; the first entry of $G$ is read as $T\varphi$ labelled by $\varphi$, since as a bare map $G$ need not be injective. Not formalized: that $T\varphi$ and $t_T \circ (s_T|T_xX)^{-1}$ are linear isomorphisms, and that $T\varphi$ is $T\hat\varphi(x)$ (gaps G.7, G.70); the M-polyfold structure transported along $G$, and the triples $(a, T\varphi, b)$. The remark writes "$T\varphi : T_xX \to T_yY$" for $T_yX$, and calls $T\varphi$ the linearization "at $x$" and later "at $\varphi$" (possible misprints) (Findings, items 10, 112, 113).

HWZ §8.1, Definition 8.1.13 (2017: 8.1), p. 367 (2017 p. 266)

If $F, G : X \to Y$ are two sc-smooth functors between the ep-groupoids $X$ and $Y$, then $F$ is naturally equivalent to $G$, $F \simeq G$, if there exists an sc-smooth map $\tau : X \to \mathbf Y$ which associates with every object $x \in X$ a morphism $\tau(x) : F(x) \to G(x)$ in $\mathbf Y$ such that $\tau(x') \circ F(h) = G(h) \circ \tau(x)$ for every morphism $h : x \to x'$ in $\mathbf X$. The sc-smooth map $\tau$ is called a natural transformation $\tau : F \to G$.

Verified edition V8.15

A natural transformation $\tau : F \to G$ is an sc-smooth $\tau : X \to \mathbf Y$ with $\tau(x) : F(x) \to G(x)$ and $\tau(x') \circ F(h) = G(h) \circ \tau(x)$; $F \simeq G$ if one exists. Book: Definition 8.1.13 (2017: 8.1), p. 367 (2017 p. 266). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none (Findings, item 12).

(Proof: $|X^1|$ is paracompact; for $z \in |X^1|$ with representative $x_z$ take $U(x_z)$ with the natural $G_{x_z}$-action such that $TU(x_z)$ is, as a bundle over $U(x_z)_1$, sc-isomorphic to a local bundle model $TO \to O^1$ with an sc-smooth bundle action of $G_{x_z}$; then $|TU(x_z)|$ and $|U(x_z)_1|$ are metrizable. A locally finite closed subcover $(A_z)$ of $(|U(x_z)_1|)$ gives a locally finite covering $(\tilde A_z)$ of $|TX|$ by closed paracompact sets, and $|TX|$, a regular Hausdorff space, is paracompact by the topological Proposition 2.7.4 (2017: 2.17).)

A strong bundle over the ep-groupoid $X$ is a pair $(P, \mu)$ in which $P : W \to X$ is a strong bundle over the object M-polyfold $X$ and $\mu : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_P\,W \to W$ is a strong bundle map covering the target map $t : \mathbf X \to X$, so that $P \circ \mu(\psi, w) = t(\psi)$, such that (1) $\mu$ is a surjective local sc-diffeomorphism and linear on the fibres $W_x$; (2) $\mu(1_x, w) = w$ for all $x \in X$ and $w \in W_x$; (3) $\mu(\psi \circ \gamma, w) = \mu(\psi, \mu(\gamma, w))$ for all $\psi, \gamma \in \mathbf X$ and $w \in W$ with $s(\gamma) = P(w)$ and $t(\gamma) = s(\psi) = P(\mu(\gamma, w))$.

HWZ §8.5 (2017 §8.4), Definition 8.5.1 (2017: 8.8), p. 383 (2017 p. 275)

An sc-smooth functor $F : Y \to X$ between ep-groupoids is a proper covering functor if (1) the sc-smooth map $F : Y \to X$ between the objects is a surjective local sc-diffeomorphism; (2) for every object $x \in X$ the preimage $F^{-1}(x)$ is finite, and there exist an open neighborhood $U(x)$ and mutually disjoint open neighborhoods $U(y)$ of the points $y \in F^{-1}(x)$ such that $F : U(y) \to U(x)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism and $F^{-1}(U(x)) = \bigcup_{y \in F^{-1}(x)} U(y)$; (3) the map $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$, $\varphi \mapsto (F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$, is an sc-diffeomorphism.

Verified edition V8.27

(1) $F$ is a surjective local sc-diffeomorphism on objects; (2) the fibres $F^{-1}(x)$ are finite and evenly covered; (3) $\varphi \mapsto (F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$ is an sc-diffeomorphism $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$. Book: Definition 8.5.1 (2017: 8.8), p. 383 (2017 p. 275). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): in (2) $U(x)$ is open and the $U(y)$ carry local inverses $\sigma(y)$; (3) on Part I's fibred-product sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X \times Y$, as in Definition 7.1.3 (4) (2017: 7.3) (Findings, items 50, 102).

HWZ §8.5 (2017 §8.4), after Definition 8.5.1 (2017: 8.8), pp. 383 ff. (2017 pp. 275–276)

The sc-diffeomorphism $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$, $\varphi \mapsto (F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$, preserves the degeneracy index, so $d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi) = d_{\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$. The fibred product is a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X \times Y$, which has the degeneracy index $d_{\mathbf X \times Y}(\varphi, y) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) + d_Y(y)$. Since $F$ and $s$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, $d_{\mathbf X \times Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(F(\varphi)) + d_Y(s(\varphi)) = 2\,d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi)$, hence $d_{\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi)) = \tfrac12\,d_{\mathbf X \times Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$: the fibred product lies in a particular position in the full product.

Verified edition V8.28

$d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi) = d_{\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y} (F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$, $d_{\mathbf X \times Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi)) = 2\,d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi)$ and $d_{\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y} = \tfrac12 d_{\mathbf X \times Y}$ at $(F(\varphi), s(\varphi))$. Book: pp. 379–385 (2017 pp. 275–276). Hidden hypotheses: $X$ and $Y$ tame, for the product formula $d_{\mathbf X \times Y} = d_{\mathbf X} + d_Y$, which Part I proves for tame M-polyfolds (Part I's Proposition 2.5.20 (2017: 2.15) states its formula $d = \tfrac12 d_{X \times Y}$ for tame $X$, $Y$). Deviation (narrower): the first equality and $d_{\mathbf X}(F(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi)$ hold in general; the other two for tame $X$, $Y$; in general $d_{\mathbf X \times Y}(F(\varphi), s(\varphi)) \le 2\,d_{\mathbf Y}(\varphi)$ (Findings, item 51).

HWZ §8.5 (2017 §8.4), Definition 8.5.5 (2017: 8.9) and the category $\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ before it, pp. 387–389 (2017 pp. 279–280)

$\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ is the category whose objects are M-polyfolds and whose morphisms are sc-smooth diffeomorphisms between M-polyfolds. Let $D$ and $C$ be two categories with finitely many objects and morphisms, all morphisms isomorphisms, $C$ with only one object $x$. A covering functor $f : D \to C$ is a functor such that $\mathbf D \to \mathbf C\,{}_s{\times}_f\,D$, $\psi \mapsto (f(\psi), s(\psi))$, is a bijection. A geometric lift of a covering functor $f : D \to C$ consists of two functors $L_D : D \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ and $L_C : C \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ and a natural transformation $\tau : L_D \to L_C \circ f$ of the functors $L_D, L_C \circ f : D \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$.

Verified edition V8.32

$\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ has the M-polyfolds as objects and the sc-diffeomorphisms as morphisms; $f : D \to C$, $C$ with one object, is a covering functor if $\psi \mapsto (f(\psi), s(\psi))$ is a bijection $\mathbf D \to C\,{}_s{\times}_f\,D$; a geometric lift is a pair of functors $L_D$, $L_C$ into $\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ with a natural transformation $\tau : L_D \to L_C \circ f$. Book: 2017 p. 279 and Definition 8.5.5 (2017: 8.9), pp. 388–389 (2017 pp. 279–280). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): $D$ a Mathlib groupoid in Type, $C = $ SingleObj G for a group $G$ in Type, so $C\,{}_s{\times}_f\,D = G \times D$; the finiteness of $D$, its hom-sets and $G$ is carried by the results that use it; $\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ has bundled M-polyfolds of one universe; $D = \emptyset$ is allowed (Findings, items 57, 100).

Associated with a covering functor $f : D \to C$ and a geometric lift $\tau : L_D \to L_C \circ f$ of $f$ there is a natural construction of a proper covering functor $F : Y \to X$ between two ep-groupoids. (Construction: $X = G_x \ltimes U(x)$, with $s(g, z) = z$, $t(g, z) = g \ast z$; $Y = \bigcup_{y \in D} U(y)$ and $\mathbf Y = \bigcup_{(y, y') \in D \times D} [\mathrm{mor}(y, y') \times U(y)]$, with $s(\psi, z) = z$, $t(\psi, z) = \varphi_{yy'}(\psi)(z)$, $(\psi, z') \circ (\gamma, z) = (\psi \circ \gamma, z)$, units $(1_y, z)$ and inverses $(\psi^{-1}, \varphi_{yy'}(\psi)(z))$, and "one verifies" that $Y$ is an ep-groupoid; $F|U(y) := \tau(y)$ and $F(\psi, z) = (f(\psi), \tau(y)(z))$. The map (8.16) $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$, $(\psi, z) \mapsto ((f(\psi), F(z)), z)$, is a bijection, by the definition of a covering functor, and a local sc-diffeomorphism, hence an sc-diffeomorphism.)

Verified edition V8.35

A covering functor $f : D \to C$ with a geometric lift gives a proper covering functor $F : Y \to X$, $X = G_x \ltimes U(x)$, $Y = \bigsqcup U(y)$, $\mathbf Y = \bigsqcup \mathrm{mor} (y, y') \times U(y)$, $F|U(y) = \tau(y)$, $F(\psi, z) = (f(\psi), \tau(y)(z))$. Book: Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) and its proof, pp. 389–391 (2017 pp. 281–282). HWZ §8.5 (2017 §8.4), Theorem 8.5.8 (2017: 8.6) and its proof, 2017 pp. 283–284

Let $F : Y \to X$ be a proper covering functor and fix $x \in X$; let $C$ be the full subcategory of $X$ with the single object $x$ and the morphisms $G_x$, and $D$ the full subcategory with the finite object set $F^{-1}(x)$. Then $f = F|D : D \to C$ is a covering functor. Given a sufficiently small open neighborhood $U(x)$ of $x$ as in Theorem 8.5.3 (2017: 8.5), there exist a geometric lift $A : K \to L$ of $f$ and fully faithful open embedding functors $\Phi : L \to X$ and $\Psi : K \to Y$, the image of $\Phi$ the full subcategory associated with $U(x)$ and the image of $\Psi$ the full subcategory associated with $F^{-1}(U(x))$, such that $F \circ \Psi = \Phi \circ A$. (In the proof, $L_C(x) = U(x)$, $L_C(g) = \Phi(g)$, $L_D(y) = U(y)$, $L_D(\psi) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi_0))^{-1}$ for $\psi : y \to y'$ in $\mathbf U(\psi_0)$, and $\tau(y) = F|U(y)$; "one verifies" that this is a geometric lift, and $A : K \to L$, $L = G_x \ltimes U(x)$, is its functor of Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3).)

Verified edition V8.36

For a proper covering functor $F : Y \to X$ and $x \in X$: $f = F|D : D \to C$ is a covering functor ($C$ on $x$, $D$ on $F^{-1}(x)$), and for $U(x)$ as in Theorem 8.5.3 (2017: 8.5) there are a geometric lift with associated proper covering functor $A : K \to L$ and fully faithful open embeddings $\Phi : L \to X$, $\Psi : K \to Y$ with images the full subcategories on $U(x)$ and $F^{-1}(U(x))$ and $F \circ \Psi = \Phi \circ A$. Book: Theorem 8.5.8 (2017: 8.6) and its proof, 2017 pp. 283–284. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): for ep-groupoids whose objects and morphisms are in Type, since Definition 8.5.5 (2017: 8.9) is stated there; "a sufficiently small $U(x)$ as in Theorem 8.5" is any chart of Theorem 8.5.3 (2017: 8.5) (which exist inside every open $V \ni x$, part (b)); "a geometric lift $A : K \to L$" is a geometric lift with its functor $A$ of Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3); $L_D$ on the morphism $\psi_0$ of $D$ is $t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi_0))^{-1}$ (the text's "$\psi \in \mathbf U(\psi_0)$" read as $\psi = \psi_0$); both "one verifies" are carried out. HWZ §8.5 (2017 §8.4), Definition 8.5.9 (2017: 8.10), p. 394 (2017 p. 285)

Let $(W, \mu)$ and $(V, \tau)$ be strong bundles over the ep-groupoids $Y$ and $X$, $P : W \to Y$ and $Q : V \to X$. A proper strong bundle covering functor is a strong bundle map $A$ (in particular fibrewise linear) with $Q \circ A = F \circ P$ and (1) $A$ is surjective and a local strong bundle isomorphism covering an sc-smooth proper covering functor $F : Y \to X$; (2) $F^{-1}(x)$ is finite for every $x \in X$, and there are open neighborhoods $U(x)$ and mutually disjoint $U(y)$, $y \in F^{-1}(x)$, such that $A : W|U(y) \to V|U(x)$ is a strong bundle isomorphism for every $y \in F^{-1}(x)$ and $F^{-1}(U(x)) = \bigcup_{y \in F^{-1}(x)} U(y)$; (3) the map $\mathbf W \to \mathbf V\,{}_s{\times}_A\,W$, $(\psi, w) \mapsto ((F(\psi), A(w)), w)$, is a strong bundle isomorphism covering the sc-diffeomorphism $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$, $\psi \mapsto (F(\psi), s(\psi))$, where the strong bundle projection $\mathbf V\,{}_s{\times}_A\,W \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$ is $((\varphi, v), w) \mapsto (\varphi, P(w))$.

Verified edition V8.37

A strong bundle map $A$, $Q \circ A = F \circ P$, with (1) $A$ surjective and a local strong bundle isomorphism covering a proper covering functor $F$; (2) $A : W|U(y) \to V|U(x)$ strong bundle isomorphisms over an even covering; (3) $(\psi, w) \mapsto ((F(\psi), A(w)), w)$ a strong bundle isomorphism $\mathbf W \to \mathbf V\,{}_s{\times}_A\,W$ covering $\mathbf Y \to \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_F\,Y$. Book: Definition 8.5.9 (2017: 8.10), p. 394 (2017 p. 285). Hidden hypotheses: none. HWZ §8.3, Definition 8.3.5, p. 379 (new in the 2021 edition)

An auxiliary norm for the strong bundle $(P : W \to X, \mu)$ over the ep-groupoid $X$ is a continuous $N : W_{0,1} \to [0, \infty)$ which (1) restricts to a complete norm on every fibre, (2) satisfies $h_k \to 0_x$ whenever $P(h_k) \to x$ and $N(h_k) \to 0$, and (3) is invariant: $N(h) = N(k)$ if $h = \mu(\varphi, k)$.

Verified edition V8.46

For a strong bundle $(P : W \to X, \mu)$ over an ep-groupoid, an auxiliary norm is a continuous $N : W_{0,1} \to \mathbb R$ which (1) is a complete norm on every fibre, (2) has $h_k \to 0_x$ in $W_{0,1}$ whenever $P(h_k) \to x$ and $N(h_k) \to 0$ — (1), (2) and continuity are Part I's auxiliary norm — and (3) satisfies $N(h) = N(k)$ whenever $h = \mu(\varphi, k)$, $s(\varphi) = P(k)$. Condition (3) is not vacuous: $\mu(\varphi, k) \in W_{0,1}$ for $k \in W_{0,1}$. Over the trivial ep-groupoid every auxiliary norm of Part I is one, and $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^n$ has one. Book: Definition 8.3.5, p. 379, new in the 2021 edition. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): values in $[0, \infty)$ follow from (1); in (3), $h$ is given in $W_{0,1}$ and $h = \mu(\varphi, k)$ is an equation in $W$ (Findings, item 117).

HWZ §8.1, Proposition 8.1.17 (2), p. 371 (new in the 2021 edition)

If $X$ has (SLUC), so has $TX$. The proof: by (1) every $T(X^i)$ has (LUC), and naturally $(TX)^i = T(X^i)$.

An equivalence of ep-groupoids, here, is a pair of sc-diffeomorphisms of the object and the morphism M-polyfolds commuting with source and target; it maps $\mathbf X^T$ onto $\mathbf X'^T$ and so transports LUC, by Proposition 7.2.21, and it passes to the index raises. Part I's Proposition 2.3.17 for $i = 1$, on objects and morphisms, gives an equivalence $T(X^1) \cong (TX)^1$, and by recursion $T(X^i) \cong (TX)^i$ for every $i$. to confirmA branched ep⁺-subgroupoid is a nonnegative functor, supported in the smooth set with paracompact orbit support, locally a weighted sum of indicators of properly embedded smooth submanifolds through the point.

HWZ §9.1, Definition 9.1.2, p. 402 (2017: Definition 9.1, p. 292)

A branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of the ep-groupoid $X$ is a functor $\Theta : X \to \mathbb Q^+$ with (1) $\mathrm{supp}(\Theta) = \{\Theta > 0\}$ contained in $X_\infty$ and $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$ paracompact in the topology induced from $|X|$; and, at every $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$, (2) an open $U(x)$ and finitely many submanifolds $M_i \subseteq U(x)$ through $x$ with proper inclusions, (3) weights $\sigma_i \in \mathbb Q$, $\sigma_i > 0$, and (4) $\Theta(y) = \sum_{y \in M_i} \sigma_i$ for $y \in U(x)$: a local branching structure.

Verified edition V9.1

A branched ep⁺-subgroupoid is a functor $\Theta \ge 0$ whose support lies in the smooth set, whose orbit support $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$ is paracompact, and which at every $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$ has a local branching structure: an open $U(x)$, finitely many smooth submanifolds $M_i \subseteq U(x)$ through $x$ with proper inclusions, weights $\sigma_i > 0$, and $\Theta(y) = \sum_{y \in M_i} \sigma_i$ on $U(x)$. The zero functor and the indicator of a smooth point of $\mathbb R^n$ are examples. Book: Definition 9.1.2, p. 402 (2017: Definition 9.1, p. 292). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): $\Theta$ takes values in $\mathbb Q$ with $\Theta \ge 0$ a field; "the topology induced on $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$ is paracompact" is a ParacompactSpace instance on the subtype; "the inclusion $M_i \to U(x)$ is proper" is IsProperMap of the inclusion. The 2017 text's "(ii) and (iii)" in (4) is "(2) and (3)" in 2021 (possible misprint, corrected) (Findings, item 1).

HWZ §9.1, Remark 9.1.1, p. 402 (2017: Remark 9.1, p. 291), and Definition 9.1.2, last paragraph, p. 402

The dimension of $T_mM$ is locally constant in $m \in M$, the local dimension of $M$. $\Theta$ is $n$-dimensional if at every point of its support the manifolds of a local branching structure can be taken $n$-dimensional (2017: are $n$-dimensional); by a footnote (new in 2021) an $n$-dimensional $\Theta$ is not $m$-dimensional for $m \ne n$; $\Theta$ is locally equidimensional if small structures have sheets of one dimension.

Verified edition V9.2

A submanifold has dimension $k$ at $a$ if the tangent space of its sub-retract at the chart image of $a$ has dimension $k$; the value does not depend on the data and the chart, is unique, exists at every point, and is invariant under restriction to open sets and under sc-diffeomorphisms. $\Theta$ is $n$-dimensional if at every point of its support some local branching structure has only $n$-dimensional $M_i$; the zero functor is $n$-dimensional for every $n$. The dimensions of the $M_i$ of one structure through $x$ are determined. Book: Remark 9.1.1, p. 402 (2017: Remark 9.1, p. 291); Definition 9.1.2, last paragraph and footnote, p. 402. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the dimension is measured in a chart, since $T_aA$ carries no linear structure (gap G.7). The local constancy of $a \mapsto \dim T_aA$ is not proved in general; it is the hypothesis HasLocallyConstantDimAt where it is needed, proved on $\mathbb R^m$ from the trace of $Ds(y)$, and elsewhere the dimensions of the $M_i$ enter as labellings $\mathrm{dim} : I \to \mathbb N$. The footnote ($n$-dimensional $\Theta \ne 0$ is not $m$-dimensional, $m \ne n$) and "locally equidimensional" are not formalized (gap G.93) (Findings, items 2, 3).

HWZ §9.1, Remark 9.1.3 (b), p. 403 (2017: Remark 9.2 (b), p. 292)

Local branching structures are in general not unique, even close to $x$: on $\mathbb R^2$ with identity morphisms only, the graphs $G_1$, $G_2$ of smooth $\beta_1$ ($=0$ for $s \le 0$, $>0$ for $s > 0$) and $\beta_2$ ($>0$ for $s<0$, $=0$ for $s \ge 0$), with weights $1$, define $\Theta(p) = \#\{i \mid p \in G_i\}$, which is also described by the graphs of $\gamma_1 = 0$ and a $\gamma_2$ with $\gamma_2(s) > 0$ for $s \ne 0$.

Verified edition V9.4

For smooth $\beta_1, \beta_2 : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with the sign conditions of the text (satisfiable, from expNegInvGlue), $\Theta(p) = \#\{i \mid p \in \mathrm{graph}\,\beta_i\}$ is a $1$-dimensional branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^2$, equal to the one given by the graphs of $0$ and $\beta_1 + \beta_2$, and no submanifold of the one structure agrees with a submanifold of the other on any neighbourhood of the origin. Book: Remark 9.1.3 (b), p. 403 (2017: Remark 9.2 (b), p. 292). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the text gives $\gamma_2$ only by $\gamma_2(s) > 0$ for $s \ne 0$; describing the same $\Theta$ forces $\gamma_2 = \beta_1 + \beta_2$; "not unique, even close to $x$" is read as the last conjunct (Findings, item 4).

HWZ §9.1, Lemma 9.1.7, p. 405 (2017: Lemma 9.2, p. 294), with the restriction remark before it, p. 404

A local branching structure on $U(x)$ restricts to $N_i = M_i \cap V(x_0)$ on $V(x_0) \subseteq U(x)$ with the same weights (some $N_i$ may be empty). For every $x$ with $\Theta(x) > 0$ there are an open $U(x)$ with the natural $G_x$-action, properly embedded submanifolds $(M_i)_{i \in I}$, a $G_x$-action on $I$ and weights $\sigma_i > 0$ with (1) $g * M_i = M_{g(i)}$, (2) $\sigma_i = \sigma_{g(i)}$, (3) $\Theta(y) = \sum_{y \in M_i} \sigma_i$ on $U(x)$; the proof uses $J = I \times G_x$, $M_{(i,g)} = g * M_i$, $\sigma_{(i,g)} = \sigma_i/|G_x|$.

Verified edition V9.7

A local branching structure at $x$ restricts to every open $V \subseteq U(x)$ containing $x$. For a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid and $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$ there is, inside every open $V \ni x$, a symmetric local branching structure: the domain of a natural representation $(\Phi, \Gamma)$ of $G_x$, a $G_x$-action on the index set with $\Phi(g)(M_i) = M_{g \cdot i}$ and $\sigma_{g\cdot i} = \sigma_i$, and $\Theta(y) = \sum_{y \in M_i} \sigma_i$ there; it is obtained with $J = I \times G_x$, $M_{(i,g)} = \Phi(g)(M_i \cap U)$ and $\sigma_{(i,g)} = \sigma_i / |G_x|$. Book: the remark before Lemma 9.1.7, p. 404, and Lemma 9.1.7, p. 405 (2017: Lemma 9.2, p. 294). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): the symmetric structure lies inside any given $V$. The restriction remark is formalized at $x$ itself, not at a point $x_0$ of $V(x_0) \subseteq U(x)$, where the $N_i$ may miss $x_0$ (reading). That $\Phi(g)(M_i \cap U)$ is a submanifold properly embedded in $U$ through $x$, used without statement in the text, is proved (Findings, items 5, 6).

HWZ §9.1, Proposition 9.1.11, pp. 407–408 (2017: Proposition 9.2, p. 297)

A branched ep⁺-subgroupoid $\Theta$ determines a unique sequence $\Theta_0, \Theta_1, \ldots$ of branched ep⁺-subgroupoids characterized by (1) $\Theta_k$ is $k$-dimensional and (2) $\Theta = \Theta_0 + \Theta_1 + \cdots$, the sum locally finite. Proof: at $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$ take a symmetric structure, split $I = I_0 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup I_n$ by the dimension of the $M_i$ and put $\Theta_k(y) = \sum_{i \in I_k, y \in M_i} \sigma_i$; independence of the structure is Proposition 9.1.12.

Verified edition V9.9

For a local branching structure with dimension labelling, $\Theta_k(y) = \sum_{\dim M_i = k,\, y \in M_i} \sigma_i$ is represented on $U(x)$ by the $k$-dimensional structure $(M_i)_{\dim M_i = k}$, $\Theta = \sum_k \Theta_k$ on $U(x)$, and for a symmetric structure $G_x$ preserves dimension and $\Theta_k$ is $G_x$-invariant. The statement of the proposition, "a unique family $(\Theta_k)$ of branched ep⁺-subgroupoids, $\Theta_k$ $k$-dimensional, with $\Theta = \sum_k \Theta_k$ pointwise, and every such family locally finite", is Proposition_9_1_11; on the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^2$ it does not hold as we read it: for the indicator $\Theta$ of the $x$-axis $L$, both $\Theta_0 = 1_{\{0\}}$, $\Theta_1 = 1_{L \setminus \{0\}}$ and $\Theta_0 = 0$, $\Theta_1 = 1_L$ are such families. HWZ §9.2, the category $\mathrm{Gr}(X)$, p. 409 (2017 pp. 297–298)

For a smooth $x$, $\mathrm{Gr}(x)$ is the set of finite formal sums $\sum \sigma_L L$ of finite-dimensional linear subspaces $L \subseteq T_xX$ with rational weights; a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ maps them by $T\varphi$; $\mathrm{Gr}(X)$ is the category of pairs $(x, a)$, with the projection $\pi : \mathrm{Gr}(X) \to X^\infty$.

Verified edition V9.11

$\mathrm{Gr}(x)$ is the set of finite formal sums $\sum_L \sigma_L L$, $\sigma_L \in \mathbb Q$, of subsets $L$ of $T_xX$; a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ of $X^\infty$ pushes them forward by the tangent $T\varphi$ of Chapter 7, functorially; the objects $(x, a)$, $a \in \mathrm{Gr}(x)$, and the pairs $(a, \varphi)$ form a category with the projection functor $\pi$ to the full subcategory $X^\infty$ of smooth objects. Book: §9.2, p. 409 (2017 pp. 297–298). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the generators are subsets of $T_xX$ rather than linear subspaces, since $T_xX$ carries no linear structure (gap G.7); in a chart the tangent spaces of submanifolds are linear subspaces (V9.12) (Findings, item 20).

Associated with a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid $\Theta$ there is a natural section functor $T_\Theta : X^\infty \to \mathrm{Gr}(X)$, $\pi \circ T_\Theta = \mathrm{Id}$, characterized by (1) $T_\Theta(x) = \sum_i \sigma_i T_xM_i$ for any local branching structure at $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$, the zero sum otherwise, and (2) $T_\Theta(\varphi) = (T_\Theta(s(\varphi)), \varphi)$.

Verified edition V9.13

If the sums $\sum_i \sigma_i\, T_xM_i$ of any two local branching structures of $\Theta$ at $x$ agree (HasIndependentTangentSums), there is a functor $T_\Theta : X^\infty \to \mathrm{Gr}(X)$ with $\pi \circ T_\Theta = \mathrm{Id}$, $T_\Theta(x) = \sum_i \sigma_i\, T_xM_i$ for every local branching structure at $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$, $T_\Theta(x) = 0$ off the support, and $T_\Theta(\varphi) = (T_\Theta(s(\varphi)), \varphi)$. Book: Theorem 9.2.1, p. 409 (2017: Theorem 9.1, p. 298), proved on pp. 412–418 (2017 pp. 301–306). Hidden hypotheses: the independence, which the text proves through Proposition 9.2.8 (V9.14). At a bad point $x$, for a class $\Xi$ of indices with one tangent space $T_xM_i$ there are $i_1, \ldots, i_p \in \Xi$, a partition $\Xi = I^1 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup I^p$ and sequences of good points $x^e_k \to x$ with $x^e_k \in M_i$ iff $i \in I^e$. Lemmas 9.2.9–9.2.11: $L \cap C$ has interior in $L = T_0M_{i_1}$; the $M_i$, $i \in \Xi$, are graphs over a cone around $h_0$; the map $a \mapsto a + B_i(a)$ is injective with invertible derivative and its image contains a cone.

If near $x$ every $n$-dimensional submanifold through $x$ is, in one chart, a graph over a ray (or ball) in its tangent space (IsGraphChartAt, HasGraphChartAt for all dimensions at once, HasGraphBallAt), then for every class $\Xi$ of sheets with one tangent space $L$ at $x$ and every neighbourhood $W$ of $x$ there is a finite slice of points in $W$ meeting each $M_i$, $i \in \Xi$, once and missing the other $M_i$, so that $\sum_{i \in \Xi} \sigma_i = \sum_{y \in F} \Theta(y)$ (HasTangentSlicesAt), and the slice can be chosen generic. $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}(X)$ is defined like $\mathrm{Gr}(X)$ with oriented finite-dimensional subspaces $(L, o)$ of $T_xX$; forgetting orientations is a functor $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}(X) \to \mathrm{Gr}(X)$ over $X^\infty$. Remark 9.3.1 recalls an earlier notion of orientation.

An orientation of $\Theta$ is a section functor $\hat T_\Theta : X^\infty \to \widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}(X)$ lifting $T_\Theta$ such that near every $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$ there is an oriented local branching structure $(M_i, o_i)$, $(\sigma_i)$ with $\hat T_\Theta(y) = \sum_{y \in M_i} \sigma_i\, T_y(M_i, o_i)$ (9.9).

An orientation of $\Theta$ is a natural assignment $\hat T_\Theta$ of formal sums of oriented tangent spaces at smooth points, lifting $T_\Theta$, which near every $x \in \mathrm{supp}(\Theta)$ is $\sum_i \sigma_i\, T_y(M_i, o_i)$ for an oriented local branching structure (continuous orientations $o_i$ of the $M_i$); it defines a section functor of $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}(X)$ over $X^\infty$. HWZ §9.4, Definition 9.4.1, p. 429 (2017: Definition 9.12, p. 315)

For $K \subseteq M$, $M$ a smooth manifold with boundary and corners, $T^K_zM$ is the linear hull of the unit vectors $e = \lim \varphi(z_k)/|\varphi(z_k)|$, $z_k \to z$ in $K \setminus \{z\}$, in a chart centred at $z$, independent of the chart; $z \in K$ is essential if it is a limit of $z_k \in K$ with $T^K_{z_k}M = T_{z_k}M$.

Verified edition V9.39

For a subset $K$ of a finite-dimensional manifold with corners, $T^K_zM$ is the span of the limits of unit directions $\varphi(z_k)/|\varphi(z_k)|$, $z_k \to z$ in $K \setminus \{z\}$, in a chart centred at $z$, independent of the chart; $z \in K$ is essential if it is a limit of $z_k \in K$ with $T^K_{z_k}M = T_{z_k}M$. For two crossing lines in $\mathbb R^2$ the essential set is $\{0\}$. Book: Definition 9.4.1, p. 429 (2017: Definition 9.12, p. 315). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): on Mathlib manifolds with corners, the span of Mathlib's tangent cone in a chart (Findings, item 70).

HWZ §9.5, Lemma 9.5.9, p. 442 (2017: Lemma 9.18, p. 326)

For $U(x)$ with the natural $G_x$-action and a local branching structure, $y \in U(x)$ and a small $V(y)$ with the natural $G_y$-action, $\mu^U_\omega(K) = \mu^V_\omega(K)$ for $K \in L(S)$, $K \subseteq |M_V|$. Proof: $H \cong G_y$, $G = \bigcup_{r \in R} rH$, $V$ invariant under $H$ and disjoint from its other translates, the preimage of $K$ is $\bigcup_r \varphi_r(\tilde K)$, and $\#R = \#G/\#H$.

Verified edition V9.54

For a natural representation of $G_x$ on $U(x)$ and $y \in U(x)$ with stabilizer $H$: $\#(G_x/H) \cdot \#G_y = \#G_x$; there is an open $V \ni y$ inside any given neighbourhood with $\varphi_g(V) = V$ for $g \in H$ and $\varphi_g(V) \cap V = \emptyset$ otherwise; for $K \subseteq |M_U \cap V|$ the preimage $M_U \cap \pi^{-1}(K)$ is the union over coset representatives $r$ of $\varphi_r(M_U \cap V \cap \pi^{-1}(K))$, and the union is disjoint. Book: Lemma 9.5.9, p. 442 (2017: Lemma 9.18, p. 326). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the equality of the measures $\mu^U_\omega$, $\mu^V_\omega$ is not stated (forms and integrals, gap G.107); the representatives $R$ are Quotient.out on $G_x/H$, and the restriction $\tilde M_j = V \cap M_j$ keeps the sheets through $y$ (restrictAt) (Findings, item 84).

712V10.1

Definition 10.1.1 (2017: 10.1), equivalences and the class $E$

as in the book

to confirmAn equivalence of ep-groupoids is a full and faithful sc-smooth functor, a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects, inducing a homeomorphism of orbit spaces.

as statedwitness: pair groupoid of ℤ → point
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §10.1, Definition 10.1.1, p. 461 (2017: Definition 10.1, p. 333)

An equivalence $F : X \to Y$ of ep-groupoids is an sc-smooth functor which is faithful and full, induces a homeomorphism $|F| : |X| \to |Y|$, and is a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects; $E$ is the class of equivalences.

Verified edition V10.1

An equivalence $F : X \to Y$ of ep-groupoids is an sc-smooth functor which is full and faithful (every $\psi : F(x) \to F(x')$ is $F(\varphi)$ for some $\varphi : x \to x'$, and $F$ is injective on each set of morphisms $x \to x'$), induces a homeomorphism $|F| : |X| \to |Y|$ of the orbit spaces, and is a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects. The equivalences form a class $E$ of morphisms of $\mathcal{EP}$ containing the identities and closed under composition. An equivalence is essentially surjective: every $y$ is the target of a morphism from some $F(x)$. The identity and the functor from the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$ to the point are equivalences. Book: Definition 10.1.1, p. 461 (2017: Definition 10.1, p. 333), with the category notions recalled on pp. 461–462. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): none (Findings, item 1).

Lemma 10.1.2 (2017: 10.1) and the remarks around it

stronger

to confirmAn sc-smooth functor is an equivalence iff it is an equivalence of categories and a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects.

with the conversenot invertible: a witness
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §10.1, Lemma 10.1.2, p. 462 (2017: Lemma 10.1, p. 334)

An sc-smooth functor which is a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects and an equivalence of categories is an equivalence; equivalences need not be invertible as functors.

Verified edition V10.2

An sc-smooth functor which is an equivalence of categories and a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects is an equivalence, and conversely every equivalence is both. For a functor of groupoids, $|F|$ is injective if $F$ is full, surjective if and only if $F$ is essentially surjective, and bijective for an equivalence of categories; $|F|$ is continuous, and open if $F$ is open on objects. The composite of two equivalences is an equivalence, and the equivalence from the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$ to the point has no left inverse on objects. Book: Lemma 10.1.2, p. 462 (2017: Lemma 10.1, p. 334), and the remarks on pp. 461–462. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): the lemma is stated with its converse; "not invertible as a functor" gets a witness.

Proposition 10.1.3 (2017: 10.1), the refinement $X_{\mathcal U}$

hypotheses explicit

to confirmThe refinement of a nonempty ep-groupoid along an open covering is an ep-groupoid, and its projection to the ep-groupoid is an equivalence.

nonempty object setindexed covering$(U, \varphi, v)$: possible misprint
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §10.1, Proposition 10.1.3, p. 462 (2017: Proposition 10.1, p. 334)

For an open covering $\mathcal U$ of the object M-polyfold of $X$, the ep-groupoid $X_{\mathcal U}$ of pairs $(U, x)$ and triples $(U, \varphi, V)$, with the structure induced from $X$ and $\mathbf X$, and the functor $(U, x) \mapsto x$, $(U, \varphi, V) \mapsto \varphi$ is an equivalence.

Verified edition V10.3

For a covering of the object M-polyfold of $X$ by open sets $U_i$, $i \in \iota$, the refinement $X_{\mathcal U}$ has as objects the pairs $(i, x)$ with $x \in U_i$, an open subset of $\iota \times X$ with $\iota$ discrete, and as morphisms the triples $(i, \varphi, j)$ with $s(\varphi) \in U_i$, $t(\varphi) \in U_j$, an open subset of $(\iota \times \iota) \times \mathbf X$, with $s(i, \varphi, j) = (i, s(\varphi))$, $t(i, \varphi, j) = (j, t(\varphi))$, $(j, \psi, k) \circ (i, \varphi, j) = (i, \psi \circ \varphi, k)$, units $(i, 1_x, i)$ and inverses $(j, \varphi^{-1}, i)$. If $X$ has an object, $X_{\mathcal U}$ is an ep-groupoid and $F : X_{\mathcal U} \to X$, $(i, x) \mapsto x$, $(i, \varphi, j) \mapsto \varphi$, is an equivalence. For the covering $\{x > -1\}$, $\{x < 1\}$ of $\mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$ this $F$ is an equivalence which is not injective on objects. Book: Proposition 10.1.3, p. 462 (2017: Proposition 10.1, p. 334), with the construction of $X_{\mathcal U}$ on p. 462. Hidden hypotheses: the object set is nonempty (the open-subset M-polyfold structure needs a nonempty set; for an empty $X$ the statement is trivial). Deviation (explicit): the covering is indexed by a type, the text's index set being the covering itself; "induced from $X$ and $\mathbf X$" is read as open subsets of products with a discrete factor; the printed $(U, \varphi, v)$ in the formula for $F$ is read $(U, \varphi, V)$ (possible misprint) (Findings, item 2). Proof: the properness at $(i, x)$ takes a closed neighbourhood of $x$ inside $U_i$ and a neighbourhood with the properness property of $X$, and is proved with ultrafilters instead of sequences.

Definition 10.1.4 (2017: 10.2), natural equivalence

as in the book

to confirmNatural equivalence of sc-smooth functors is an equivalence relation compatible with composition on both sides.

as statedDefinition 8.1.13 reused
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §10.1, Definition 10.1.4, p. 463 (2017: Definition 10.2, p. 335)

A natural transformation $\tau : F \to G$ of sc-smooth functors is an sc-smooth $\tau : X \to \mathbf Y$ with $\tau(x) : F(x) \to G(x)$ and $\tau(x') \circ F(\varphi) = G(\varphi) \circ \tau(x)$; $F \simeq G$ is an equivalence relation compatible with composition.

Verified edition V10.4

A natural transformation $\tau : F \to G$ of sc-smooth functors $X \to Y$ is an sc-smooth map $\tau : X \to \mathbf Y$ with $\tau(x) : F(x) \to G(x)$ and $\tau(x') \circ F(\varphi) = G(\varphi) \circ \tau(x)$ for $\varphi : x \to x'$; $F \simeq G$ if one exists. $\simeq$ is an equivalence relation, and $F \simeq G$ implies $F \circ \Psi \simeq G \circ \Psi$ and $\Phi \circ F \simeq \Phi \circ G$. A natural transformation is a natural isomorphism of the underlying functors. Book: Definition 10.1.4, p. 463 (2017: Definition 10.2, p. 335), and the claims after it, p. 464. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): none; the definition is Definition 8.1.13 (Findings, item 3).

HWZ §10.2, Definition 10.2.1, p. 477 (2017: Definition 10.3, p. 342)

For $F : X \to Y$, $G : Z \to Y$, $X \times_Y Z$ has objects $(x, \phi, z)$ with $\phi : F(x) \to G(z)$ and morphisms $(h, \phi, k)$, with source, target, units, inverses $\iota$ and composition as listed.

Verified edition V10.17

For sc-smooth functors $F : X \to Y$ and $G : Z \to Y$, the objects of $X \times_Y Z$ are the triples $(x, \phi, z)$ with $\phi : F(x) \to G(z)$, the morphisms the triples $(h, \phi, k)$ with $\phi : F(s(h)) \to G(s(k))$; $s(h, \phi, k) = (s(h), \phi, s(k))$, $t(h, \phi, k) = (t(h), G(k) \circ \phi \circ F(h)^{-1}, t(k))$, the unit at $(x, \phi, z)$ is $(1_x, \phi, 1_z)$, the inverse is $(h^{-1}, G(k) \circ \phi \circ F(h)^{-1}, k^{-1})$ and the product of a composable pair is $(h \circ h', \phi', k \circ k')$. This is a groupoid. Book: Definition 10.2.1, p. 477 (2017: Definition 10.3, p. 342). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): objects and morphisms are elements of iterated fibred products, $X \,{}_F\!\times_s (\mathbf Y \,{}_t\!\times_G Z)$ and $\mathbf X \,{}_{F \circ s}\!\times_s (\mathbf Y \,{}_t\!\times_{G \circ s} \mathbf Z)$; the multiplication is a total map whose value off composable pairs is not used; the printed inverse $\iota(h, \psi, k) = (h^{-1}, G(k) \circ \phi \circ F(h)^{-1}, k^{-1})$ is read with $\psi = \phi$ (possible misprint) (Findings, item 20).

as in the book

to confirmFor $F$ an equivalence, $\pi_Z$ is an equivalence, $F \circ \pi_X \simeq G \circ \pi_Z$, $d = d_Z \circ \pi_Z$, and tameness and paracompactness of the orbit space pass from $Z$.

as statedfullness composite: possible misprint

HWZ §10.2, Theorem 10.2.2, pp. 477–478 (2017: Theorem 10.2, p. 343), proof pp. 481–482

If $F$ is an equivalence, $\pi_Z$ is an equivalence, $F \circ \pi_X \simeq G \circ \pi_Z$, $d_{X \times_Y Z} = d_Z \circ \pi_Z$, and tameness and a paracompact orbit space pass from $Z$.

Verified edition V10.19

The projections $\pi_X$ and $\pi_Z$ are sc-smooth functors and $\sigma(x, \phi, z) = \phi$ is a natural transformation $F \circ \pi_X \to G \circ \pi_Z$ whenever $X \times_Y Z$ is defined. If $F$ is an equivalence and $G$ is sc-smooth, then $\pi_Z$ is an equivalence, $F \circ \pi_X \simeq G \circ \pi_Z$, $d_{X \times_Y Z}(x, \phi, z) = d_Z(z)$, and if $Z$ is tame, or has a paracompact orbit space, so has $X \times_Y Z$. An equivalence preserves the degeneracy index and pulls back tameness and the paracompactness of the orbit space. The weak fibred product of the equivalence from the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$ to the point with the identity of the point is a nonempty ep-groupoid whose projection to the point is an equivalence. Book: Theorem 10.2.2, pp. 477–478 (2017: Theorem 10.2, p. 343), with the paragraph after it, p. 478, and its proof, pp. 481–482. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): in the fullness step the printed $\phi' \circ G(k) \circ \phi^{-1}$, which does not compose, is read $\phi'^{-1} \circ G(k) \circ \phi : F(x) \to F(x')$ (possible misprint); essential surjectivity is taken from that of $F$ (Findings, item 23). Proof: $\pi_Z$ is full and faithful because the unique morphism over $k : z \to z'$ is $(h, \phi, k)$ with $F(h) = \phi'^{-1} \circ G(k) \circ \phi$, essentially surjective because every $G(z)$ receives a morphism from some $F(x)$, and Lemma 10.1.2 applies.

Definition 10.4.1 (2017: 10.10), strong bundle equivalences

restated

to confirmA strong bundle equivalence is a strong bundle functor over an equivalence, an equivalence at level $[0]$, a homeomorphism of $|W[1]|$, and locally a strong bundle isomorphism on objects and morphisms.

level $[1]$: homeomorphism of $|W[1]|$rest of $[1]$ from (2)witness over $-\mathrm{id}$
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §10.4, Definition 10.4.1, p. 496 (2017: Definition 10.10, p. 357)

A strong bundle equivalence is a strong bundle functor $\Phi$ covering an equivalence $\phi$ such that (1) $\Phi : W[i] \to W'[i]$, $i = 0, 1$, are equivalences and (2) $\Phi$ is locally a strong bundle isomorphism on objects and morphisms.

Verified edition V10.22

A strong bundle equivalence $\Phi : (P : W \to X, \mu) \to (P' : W' \to X', \mu')$ is a strong bundle functor $\Phi : (W, \mathbf W) \to (W', \mathbf W')$ (linear on fibres, satisfying (10.14)) covering an equivalence $\phi : X \to X'$, with (1) $\Phi : W[0] \to W'[0]$ an equivalence of ep-groupoids and $|\Phi| : |W[1]| \to |W'[1]|$ a homeomorphism, and (2) every point of $X$, and every morphism of $\mathbf X$, having an open neighbourhood over which $\Phi$ on objects, respectively on morphisms, is a strong bundle isomorphism covering $\phi$. The fibre maps $W_x \to W'_{\phi(x)}$ are then topological linear isomorphisms and $\Phi : W[1] \to W'[1]$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism. The identity and composites of strong bundle equivalences are strong bundle equivalences, and so is every isomorphism of strong bundles over ep-groupoids; the projection $(-\mathrm{id})^(\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k) \to \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k$ over $-\mathrm{id}$ is one, not over the identity for $n \ge 1$. *Book: Definition 10.4.1, p. 496 (2017: Definition 10.10, p. 357). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): $W[1]$ is not built as an ep-groupoid in the project; (1) at level $[1]$ is read as the homeomorphism of $|W[1]|$, the quotient of $W_{0,1}$ by the orbit relation of $W$; the local sc-diffeomorphism property at level $[1]$ follows from (2), and fullness and faithfulness at level $[1]$ are those at level $[0]$ restricted (Findings, item 40).

Book: Theorem 10.3.10, p. 489 (2017: Theorem 10.4, p. 353), proved in Appendix §10.6.2, pp. 515–519. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): in (C1) the text's $A \times_X B$, $\mathrm{mor}_Y(\Psi(a), \Psi(a'))$ and "$x$" are read $A \times_Y B$, $\mathrm{mor}_X(\Psi(b), \Psi(b'))$ and "$y$", and in (C2) $(s|U)^{-1}(b')$ is read $(s|U)^{-1}(\Psi(b'))$ (possible misprints); the step of (C2) that $\Gamma'$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism does not hold as we read it without the other half of (C2), and the local sc-diffeomorphism property of $\Phi$ is proved from a local right inverse obtained from the equivalence $\Phi \circ \pi_{A'}$ and from local injectivity (Findings, items 34, 61).

the diagrams of strong bundles, their refinements and equivalence

HWZ §10.5, the diagrams of strong bundles, p. 504 (2017 p. 364)

Diagrams $W \xleftarrow{\Phi} W'' \xrightarrow{\Psi} W'$ with $\Phi$ a strong bundle equivalence and $\Psi$ a strong bundle functor; refinements and equivalence (having a common refinement) as for ep-groupoids; the class $[D]$ is a generalized strong bundle map.

Verified edition V10.51

A diagram $D : W \xleftarrow{\Phi} W'' \xrightarrow{\Psi} W'$ between strong bundles $(P : W \to X, \mu)$ and $(P' : W' \to X', \mu')$ over ep-groupoids consists of a strong bundle $(P'' : W'' \to X'', \mu'')$ over an ep-groupoid, a strong bundle equivalence $\Phi$ and a strong bundle functor $\Psi$ (morphisms of $\mathcal{SEP}$). $D'$ refines $D$ if a strong bundle equivalence $H : W''' \to W''$ has $\Phi \circ H \simeq \Phi'$ and $\Psi \circ H \simeq \Psi'$ (natural equivalence of strong bundle functors, Definition 10.4.8); every diagram refines itself, composing both legs with a strong bundle equivalence or replacing them by naturally equivalent ones gives a refinement, and a refinement of a refinement is one. Two diagrams are equivalent if they have a common refinement, an equivalence relation (V10.69); a generalized strong bundle map $[D] : W \to W'$ is the class of $D$, and $[D] = [D']$ iff $D$ and $D'$ have a common refinement. For $W' = \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^n$, $W' \xleftarrow{P'} (-\mathrm{id})^W' \xrightarrow{P'} W'$ refines $1_{W'}$, so its class is $[1_{W'}]$. *Book: §10.5, p. 504 (2017 p. 364), "following our earlier construction". Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): none; the classes are formed for the generated equivalence relation, which is having a common refinement by the transitivity, the strong bundle version of Lemma 10.3.4 (V10.69) (gap G.123, closed since; Findings, items 18, 50).

HWZ §10.1, Proposition 10.1.9, pp. 468–470 (new in the 2021 edition)

If $F : X \to Y$ is an equivalence and one of $X$, $Y$ has the local regularity property, so has the other. The proof transports $U(x)$ along $Q = \hat\psi \circ F$ for $\psi : F(x) \to y$, with $Q(g * z) = (\psi \circ F(g) \circ \psi^{-1}) * Q(z)$ ((10.1)–(10.3)).

Verified edition V10.62

If $F : X \to Y$ is an equivalence, $X$ has the local regularity property (Definition 7.4.19) if and only if $Y$ has it. For a morphism $\psi : F(x) \to y$, the composite $Q = \hat\psi \circ F$ is an sc-diffeomorphism of a neighbourhood of $x$ onto one of $y$, $g \mapsto \psi \circ F(g) \circ \psi^{-1}$ is an isomorphism $G_x \to G_y$ with $Q(g * z) = (\psi \circ F(g) \circ \psi^{-1}) * Q(z)$ ((10.2), (10.3)), natural representations are carried along $Q$ in both directions, and an equivariant sc-diffeomorphism $U(x) \to U(y)$ along a surjection $G_x \to G_y$ carries the condition of (LR) both ways. The equivalence of diagrams of strong bundles is transitive: if $w$ refines $D$ by $H$ and $D'$ by $H'$, and $w'$ refines $D'$ by $K$ and $D''$ by $K'$, the diagram on the weak fibred product of $H'$ and $K$ (V10.68) refines $D$ by $H \circ \Pi_X$ and $D''$ by $K' \circ \Pi_Z$. as in the book

to confirmThe tangent functor induces a functor $T : \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1}) \to \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1})$, $[X \leftarrow A \to Y] \mapsto [TX \leftarrow TA \to TY]$, extending $T$ on $\mathcal{EP}$.

as statedcomposition supplieduniverse of Chapter 8’s $T$

HWZ §11.1, Theorem 11.1.1, p. 521 (2017: Theorem 11.1, p. 375)

The tangent functor $T : \mathcal{EP} \to \mathcal{EP}$ induces a functor $T : \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1}) \to \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1})$ by $[X \xleftarrow{F} A \xrightarrow{\Phi} Y] \mapsto [TX \xleftarrow{TF} TA \xrightarrow{T\Phi} TY]$, compatible with $i : \mathcal{EP} \to \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1})$.

Verified edition V11.1

The assignment $X \mapsto TX$, $[X \xleftarrow{F} A \xrightarrow{\Phi} Y] \mapsto [TX \xleftarrow{TF} TA \xrightarrow{T\Phi} TY]$ is a functor $T : \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1}) \to \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1})$: a refinement $H : d' \to d$ gives the refinement $TH : Td' \to Td$, equivalent diagrams have equivalent tangent diagrams, $T$ preserves identities and composition, and $T(i(\Phi)) = i(T\Phi)$ for the localization functor $i : \mathcal{EP} \to \mathcal{EP}(E^{-1})$. $T$ maps generalized isomorphisms to generalized isomorphisms. For functors $P : C \to X$, $Q : C \to Z$ and a natural transformation $\tau : \Phi \circ P \to G \circ Q$, $c \mapsto (P(c), \tau(c), Q(c))$ is a functor $C \to X \times_Y Z$ with $\pi_X$ and $\pi_Z$ composites $P$ and $Q$. Book: Theorem 11.1.1, p. 521 (2017: Theorem 11.1, p. 375), with its proof, pp. 521–522. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (same): the text checks refinements and leaves "the remaining argument" to the reader; that $T$ preserves composition needs the comparison $T(A \times_Y B) \to TA \times_{TY} TB$, $v \mapsto (T\pi_A(v), T\sigma(v), T\pi_B(v))$, an equivalence by two out of three, through which $T(d \circ e)$ refines $Td \circ Te$; $T$ is defined on the ep-groupoids of Chapter 8's tangent universe (Findings, item 1). Proof: $TF$ is an equivalence (Theorem 10.1.7); a natural transformation $\sigma : G \to F \circ H$ gives $T\sigma : TG \to TF \circ TH$ (Proposition 8.1.14).

Definition 11.1.3 (2017: 11.1), faces in the ep-groupoid sense

restated

to confirmA face of a tame ep-groupoid is the full subcategory over the closure in $|X|$ of a connected component of $\{d_{|X|} = 1\}$; face structured means every $z$ lies in exactly $d_{|X|}(z)$ faces of $|X|$.

HWZ §11.1, Definition 11.1.3, p. 523 (2017: Definition 11.1, p. 377)

A face of $|X|$ is the closure of a connected component of $\{d_{|X|} = 1\}$; a face of $X$ is the full subcategory $X_\theta$ over a face $\theta$; $X$ is face structured if it is tame and every $z$ lies in exactly $d_{|X|}(z)$ faces of $|X|$, weakly face structured if the object M-polyfold is face structured.

Verified edition V11.3

A face of $|X|$ is the closure in $|X|$ of the connected component, in $\{z \in |X| \mid d_{|X|}(z) = 1\}$, of a point of that set; for $\theta \subseteq |X|$, $X_\theta$ is the full subcategory on the objects $x$ with $|x| \in \theta$, recorded by its object set $\pi^{-1}(\theta)$, a saturated set, and its morphisms are those with source in it; a face of $X$ is $X_\theta$ for a face $\theta$ of $|X|$. $X$ is face structured if it is tame and every $z \in |X|$ lies in exactly $d_{|X|}(z)$ faces of $|X|$ (counted in $\mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$), and weakly face structured if it is tame and its object M-polyfold is face structured (Definition 2.5.10). The faces of $|X|$ are Chapter 2's faces for the index $d_{|X|}$ on the open set $|X|$. Book: Definition 11.1.3, p. 523 (2017: Definition 11.1, p. 377). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): a face of $X$ is recorded by its object set; its ep-groupoid structure is Proposition 11.1.6 (V11.6) (Findings, item 3).

HWZ §11.3, Lemma 11.3.2, p. 536 (2017: Lemma 11.5, p. 389)

For an equivalence $F$: $F_*\Theta$ is well defined and a functor, $F^F_\Theta = \Theta$; $F_*F^*\Theta' = \Theta'$; naturally equivalent equivalences have the same push-forwards and pull-backs.

Verified edition V11.15

(1) If $F$ is full and $\Theta$ is a functor, then $(F_*\Theta)(y) = \Theta(x)$ for every $x$ with a morphism $F(x) \to y$, $F_*\Theta$ is a functor and $F^F_\Theta = \Theta$; (2) if $F$ is essentially surjective and $\Theta'$ is a functor, $F_*F^\Theta' = \Theta'$; (3) naturally equivalent full functors $F \simeq G$ have $F_\Theta = G_*\Theta$, and naturally equivalent functors have $F^\Theta' = G^\Theta'$. Moreover $F^$ of a functor is a functor, $(G \circ F)^ = F^* \circ G^$, $(G \circ F)_ = G_* \circ F_*$ for full $F$, $G$, $G \circ F$, and $1_*\Theta = \Theta$. Definition 11.6.4 (2017: 11.6), functors and equivalences between proper coverings

stronger

to confirmA functor between proper coverings is a commuting pair $(\Psi, \Phi)$; it is an equivalence iff $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ are equivalences, the fibre condition being automatic.

fibre condition redundantwitness: $\mathbb Z$-pair → point
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §11.6, Definition 11.6.4, p. 553 (2017: Definition 11.6, p. 404)

(1) A functor $(\Psi, \Phi) : F \to F'$ with $\Phi \circ F = F' \circ \Psi$; (2) an equivalence if $\Psi$, $\Phi$ are equivalences and $\Psi$ maps each fibre $Y_x$ bijectively onto $Y'_{\Phi(x)}$.

Verified edition V11.36

(1) An sc-smooth functor $(\Psi, \Phi) : F \to F'$ between functors $F : Y \to X$, $F' : Y' \to X'$ is a pair of sc-smooth functors $\Psi : Y \to Y'$, $\Phi : X \to X'$ with $\Phi \circ F = F' \circ \Psi$ on objects and on morphisms; $\Psi$ then maps $Y_x$ into $Y'_{\Phi(x)}$; identities and composites are such pairs. (2) It is an equivalence if $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ are equivalences and $\Psi$ maps $Y_x$ bijectively onto $Y'_{\Phi(x)}$ for every $x$; identities and composites of equivalences are equivalences. If $F$ and $F'$ are proper covering functors, the fibre condition follows from the other two, so that $(\Psi, \Phi)$ is an equivalence if and only if $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ are. The pair $(\mathbb Z\text{-pair} \to \mathrm{pt}, \mathbb Z\text{-pair} \to \mathrm{pt})$ between the identity coverings is an equivalence, though it has no inverse functor. Book: Definition 11.6.4, p. 553 (2017: Definition 11.6, p. 404). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): the redundancy of the fibre condition for proper coverings is added; the text's remark after the definition treats the fibre bijection as defining a subclass of the functors of (1) (Findings, item 72). Proof: injectivity from the faithfulness of $\Phi$ and unique lifting along $F$; surjectivity from the essential surjectivity of $\Psi$, the fullness of $\Phi$ and unique lifting along $F'$.

Proper coverings and their functors form a category $\mathcal{PC}$ with the class $E_{\mathcal{PC}}$; a diagram is $F \xleftarrow{\Gamma} A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} F'$ with $\Gamma \in E_{\mathcal{PC}}$, and two diagrams have a common refinement if there are equivalences $H$, $H'$ with $\Gamma \circ H \simeq \Gamma' \circ H'$, $\varepsilon \circ H \simeq \varepsilon' \circ H'$.

A diagram $d : F \to F'$ is $F \xleftarrow{\Gamma} A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} F'$ with $\Gamma$ an equivalence of proper coverings; a common refinement of $d$, $d'$ consists of equivalences $H : A'' \to A$, $H' : A'' \to A'$ with $\Gamma \circ H \simeq \Gamma' \circ H'$ and $\varepsilon \circ H \simeq \varepsilon' \circ H'$.
